PowerInfer [23] serves LLMs on a consumer-grade GPU. Quest [24] shows that which KV entries matter depends on the query. The LLM setting differs from ours in two ways that change the design: a decoding step is short, so moving KV is bandwidth-bound, and a selective access set is known only after the query is computed. In a world model a chunk computes for about a second and its access set follows from the camera pose, which makes zero-stall prefetching from NVMe possible on a consumer machine.

    Long video beyond the native horizon. StreamingLLM [14] keeps attention-sink tokens and assigns positions within the cache. Rolling Forcing [15] re-applies RoPE to cached keys at effective indices so that they keep a fixed relative position to the frames being denoised, and Deep Forcing [16] shifts the temporal RoPE phase of sink tokens to the current timeline. WorldPlay applies a related reframing to retrieved memory in an interactive world model. WorldPager’s position handling follows this practice; we apply it to pose-retrieved long-term memory that may be read back from NVMe and enable it only beyond the native horizon, so that the first 341 chunks stay bit-identical.

    VII Limitations and Conclusion

    Limitations. Our evidence has the following scope.

  • •

    One machine, one drive. All timing comes from one RTX 4090 with one NVMe SSD; slower drives are emulated with a software token bucket, including the SATA-class case.

  • •

    One scene and one seed for timing. System measurements use one starting image and one seed per configuration (with up to five rollouts), so we do not report confidence intervals for them.

  • •

    Quality on one model. Image-quality and consistency results are for MG2 only; on LingBot-World retrieval did not improve consistency, so we report system metrics only for it.

  • •

    Long-gap image quality. int4 tiered storage lowers MUSIQ on long-gap revisits by about one point (-1.28 [-2.25, -0.36]), within the registered tolerance; scene 0000 keeps only two seeds after drifting runs are excluded.

  • •

    Long-range texture drift. Memory-conditioned generation develops a repeated texture after about 100 chunks, independently of KV precision (Sec. V).

  • •

    Model accuracy. Three held-out predictions miss (near the failure bandwidth, LingBot at 0.075 GB/s, and LingBot read-back volume), and int8 was emulated by byte accounting only.

  • •

    Speed. At about 9.5 frames per second, WorldPager generates video continuously but not in real time.

    • Conclusion. On a single consumer machine, long sessions of a memory-augmented world model stop at two walls: host memory runs out after 45 seconds of video, and the model’s positions run out after 4.3 minutes. The memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound, and its access set is known before compute, so an analytical model can predict where each budget spills and what bandwidth prefetching needs. WorldPager follows that model: it stores int4 KV in a GPU, DRAM, and NVMe hierarchy, prefetches from the extrapolated pose without ever waiting, writes back in the background, and handles positions at inference time. One RTX 4090 with 32 GiB of host memory and one NVMe drive then generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously, with zero stalls and constant host memory.

    Use of AI

    Large language models (Anthropic’s Claude) were used to draft and revise the text of this paper, to write the figure-generation scripts, and to write and run parts of the experiment code under the authors’ direction. All experimental designs were registered before the runs, every number in the paper was traced to a result file, and the authors reviewed the full text and take responsibility for its content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Per-scene and per-seed results for int4 versus bf16 long-gap recall

    Table IX lists, for each scene and seed, the paired differences (int4 minus bf16) averaged over the 13 revisit events of each gap tier, and the drift flag. A run is flagged when the two arms differ by more than two MUSIQ points on the outbound leg (chunks 3–299) or on the first-visit frames, that is, before any revisit.

item.title: agent 从建游戏到看数据全包：Summer 4.0 把整个引擎收成一个 API，Claude Code / Codex / Cursor 都能直接驱动 ｜ Summer 4.0, the Game Engine for AI Agents
item.description:
一句话：从写游戏、出美术音效、发布到读数据，全链路给 agent；发布/删除这类动作要先问人。

要点：

  • 任意 agent（Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Claude、ChatGPT）都能驱动：做完一款完整多人游戏、生成美术与音效、发布到 Summer Games、再回读表现数据
  • 此前的问题是引擎核心能被 agent 驱动，但 Summer 的其余部分只能以「一长串工具」的形式暴露；4.0 把它收成一条链、一个账号覆盖全部应用

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Blog·Summer Engine（English）

原文发布：2026-10-16

本期推送：2026-10-28

Your AI agent can now reach every part of Summer. Summer 4.0 is the game engine for AI agents. Any agent, from Claude Code, Codex and Cursor to Claude and ChatGPT, can use it. Your coding agent builds a full multiplayer game in Summer Engine, makes its art and sound, publishes it on Summer Games and then reads how it does. One link connects Summer's cloud. One Summer account covers every app. Publishing a game, live changes, deleting for good and contacting people ask you first.

Summer was always the game engine built for AI. Agents drove the engine well, but the rest of Summer reached them as a long list of tools that grew one feature at a time. 4.0 replaces that list with one catalog of operations. An agent finds the right action, knows what it will use from your credits, and knows when to ask you.

What is new in Summer 4.0?

  • One catalog for everything. Assets, publishing, analytics, plans, Summer Apps, the Studio and the engine are operations with plain names, such as 
    assets.generate_3d
    , 
    store.publish
    and 
    analytics.summary
    . The operations reference lists every one.
  • One link and one Summer account for every agent app.
  • A short list of everyday tools, including search and call for everything else.
  • The same commands in your terminal, as 
    summer
    .
  • Agent permissions. Building and generating run on their own. Publishing a game, live changes, deletes and invites ask you first.
  • Approval cards in your Studio tab when your agent needs you.
  • Agent activity with Undo, so you see what your agent changed and undo the changes that support it.
  • Auto top-up, so agents keep going when credits run low.
  • Versions for the ChatGPT and Claude app directories.

    • What does a game engine for AI agents need?

    An agent that makes games does more than edit scenes. It makes art, uploads a build, fills in a store page, checks the numbers and changes what players see. Each step touches a different service and carries a different risk. A wrong scene edit is undone with one key. A wrong store page reaches every player.

    So every operation in 4.0 follows the same rules:

  • Names in plain words. Each operation is 
    area.action
    , like 
    assets.search
    or 
    jobs.wait
    . The area is a word you would use yourself.
  • Typed input and one answer shape. One flat input, and the same kind of answer every time, so the agent never guesses.
  • A dry run for every change. The agent can ask what would happen before anything changes. For asset generation, the dry run shows the most credits it will use.
  • Jobs for long work. A 3D model or a video answers at once with a job, and the agent waits on it with 
    jobs.wait
    . Nothing in the cloud blocks for minutes.
  • One error shape. Out of credits or signed out, the answer has a stable code, a plain message and the next step to take. How Summer answers lists the codes.
  • A clear risk level. Each operation is marked by the strongest thing it can do: read, change your own drafts, spend credits, publish, change what players see, or delete for good. Your agent permissions decide which of those run without asking.

    • How do you connect any agent with one link?

    The Summer address works in every agent app that can add an MCP server by its address:

    https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp

    In Claude Code, run this in your terminal, then type 

    /mcp
    and sign in:

    claude mcp add --transport http summer https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp

    In Codex, run 

    codex mcp add summer --url https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp
    , then 
    codex mcp login summer
    . Cursor and VS Code take the address in their MCP config. Claude and ChatGPT take it as a custom connector. The Summer MCP page has the exact line for every app. The connect your agent guide covers Claude and ChatGPT step by step.

    The first time, a Summer sign-in page opens in your browser. Every app you connect after that uses the same Summer account and the same agent permissions.

    The link reaches everything that runs in Summer's cloud. To let your agent build and play the game in Summer Engine on your computer, add the local server too:

    npx -y summer-engine@latest setup claude-code --yes

    Replace 

    claude-code
    with your agent, or just tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game." Already use Summer? Run 
    npx -y summer-engine@latest login
    once after you update.

    How does your agent find the right operation?

    The Summer link starts your agent with 20 tools for the everyday jobs: your account, Summer's docs, your games and projects, searching and generating assets, the store page and publishing, a game's numbers, and waiting on jobs. A short list keeps the agent fast and its context small.

    Everything else is two tools away. 

    summer_search
    takes plain words, like "set a new trailer on my store page", and returns the matching operation with its exact input. 
    summer_call
    runs it by name. The rules hold either way. Dry runs, permissions and approvals are checked on Summer's side, not in the prompt.

    Can you run the same commands in the terminal?

    Yes. Every operation is also a command, 

    summer
    , with its input as flags:

    summer whoami
summer ops search set a new trailer
summer assets generate-image --prompt "a cozy pixel-art tavern at night" --dry-run
summer analytics summary --game-id g_123 --days 7

    Without a global install, run them as 

    npx -y summer-engine
    . Add 
    --dry-run
    to see what would happen, 
    --wait
    to follow a job until it ends, and 
    --json
    to print the exact answer an agent gets. An agent with a terminal can script a hundred calls this way instead of making them one by one. The CLI reference has every flag.

    What can your agent do without asking?

    In Studio, Settings > Agent permissions shows six switches and their defaults. Publish and Prices and live changes show On, but today Summer Games still asks you first for those:

    PermissionWhat it coversToday
    Make and buildEdit drafts, plans and uploads, and start buildsRuns on its own
    Spend creditsGenerate assets and run paid builds, within your credits and auto top-up limitRuns on its own
    PublishPublish store pages, versions and releases. The game goes live as soon as Summer's automatic checks passAsks you once, as the game's owner
    Prices and live changesChange prices and sales, start or stop A/B tests, change member rolesAsks you
    Delete for goodDelete or remove things for goodAsks you
    Contact peopleSend invites and other emails to real peopleAsks you

    Reading never asks. Changing these switches yourself is coming soon, and only you will be able to turn one on. The permissions guide explains each group. A few things always ask: changing these permissions or auto top-up, entering a game jam (it agrees to the jam's rules) and changing your event limit.

    What happens when your agent needs your approval?

    When something needs you, the agent does not fail. It asks. If Summer Studio is open in your browser, a card appears in that tab. It starts with "Your agent wants to", says exactly what would change, before and after, and which agent asked. Owner requests show Approve and Decline. Other requests show the action's own word, such as Invite or Remove, and Cancel. With no Studio tab open, the agent gives you the link instead.

    Nothing changes until you press it. If what the request would change has changed since, it stops instead of overwriting.

    Publishing to Summer Games asks you once today. Your agent uploads the build, fills in the store page and sends you one link to publish. You approve once, then the game goes live as soon as Summer's automatic checks pass, with no review. Our guide to store art from your agent covers the store page itself, and the publishing docs cover the checks.

    How do you see and undo what your agent did?

    Under the switches, Agent activity lists what your agents changed or asked for through the Summer link, newest first, each marked Done, Waiting for you, Started or Undone. Changes to prices, sales, member roles, team names and the event limit have an Undo button. Only you can press it, and it runs once. For prices, roles and the event limit, it refuses if the value changed again since.

    How do agents keep going when credits run low?

    Generation and paid builds use your Summer credits. Before an asset generation runs, the agent can see the most credits it will use. When you run out, the answer says so and gives one link to add more.

    Auto top-up can keep your agents going. Turn it on in Studio on the Billing page or in the Add credits step. You set when credits fall below an amount, how much to add, and a monthly limit. Summer charges your saved card only by that rule, emails a receipt for every charge, and turns the rule off if a charge fails. Your agent never buys credits on its own.

    Is Summer in ChatGPT and Claude?

    Summer has versions made for the ChatGPT and Claude app directories. Each follows its store's rules. Every action is its own tool, with no search-and-run tool, and the ChatGPT version never shows checkout or billing links. Until the listings are live, add the Summer address as a custom connector in either app. The ChatGPT and Claude guide shows how.

    What does a full session look like?

    Each line is one ask to your agent.

  • "Make a two-player co-op game about frogs racing on lily pads." The agent builds it in Summer Engine and tests it with two players on your computer. Read how to add multiplayer to your game for that step.
  • "Make the frog model and a jump sound." The model runs as a job, and the sound comes back at once. Our post on game audio with your AI agent goes deeper.
  • "Publish it on Summer Games." The agent fills in the store page and sends you the publish link.
  • "How did it do this week?" The agent reads page views, launches, sessions and play time, with one reading of what to fix. It is the same data you see in Grow in Summer Studio.
  • "Invite sam@example.com to the team." Contacting people asks you first, so a card appears, and the invite goes out when you press Invite.

    • What are the limits today?

  • The engine runs on your computer. The hosted link cannot edit scenes. Add the local server for that. Scene edits show in the editor, where undo works, not in Agent activity.
  • Publishing asks you once, then the game goes live as soon as Summer's automatic checks pass.
  • Game numbers come from Summer Games. Games launched in other stores are not counted. The analytics guide explains what is tracked.
  • Some Grow tools are still rolling out, such as store page A/B tests.

    • What should you do next?

    Connect one agent with the link above and ask it what it can do for your game. Then let it make something.

    Tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game."

    Frequently asked questions

    What is a game engine for AI agents?

    It is a game engine where an AI agent can do every step of making and running a game, not only edit code. In Summer 4.0, assets, publishing, analytics, plans and the Studio are one catalog of operations with plain names, typed inputs, dry runs and one error format, so any agent can find the right action and use it safely.

    Which AI agents work with Summer 4.0?

    Any agent app that can add an MCP server by its address, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Claude and ChatGPT. Agents with a terminal can also run the same operations as summer commands.

    What can my agent do without asking me?

    It can make and build, and spend credits within your credits and auto top-up limit. Today it asks you first before it publishes a game, makes a live change such as a price or an A/B test, changes a member, deletes anything for good or contacts a real person. Agent permissions in Studio settings shows the switches; changing them is coming soon.

    Can I undo what my agent did?

    Agent activity in Studio settings lists the changes and requests your agents made through the Summer link, newest first. Changes to prices, sales, member roles, team names and the event limit have an Undo button that only you can press.

    What happens when my agent runs out of credits?

    It stops, says it needs more credits, and gives one link to add more. If you turn on auto top-up, Summer adds credits from your saved card when your balance runs low, up to the monthly limit you set, so your agents keep running.

    Do the old Summer tool names still work?

    Yes. summer_call runs any earlier Summer tool name, within your agent permissions. While your installed Summer skills are older than 4.0, the local server also lists the earlier names again. Engine tools keep their names.

    All posts
  • MCP·Oct 16, 2026·6min read

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI. Add one link to your AI agent, or let it run Summer as commands in its terminal. Here is how both work.

  • MCP·Oct 16, 2026·9min read

    Designing an MCP Server for AI Agents

    How we went about designing an MCP server for AI agents in Summer MCP and CLI 4.0. One catalog, plain names, dry runs, retry keys and a 168-run eval.

  • MCP·Jun 7, 2026·5min read

    Summer Engine MCP Prompt Templates for AI Game Development

    Copyable prompts for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Devin Desktop, and other MCP agents using Summer Engine's MCP bridge.

要点：

  • 起点是承认 3.x 的失败：工具是一个一个长出来的，最终变成 agent 难以发现与组合的长清单——于是 4.0 重做成「每个能力一个带类型的操作」
  • 设计目标是让 agent 用平白的语言就能找到操作，并在真正执行前用 dry run 预检——把「猜工具」变成「查契约」
  • 作者用 168 次运行的评测来说明取舍，并明确写了哪里还不行（不是只讲成功）

为什么值得看：MCP 现在被当成万能胶，但「工具列表」和「可供 agent 推理的 API 契约」是两件事。这篇是目前少见的、带评测数字与失败清单的接口设计复盘，任何要把编辑器/引擎暴露给 agent 的团队都该先读。

中文摘要：Summer 团队把引擎重做成「一个 API」时，顺手写下这份给 agent 设计 MCP Server 的复盘：为什么推倒重来、选了什么、168 次运行的评测说明了什么、以及哪里还不行。核心判断是 3.x 的增长方式会失败——工具一个一个长出来，最后成为 agent 既难发现也难组合的长清单；4.0 改为「每个能力一个带类型的操作」，让 agent 用自然语言就能找到，并在执行前用 dry run 做预检，把「猜工具」换成「查契约」。发布同时包含 4.0 导览与 MCP/CLI 的安装方式，CLI、本地 MCP 与 skills 都放在一个开源包 summer-engine 里。对做引擎接口的人来说，这类带评测与失败清单的复盘，比功能列表有用得多。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Blog·Summer Engine（English）

原文发布：2026-10-16

本期推送：2026-10-28

Summer MCP and CLI 4.0 are out (npm 

summer-engine
4.2.0). Summer Engine is a game engine that AI agents drive, with a store, Summer Games, where the games go live. Every part of it is now one typed operation that your agent finds in plain words and checks with a dry run. This post is about designing an MCP server for AI agents: what we chose, why, what a 168-run eval showed, and where it falls short.

The tour of 4.0 is in Summer 4.0, the game engine for AI agents, and the setup lines are in Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI.

Why did we start over with one API?

Summer 3.x grew one tool at a time. Signed in, the last 3.x build listed 217 tools. Some tools mixed a read with a change. Asked to change a price on 3.x, one agent re-submitted the whole store page in 5 of 6 runs, because that tool happened to take a price too.

So 4.0 starts from one catalog. Each operation is declared once: a permanent name, a summary, one effect (read, write, spend, publish, change what players see, or delete), an input and output schema, and at least one example that a test checks against the input. The hosted MCP, the npm MCP, the CLI and the approval cards in Summer Studio are views of that catalog. A view adds no behavior, so a fix to an operation is a fix everywhere.

The catalog holds 320 operations: 229 run on Summer's servers and 91 on your computer, most of them in the Summer Engine editor. Each lives next to the code that runs it, and all pass one public contract schema. We share the contract, not the code, because the contract changes rarely and the operations change daily. The operations reference is generated from the same catalog.

How did we choose the names?

We asked the models first. Two fresh model runs got four tasks, such as a weekend sale, with only a one-line description of Summer, and were asked how they would most want to reach it.

Both asked for an MCP server with typed tools, plus a CLI that mirrors it. One wrote names like 

games.list
, 
analytics.summary
, 
store.publish
and 
jobs.wait
; the other wrote 
store_publish
. Both asked for dry runs, retry keys, job ids, structured errors, scoped permissions and an audit log.

So every name is 

area.action
; only 
whoami
stands alone. The area is a word a person uses, such as 
pricing
, and the action is usually a verb. A read and a change are never one operation. A name is permanent, so a new meaning gets a new name.

On MCP, 

store.get_listing
is the tool 
summer_store_get_listing
, because some clients reject dots in tool names. In a terminal it is 
summer store get-listing
. Two exceptions: engine tools kept their 3.x names, such as 
summer_add_node
, and makers kept 
summer_tool_
. 78% of the 3,141 tool mentions in our skills library name engine and file tools, so a rename would churn most skills for no gain.

Why search and call instead of 320 tools?

The hosted MCP lists 20 tools: 18 everyday operations, plus 

summer_search
and 
summer_call
. 
summer_search
takes the job in plain words and returns the matching operations with their exact input schema, so the next call needs no second lookup. 
summer_call
runs any operation by name, with the same input checks, dry runs and approvals as its own tool. Its MCP hints state the worst case, so clients ask before it runs.

Input tokens on the first model call, measured once per client (with no Summer server, about 2,700, or 13,161 in Codex CLI):

Client3.x4.0Change
npm server, client loads every tool147,36664,74756% less
Hosted server, client loads every tool43,06212,91570% less
npm server, Claude Code7,5015,93821% less
npm server, Codex CLI13,16113,161none

Claude Code and Codex already defer MCP tools, so they gain little or nothing. The 4.0 npm list still has 106 tools, because most of them are engine tools. Against 3.x with short descriptions and the engine toolset picked by hand, 4.0 saved 8%, and a hand-picked cloud-only 3.x toolset was smaller than 4.0. The gain over tuned 3.x is never picking toolsets by hand.

This only works if search is good, and in 4.0.0 it was not. "Publish my game" missed 

store.publish
. Agents in our eval searched with keywords, so they still found the right operation 50 of 55 times, but people type sentences. A test holds 35 real phrases, such as "lower my price", and all pass. It is live on the hosted server and in 4.2.0.

What does every answer look like?

Every operation answers one shape, on every surface:

{ "ok": true, "status": "done", "result": { "items": [] } }
{ "ok": true, "status": "running", "job": { "id": "gen:", "state": "running" } }
{ "ok": true, "status": "needs_approval",
  "approval": { "id": "apr_", "url": "https://www.summerengine.com/studio/approvals/apr_" },
  "job": { "id": "apr:", "state": "awaiting_approval" } }
{ "ok": false, "error": { "code": "no_credits", "message": "Not enough credits for this call.",
  "next": { "url": "https://www.summerengine.com/studio/credits", "label": "Add credits" }, "retry": "no" } }
  • Waiting for a person is a status, not an error.
    needs_approval
    tells the agent to hand you a link and wait, not to retry.
  • Slow cloud work never blocks. Anything that can take more than about 20 seconds answers 
    running
    with a job id, and 
    jobs.wait
    waits up to 50 seconds at a time. An engine export still blocks, by default up to 15 minutes.
  • Errors come from a closed list of 18 codes. Each has a plain message, at most one 
    next
    step (an operation, a link, or a sentence to tell you) and a 
    retry
    hint: 
    no
    , 
    safe
    , 
    same_key
    , or 
    after
    a wait. One step, not a list, so the agent does not have to choose. 
    invalid_input
    names the failed field in 
    details.path
    .

    • A last fix before 4.0.0 split the cloud failure that always said "sign in" into 

    not_signed_in
    , 
    forbidden
    , 
    unavailable
    and 
    outcome_unknown
    . The last means a change may have run: retry only with the same key, or check first. How Summer answers lists every code.

    How do dry runs and retry keys work?

    Every operation that changes something takes 

    dryRun: true
    . Summer checks the call and describes it, and nothing changes, is spent or is sent. The preview gives the approval a call needs, the estimated credits for generation, and before and after for publishing, live changes and deletes. The types enforce it: a spend operation cannot be defined without a cost estimate, and one that publishes, changes what players see or deletes cannot be defined without a preview.

    Every change on Summer's servers also takes an 

    idempotencyKey
    . The same key with the same input within 24 hours returns the first answer, marked 
    replayed
    , and never does the work twice. The same key with different input is an 
    idempotency_conflict
    . Publishing, releasing and the five price and sale changes require a key. Generation keeps it optional, because "the same prompt again" is often what you want. Engine edits on your computer have no retry key.

    What may an agent do without asking?

    Both blind-test runs asked for scoped permissions. Most operations that change something belong to one of six switches in Summer Studio under Settings > Agent permissions:

    SwitchDefaultOperations
    Make and buildOn120
    Spend creditsOn51
    PublishOn, but Summer Games still asks the owner today8
    Prices and live changesOn, but Summer Games still asks you today9
    Delete for goodOff, asks you18
    Contact peopleOff, asks you5

    The 104 reads never ask. Five operations always ask, such as auto top-up settings, and an agent can never turn a switch on by itself. The defaults trust the agent, and the approval card is the fallback.

    When something asks, the answer is 

    needs_approval
    with a link, and an open Studio tab shows a card too. The request is bound to its exact input. If the value changed since the agent asked, it ends 
    stale
    instead of overwriting. Agent activity lists what your agents did, with Undo for prices, sales, member roles, team names and the analytics event limit.

    What is live today: the switches show their defaults, and changing them is not available yet. Summer Games runs its own check on agent changes, and that check does not yet follow saved permissions. Until it does, an agent's publish always asks the game's owner, and price, A/B test and member changes always ask you. The agent permissions guide has the details.

    The approval lives on Summer's side, not in the prompt or the client, and 

    summer_call
    passes the same checks as a direct tool. For terminal agents, 
    npx -y summer-engine@latest setup claude-code --cli --allow-rules --yes
    adds allow rules for read commands and for dry runs of spend commands. Everything else still asks.

    How did we test 4.0 against 3.x?

    Right after 4.0.0 shipped, we ran 168 agent sessions: two clients (Claude Code and Codex CLI), four setups, seven tasks, three runs each. The setups were 3.x in full, 3.x tuned with short descriptions and toolsets picked per task, 4.0, and 4.0 with the old names too. The tasks were real asks, from "How did my game do this week?" (the numbers in Grow) to a price change, a publish and fixing an error on play. The npm server was real; the hosted server was a stand-in with the real catalog and search. Account and engine answers were fixtures with the real shapes.

  • Success was the same. 4.0 passed 21 of 21 in both clients. So did tuned 3.x.
  • No false claims. In all 168 runs, no agent said a change was live while it waited for approval. On 4.0, price, invite and publish gave the approval link 18 of 18 times.
  • The right operation. On 4.0, every price change used 
    pricing.set_base
    and every invite made an approval card. Our 3.x setup could not invite.
  • More first-try mistakes. 4.0 had 4 bad calls where tuned 3.x had none, such as 
    name
    instead of 
    op
    and a 
    limit
    over the maximum. Each was fixed on the next call, and 4.2.0 also accepts 
    name
    .
  • Upgrades hid the gain. While installed skills were older than 4.0, the old names stayed listed. That gave back about half the token saving, and Claude Code picked the old tools. 4.2.0 refreshes the skills on first start.

    • Three of our five pass rules held. The 50% token rule held only for clients that load every tool, and "no more bad calls than tuned 3.x" failed narrowly. The tasks were too easy to tell setups apart on success, three runs per cell is a small sample, and no editor client such as Cursor ran; the "loads every tool" rows count what such a client would load.

    What did we learn designing an MCP server for AI agents?

  • Ask a model with little context first. It named the operations the way agents look for them.
  • Test search with the sentences people type, not keywords.
  • Ship the switch with the gate. We showed the switches before Summer Games could follow them.

    • What comes next?

  • A harder eval with real accounts and a running engine.
  • An HTTP API and a typed SDK from the same catalog, for agents that script hundreds of calls. Specified, not built.
  • A tool list that follows use: once there is enough 4.0 data, the 18 direct operations are re-picked each month by how many people call each one. Telemetry records the operation name, never its arguments or results.

    • To try it, follow the MCP setup guide.

    Tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game."

    Frequently asked questions

    What is Summer MCP and CLI 4.0?

    It is how AI agents use Summer Engine. Every part of Summer is one operation with a plain name such as store.publish or assets.generate_3d. Agents reach the operations through the hosted MCP at https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp, the local npm MCP, or the summer CLI in a terminal. The current npm release is summer-engine 4.2.0.

    Why not list every operation as its own MCP tool?

    A client that loads every tool pays for all of them before the agent reads a word. The hosted MCP lists 20 tools for everyday jobs, and summer_search finds any other operation on Summer's servers from plain words and returns its exact input. In our tests this cut the first model call by 70% on the hosted server for clients that load every tool. Clients that already defer tools, such as Claude Code and Codex, gained little.

    What do dry runs and idempotency keys do?

    A dry run checks a change and describes it, often with before and after and the credits it would use, and changes nothing. An idempotency key makes a retry of a change on Summer's servers safe. The same key with the same input within 24 hours returns the first answer again and never does the work twice. Publishing and price changes require a key.

    Can my agent publish or change prices without asking me?

    Not today. Agent permissions in Summer Studio show their defaults, and changing them comes soon. Until Summer Games follows saved permissions, an agent's publish asks the game's owner, and price, A/B test and member changes ask you. Your agent gives you an approval link, and nothing changes until you approve.

    How did you test Summer 4.0 against 3.x?

    We ran 168 agent sessions in Claude Code and Codex CLI, across four setups, seven real tasks and three runs each. 4.0 matched a tuned 3.x setup on success, and no run claimed a change was live while it waited for approval. Account and engine answers were fixtures, so the test did not touch a real account or a running engine.

    Do the old 3.x tool names still work?

    Yes, for all of 4.x. summer_call accepts any 3.x tool name and runs the operation that replaced it. Engine tools keep their 3.x names. To get the full 3.x tool list back, run the local server with --surface v3.

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI. Add one link to your AI agent, or let it run Summer as commands in its terminal. Here is how both work.

  • Summer Engine·Oct 16, 2026·8min read

    Summer 4.0, the Game Engine for AI Agents

    Summer 4.0 is the game engine for AI agents. Any agent can build your game, make its assets and publish it once you approve.

  • MCP·Jun 7, 2026·5min read

    Summer Engine MCP Prompt Templates for AI Game Development

    Copyable prompts for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Devin Desktop, and other MCP agents using Summer Engine's MCP bridge.

    adds allow rules for read commands and for dry runs of spend commands. Everything else still asks.

    How did we test 4.0 against 3.x?

    Right after 4.0.0 shipped, we ran 168 agent sessions: two clients (Claude Code and Codex CLI), four setups, seven tasks, three runs each. The setups were 3.x in full, 3.x tuned with short descriptions and toolsets picked per task, 4.0, and 4.0 with the old names too. The tasks were real asks, from "How did my game do this week?" (the numbers in Grow) to a price change, a publish and fixing an error on play. The npm server was real; the hosted server was a stand-in with the real catalog and search. Account and engine answers were fixtures with the real shapes.

  • Success was the same. 4.0 passed 21 of 21 in both clients. So did tuned 3.x.
  • No false claims. In all 168 runs, no agent said a change was live while it waited for approval. On 4.0, price, invite and publish gave the approval link 18 of 18 times.
  • The right operation. On 4.0, every price change used 
    pricing.set_base
    and every invite made an approval card. Our 3.x setup could not invite.
  • More first-try mistakes. 4.0 had 4 bad calls where tuned 3.x had none, such as 
    name
    instead of 
    op
    and a 
    limit
    over the maximum. Each was fixed on the next call, and 4.2.0 also accepts 
    name
    .
  • Upgrades hid the gain. While installed skills were older than 4.0, the old names stayed listed. That gave back about half the token saving, and Claude Code picked the old tools. 4.2.0 refreshes the skills on first start.

    • Three of our five pass rules held. The 50% token rule held only for clients that load every tool, and "no more bad calls than tuned 3.x" failed narrowly. The tasks were too easy to tell setups apart on success, three runs per cell is a small sample, and no editor client such as Cursor ran; the "loads every tool" rows count what such a client would load.

    What did we learn designing an MCP server for AI agents?

  • Ask a model with little context first. It named the operations the way agents look for them.
  • Test search with the sentences people type, not keywords.
  • Ship the switch with the gate. We showed the switches before Summer Games could follow them.

    • What comes next?

  • A harder eval with real accounts and a running engine.
  • An HTTP API and a typed SDK from the same catalog, for agents that script hundreds of calls. Specified, not built.
  • A tool list that follows use: once there is enough 4.0 data, the 18 direct operations are re-picked each month by how many people call each one. Telemetry records the operation name, never its arguments or results.

    • To try it, follow the MCP setup guide.

    Tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game."

    Frequently asked questions

    What is Summer MCP and CLI 4.0?

    It is how AI agents use Summer Engine. Every part of Summer is one operation with a plain name such as store.publish or assets.generate_3d. Agents reach the operations through the hosted MCP at https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp, the local npm MCP, or the summer CLI in a terminal. The current npm release is summer-engine 4.2.0.

    Why not list every operation as its own MCP tool?

    A client that loads every tool pays for all of them before the agent reads a word. The hosted MCP lists 20 tools for everyday jobs, and summer_search finds any other operation on Summer's servers from plain words and returns its exact input. In our tests this cut the first model call by 70% on the hosted server for clients that load every tool. Clients that already defer tools, such as Claude Code and Codex, gained little.

    What do dry runs and idempotency keys do?

    A dry run checks a change and describes it, often with before and after and the credits it would use, and changes nothing. An idempotency key makes a retry of a change on Summer's servers safe. The same key with the same input within 24 hours returns the first answer again and never does the work twice. Publishing and price changes require a key.

    Can my agent publish or change prices without asking me?

    Not today. Agent permissions in Summer Studio show their defaults, and changing them comes soon. Until Summer Games follows saved permissions, an agent's publish asks the game's owner, and price, A/B test and member changes ask you. Your agent gives you an approval link, and nothing changes until you approve.

    How did you test Summer 4.0 against 3.x?

    We ran 168 agent sessions in Claude Code and Codex CLI, across four setups, seven real tasks and three runs each. 4.0 matched a tuned 3.x setup on success, and no run claimed a change was live while it waited for approval. Account and engine answers were fixtures, so the test did not touch a real account or a running engine.

    Do the old 3.x tool names still work?

    Yes, for all of 4.x. summer_call accepts any 3.x tool name and runs the operation that replaced it. Engine tools keep their 3.x names. To get the full 3.x tool list back, run the local server with --surface v3.

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI. Add one link to your AI agent, or let it run Summer as commands in its terminal. Here is how both work.

item.title: DLSS 5 上 RTX Spark：10 月模型比 9 月快 2 倍，4K 下显存再省 20%、GPU 开销减半 ｜ NVIDIA RTX Spark Powers Neural Rendering and AI Characters in Games
item.description:

要点：

  • RTX Spark 是面向 AI 开发、创作与游戏的 Windows PC 平台，最高 128 GB 统一内存，带完整 CUDA 栈与光追/DLSS 5
  • DLSS 5（3D 引导神经渲染）在 RTX Spark 上跑起来，首发作品是 NBA 2K27；10 月模型比 9 月版快 2 倍，GPU 开销减半，4K 下显存占用再降 20%

为什么值得看：两个数字值得记：神经渲染模型在上线后一个月还能再快一倍，说明这条路的成本曲线还在快速下降；而「4K 省 20% 显存」直接决定了能不能和传统管线共存。做渲染预算的人应当把这类月度更新当成变量，而不是一次性选型。

中文摘要：NVIDIA 把 RTX Spark 定位成面向 AI 开发、创作与游戏的 Windows PC 平台：最高 128 GB 统一内存，配完整 CUDA 栈，并包含光追与 DLSS 5。DLSS 5 的 3D 引导神经渲染已在 RTX Spark 上运行，首发作品是 NBA 2K27；更值得注意的是迭代速度——10 月版本的模型比 9 月快 2 倍，GPU 开销减半，4K 下显存占用再降 20%。同批更新还包括 ACE 的端侧 AI 角色能力、Nemotron 3.5 系列以及 RTX Kit 的多项改进。对做渲染预算的团队，这意味着神经渲染不再是一个「选定就不动」的模块：它的性能与显存画像每个月都在变，规划时得把它当变量。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：NVIDIA Developer（English）

原文发布：2026-10-27

本期推送：2026-10-28

Content Creation / Rendering

NVIDIA RTX Spark Powers Neural Rendering and AI Characters in Games

Oct 27, 2026 By Phillip Singh
  • L
  • T
  • F
  • R
  • E
  • NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new Windows PC platform for AI development, creation, and gaming in slim laptops and compact desktops, combining up to 128 GB of unified memory with the full NVIDIA CUDA stack and RTX technologies including ray tracing and DLSS 5.
  • DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering runs on RTX Spark, starting with NBA 2K27, and an October model update runs 2x faster than the September version while halving GPU overhead and reducing VRAM use at 4K by 20%.
  • Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB offers ~40% higher average quality against the prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens versus peers, enabling responsive local AI character interactions on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark.
  • NVIDIA RTX Kit brings eight neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark, including RTX Neural Texture Compression, RTX Mega Geometry, and RTX Character Rendering for strand-based hair and skin with path tracing.
  • NVIDIA Nsight tools support graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications on RTX Spark from day one, with Nsight Graphics 2026.3 introducing a Windows on Arm installer and Nsight Systems 2026.5 providing a single installer for all Windows versions.
  • The NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 provides an updated foundation for advanced ray tracing and neural graphics in UE 5.8 projects, while MotionBricks adds new SOMA human-motion models, downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and an interactive reference implementation built with Newton.

    • Next Steps

  • Download the In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK to access Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB for on-device AI characters.
  • Download Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark to capture, inspect, and profile frames for native Arm64 and emulated applications.
  • Explore the RTX Neural Texture Compression repository to integrate AI-powered texture compression into game projects.
    • Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more

    NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new Windows PC platform for AI development, creation, and gaming in slim laptops and compact desktops. Powered by an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and NVIDIA Grace CPU, it combines up to 128 GB of unified memory with the full NVIDIA CUDA stack and RTX technologies including ray tracing and DLSS 5.

    This post covers the following technologies for game developers building on RTX Spark:

  • DLSS suite of technologies that boost FPS and improve image quality
  • NVIDIA ACE updates for responsive, on-device AI characters
  • RTX Kit SDKs for neural rendering, geometry, and character rendering
  • NVIDIA Nsight tools for optimizing and debugging native Arm64 and x64 applications
  • NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 for integrating RTX technologies into your Unreal Engine projects
  • MotionBricks update for human-character motion

    • DLSS on RTX Spark

    RTX Spark benefits from the full suite of DLSS technologies in supported games, including Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, and 3D-Guided Neural Rendering.

    DLSS Super Resolution reconstructs frames from a lower resolution input to improve performance. DLSS Ray Reconstruction generates additional pixels to enhance ray-traced scenes. DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation can generate up to 5 additional frames per rendered frame, automatically adjusting the multiplier to maximize smoothness.

    The latest NVIDIA app beta also brings a faster Performance Mode (Preset C) for Frame Generation, with minor trade-offs in image quality.

    DLSS 5 brings 3D-Guided Neural Rendering to RTX Spark

    DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is supported on NVIDIA RTX Spark, starting with NBA 2K27.

    An October model update runs 2x faster than the September version and halves GPU overhead while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. It also reduces VRAM use at 4K by 20%. The model will ship by default in future DLSS 5 games.

    For developers, DLSS 5 adds a final stage to the graphics pipeline that enhances lighting and material detail. The engine-rendered frame, including artist-designed geometry, textures, and lighting buffers, remains the foundation, while developer controls determine what can change. Avalanche Software has taken advantage of DLSS 5’s SDK controls to tune the integration to maintain the artistic intent and style of the game.

    Read the full DLSS 5 update here.

    DLSS 4.5 Unreal Engine plugin

    The updatedNVIDIA DLSS 4.5 plugin for Unreal Engine gives developers powerful tools for delivering sharper images and smoother gameplay. Its second-generation transformer model for Super Resolution improves image stability, anti-aliasing, and visual clarity, while Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced image quality.

    On supported GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX PRO Blackwell GPUs, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation adapts the frame-generation multiplier as workloads change, with 6x Multi Frame Generation producing up to five additional frames per rendered frame.

    A key addition in plugin version 8.9.0 is official Windows on Arm (WoA) support for Unreal Engine 5.8. Native ARM64 binaries and support for building and packaging UE 5.8 applications give developers a supported path to bring DLSS-enabled projects to RTX Spark systems. Alongside updated Streamline and NGX components and fixes for UE 5.8 Frame Generation issues, this release expands the plugin’s platform reach and helps developers prepare their applications for RTX Spark.

    NVIDIA ACE introduces Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for on-device AI characters

    NVIDIA ACE is our technology suite for creating in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences, and we’ve shared two exciting showcases this year:

  • PUBG rolled out AI teammates in a public beta powered by our first-generation Nemotron small language model (SLM). It helped new players land their first chicken dinners and generated viral clips across social media.
  • Aniimo debuted our more efficient second-generation Nemotron SLM, turning standard in-game pets into responsive AI companions that react to your voice. Players can check in on their pets’ feelings or teach them new tricks, which will bring a new level of immersion when it releases in early 2027.

    • More intelligence, less memory

    Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available. This model offers ~40% higher average quality against our prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens vs peers.

    It is purpose-built to power richer, faster in-game character interactions, with strong conversational capability, autonomous multi-turn tool use, instruction adherence, and grounding to game state, all running locally on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark.

    Engineered for maximum intelligence and speed per GB of memory, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB enables responsive local experiences while preserving headroom for graphics rendering and local speech models. Key features include:

  • Multi-turn tool use: Call application APIs to carry out tasks across a conversation, with integration guidance for asynchronous tool calls
  • Conversational mode: Toggle to encourage concise, speech-ready responses for natural back-and-forth interactions.
  • Configurable reasoning: Enable reasoning for complex requests or disable it for faster responses, with integration options to cap thinking to meet latency targets.
  • 64k context: Accommodate conversation history, instructions, tool definitions, retrieved information and game state.
  • Multilingual capability: Support for 35 languages, building on a base model pre-trained on more than 140 languages.

    • Get started with NVIDIA ACE

    Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is available to developers via the In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK.

    To test it in a game, check out SkyrimNET, an AI NPC modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character with personal memory, voice, and autonomy, enabling dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly. The platform supports both cloud and local inference across multiple language models.

  • Download the SkyrimNET Plugin:GitHub Repository
  • Download the ARM-Supported Loader:Mod Organizer Release

    • NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark

    NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering, complex geometry, and realistic character rendering to game development. Eight RTX Kit technologies are published with support for RTX Spark:

  • RTX Neural Texture Compression (NTC): Uses AI to shrink texture storage while maintaining visual fidelity comparable to traditional block compression.
  • RTX Texture Filtering: Uses stochastic texture sampling after shading to reduce artifacts and improve image quality, including for difficult volumes.
  • RTX Neural Shaders: Lets developers train neural networks and run them within shaders for new asset compression and approximation techniques.
  • RTX Mega Geometry: Speeds up bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction for cluster-based geometry, helping developers ray trace more triangles and improve performance in complex scenes.
  • NVIDIA Real-Time Denoisers (NRD): Provides denoisers for diffuse and specular lighting and shadows, producing cleaner images from low ray-per-pixel inputs.
  • RTX Character Rendering: Provides tools for rendering strand-based hair and skin with path tracing, including subsurface scattering and Blackwell-accelerated hair primitives.
  • RTX Global Illumination (RTXGI): Provides several techniques for efficient indirect lighting for ray traced and path traced applications.
  • Opacity Micro-Maps (OMM): Used to accelerate ray tracing of high detail geometry by efficiently encoding the opacity states of micro-triangles and micro meshes.

    • Optimizing and debugging RTX Spark applications

    NVIDIA Nsight tools are ready for RTX Spark from day one, supporting graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications.

    Nsight Graphics lets developers capture, inspect, and profile individual frames, examining every draw call, shader, and resource to diagnose rendering bugs and tune GPU performance. Nsight Graphics release 2026.3 introduces a new Windows on Arm installer for RTX Spark systems, supporting native Arm64 target applications as well as emulated x64 and Arm64EC targets.

    Nsight Systems delivers a system-wide view of application performance, correlating CPU threads, GPU workloads, API calls, and memory activity on a single timeline so developers can pinpoint bottlenecks and balance work across the platform. Starting with Nsight Systems 2026.5, a single installer for all versions of Windows supports both native Arm64 and emulated applications.

    Nsight Aftermath helps teams resolve GPU crashes and hangs by generating detailed crash dumps that show what the GPU was doing at the moment of failure, both during development and in the field. Nsight Aftermath SDK 2026.3 includes a Windows on Arm version for integrating into native Arm64 applications. Crash dumps from emulated x64 applications will continue to function as expected with the x64 version of the SDK.

  • Download Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Systems for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Aftermath SDK for RTX Spark here

    • NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8

    The release ofNVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 (NvRTX 5.8) gives developers an updated foundation for bringing advanced ray tracing and neural graphics to UE 5.8 projects. This update focuses on codebase refactoring, stabilization, and compatibility improvements. Developers can access the branch source through GitHub to integrate and customize NVIDIA RTX technologies for their games and applications.

    Simplify runtime character animation with MotionBricks

    MotionBricks is open-source research for generating character motion in real time. Rather than hand-authoring every transition and wiring it into an increasingly complex animation graph, developers guide motion through target poses. MotionBricks generates the connecting movement at runtime and adapts as player input or game event changes.PaperGitHub

    The model supports control over speed, direction, and movement style, along with pose-guided interactions such as sitting and picking up objects. These capabilities let developers build varied character behaviors through a common pose-based interface. The original research demonstration shows these behaviors working together in Unreal Engine. Research demonstrations

    The update builds on this work with:

  • New SOMA human-motion models, alongside the existing G1 robot model.
  • Downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and export tools for developers building their own integrations.
  • An interactive reference implementation built with Newton, demonstrating pose-guided human and robot motion.

    • MotionBricks is provided as research code and models. The Unreal Engine integration shown in the research demonstration is not included in this release.

    Resources for game developers

    Check out the full list of game developer resources and stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news:

  • Subscribe to our newsletter (select gaming as your industry)
  • Follow us on social: X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube
  • Join our Discord community

    • Tags

    Content Creation / Rendering | Gaming | DLSS | Nsight Tools - Graphics | RTX Kit | Intermediate Technical | News | ACE | DGX Spark | Unreal Engine

    About the Authors

    About Phillip Singh
    Phillip Singh is a senior developer marketing manager at NVIDIA, specializing in games and consumer AI. He is dedicated to empowering the next generation of game developers through neural rendering and AI graphics technology. Phillip earned his master's in business administration from the Santa Clara University Leavey School of Business. View all posts by Phillip Singh

  • Configurable reasoning: Enable reasoning for complex requests or disable it for faster responses, with integration options to cap thinking to meet latency targets.
  • 64k context: Accommodate conversation history, instructions, tool definitions, retrieved information and game state.
  • Multilingual capability: Support for 35 languages, building on a base model pre-trained on more than 140 languages.

    • Get started with NVIDIA ACE

    Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is available to developers via the In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK.

    To test it in a game, check out SkyrimNET, an AI NPC modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character with personal memory, voice, and autonomy, enabling dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly. The platform supports both cloud and local inference across multiple language models.

  • Download the SkyrimNET Plugin:GitHub Repository
  • Download the ARM-Supported Loader:Mod Organizer Release

    • NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark

    NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering, complex geometry, and realistic character rendering to game development. Eight RTX Kit technologies are published with support for RTX Spark:

  • RTX Neural Texture Compression (NTC): Uses AI to shrink texture storage while maintaining visual fidelity comparable to traditional block compression.
  • RTX Texture Filtering: Uses stochastic texture sampling after shading to reduce artifacts and improve image quality, including for difficult volumes.
  • RTX Neural Shaders: Lets developers train neural networks and run them within shaders for new asset compression and approximation techniques.
  • RTX Mega Geometry: Speeds up bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction for cluster-based geometry, helping developers ray trace more triangles and improve performance in complex scenes.
  • NVIDIA Real-Time Denoisers (NRD): Provides denoisers for diffuse and specular lighting and shadows, producing cleaner images from low ray-per-pixel inputs.
  • RTX Character Rendering: Provides tools for rendering strand-based hair and skin with path tracing, including subsurface scattering and Blackwell-accelerated hair primitives.
  • RTX Global Illumination (RTXGI): Provides several techniques for efficient indirect lighting for ray traced and path traced applications.
  • Opacity Micro-Maps (OMM): Used to accelerate ray tracing of high detail geometry by efficiently encoding the opacity states of micro-triangles and micro meshes.

    • Optimizing and debugging RTX Spark applications

    NVIDIA Nsight tools are ready for RTX Spark from day one, supporting graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications.

    Nsight Graphics lets developers capture, inspect, and profile individual frames, examining every draw call, shader, and resource to diagnose rendering bugs and tune GPU performance. Nsight Graphics release 2026.3 introduces a new Windows on Arm installer for RTX Spark systems, supporting native Arm64 target applications as well as emulated x64 and Arm64EC targets.

    Nsight Systems delivers a system-wide view of application performance, correlating CPU threads, GPU workloads, API calls, and memory activity on a single timeline so developers can pinpoint bottlenecks and balance work across the platform. Starting with Nsight Systems 2026.5, a single installer for all versions of Windows supports both native Arm64 and emulated applications.

    Nsight Aftermath helps teams resolve GPU crashes and hangs by generating detailed crash dumps that show what the GPU was doing at the moment of failure, both during development and in the field. Nsight Aftermath SDK 2026.3 includes a Windows on Arm version for integrating into native Arm64 applications. Crash dumps from emulated x64 applications will continue to function as expected with the x64 version of the SDK.

  • Download Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Systems for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Aftermath SDK for RTX Spark here

    • NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8

    The release ofNVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 (NvRTX 5.8) gives developers an updated foundation for bringing advanced ray tracing and neural graphics to UE 5.8 projects. This update focuses on codebase refactoring, stabilization, and compatibility improvements. Developers can access the branch source through GitHub to integrate and customize NVIDIA RTX technologies for their games and applications.

    Simplify runtime character animation with MotionBricks

    MotionBricks is open-source research for generating character motion in real time. Rather than hand-authoring every transition and wiring it into an increasingly complex animation graph, developers guide motion through target poses. MotionBricks generates the connecting movement at runtime and adapts as player input or game event changes.PaperGitHub

    The model supports control over speed, direction, and movement style, along with pose-guided interactions such as sitting and picking up objects. These capabilities let developers build varied character behaviors through a common pose-based interface. The original research demonstration shows these behaviors working together in Unreal Engine. Research demonstrations

    The update builds on this work with:

  • New SOMA human-motion models, alongside the existing G1 robot model.
  • Downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and export tools for developers building their own integrations.
  • An interactive reference implementation built with Newton, demonstrating pose-guided human and robot motion.

    • MotionBricks is provided as research code and models. The Unreal Engine integration shown in the research demonstration is not included in this release.

    Resources for game developers

    Check out the full list of game developer resources and stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news:

  • Follow us on social: X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube

item.title: 别给每个高斯都配同样长的时间轴：GaussianSpline 让轨迹自适应分段的贝塞尔样条，静的地方省、动的地方密 ｜ GaussianSpline: Adaptive Bézier Splines for Highly Dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：联合学控制点与时间分段，用反射约束保证 G¹ 连续；低阶非均匀反而打败高阶均匀。

要点：

  • 每个高斯的运动用非均匀分段三次贝塞尔样条表示，控制点与「时间怎么分段」一起学：高动态区域分到更多时间容量，接近静止的区域保持紧凑轨迹
  • 相邻贝塞尔段之间用基于反射的约束强制 G¹ 连续，于是轨迹既全局平滑又保留非均匀参数化的灵活性，且全程可微
  • 消融给出一个反直觉结论：在所有样条阶数上，非均匀间距都优于或持平均匀间距，而提高阶数几乎没收益——最低阶 + 非均匀布局效果最好，说明「自适应节点放置」比「样条多灵活」更重要

为什么值得看：动态 3DGS 的容量一直花得很平均：静止的背景和飞速的手拿同样的时间分辨率。这条把时间预算变成可学的分配问题，和渲染里「把采样率放到变化的地方」是同一个直觉，但要落到可微训练里并不容易。

中文摘要：动态 4D 高斯泼溅通常用全局形变、固定阶数多项式或均匀参数化样条来描述每个高斯的运动，结果是时间容量被平均分配。GaussianSpline 改成自适应、非均匀的分段三次贝塞尔样条：它同时学习贝塞尔控制点与每个高斯轨迹的时间分段，把更多时间容量给高动态区域、让近静态区域保持紧凑，从而还原复杂快速运动。为了让整条轨迹既平滑又保留局部分辨能力，作者在相邻段之间用基于反射的约束强制 G¹ 连续，得到完全可微的运动表示。实验在 Neural 3D Video、Google Immersive 与合成场景上均显示高非均匀动态场景的重建质量提升，消融还表明「非均匀间距」比「更高阶样条」更关键。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-10-28

GaussianSpline: Adaptive Bézier Splines for Highly Dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

We present GaussianSpline, a dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models per-Gaussian motion using adaptive, non-uniform piecewise cubic Bézier splines. Unlike approaches based on global deformations, fixed-order polynomials, or uniformly parameterized splines, GaussianSpline jointly learns the Bézier control points and the temporal partition of each Gaussian’s trajectory. This adaptive representation allocates greater temporal capacity to highly dynamic regions while maintaining compact trajectories for near-static regions, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction of complex and rapidly changing motion. To jointly achieve globally smooth motion and local adaptivity, we enforce G¹ continuity between consecutive Bézier segments using a reflection-based constraint on their control points. This produces smooth, fully differentiable trajectories while preserving the flexibility of non-uniform temporal parameterization. Experiments on the Neural 3D Video benchmark, the Google Immersive dataset [BFO∗20], as well as on synthetic scenes demonstrate that GaussianSpline substantially improves reconstruction quality in scenes with highly non-uniform and challenging dynamics, while maintaining competitive performance on general dynamic scenes compared with state-of-the-art 4D Gaussian Splatting methods.

1 Introduction

Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from multi-view video is an emerging problem in computer graphics and vision, with applications in virtual reality, telepresence, and film production. The recent success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] has demonstrated that explicit, differentiable representations based on anisotropic Gaussians can achieve high-quality reconstruction and real-time rendering of static 3D scenes, motivating their extension to dynamic 4D content. However, moving from static to dynamic Gaussian Splatting introduces a fundamental challenge: the representation must simultaneously capture the spatial structure of the scene and the complex temporal evolution of potentially millions of Gaussians. In particular, accurately modeling highly dynamic regions requires flexible motion trajectories, while avoiding unnecessary temporal degrees of freedom in near-static regions.

Existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods typically rely on neural deformation fields or fixed spatial-temporal representations. Neural deformation approaches augment canonical Gaussians with MLP-based motion predictors [HSY∗23, YGZ∗24, LKL∗25], introducing additional per-Gaussian computation during rendering. Structured 4D approaches instead factorize spacetime using voxel grids or plane-based representations [XPL∗24, WYF∗24], but rely on predefined spatial-temporal resolutions. These representations therefore face a trade-off between computational or memory cost and reconstruction fidelity, particularly for scenes with highly non-uniform dynamics, where different regions require different levels of temporal modeling.

To avoid the overhead of neural deformation networks, explicit trajectory-based methods [LCLX24, LDZY24] model Gaussian motion using global parametric functions, such as polynomials or Fourier bases. More recently, piecewise spline representations have been explored for trajectory modeling, offering local control and compact parameterization [PBB∗25, YHOL25]. However, these approaches typically employ a uniform temporal parameterization across Gaussian trajectories, allocating the same temporal capacity regardless of the underlying motion. This limits their ability to efficiently capture the highly heterogeneous dynamics of real-world scenes, where different regions may exhibit slow, smooth motion or rapid and complex changes.

To address these limitations, we introduce GaussianSpline, a per-Gaussian trajectory-based 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that models motion using adaptive piecewise cubic Bézier splines with learnable, non-uniform temporal parameterization. Each Gaussian is assigned an independent trajectory initialized with a minimal number of spline segments. During optimization, the Bézier control points and segment intervals are jointly learned, allowing each trajectory to allocate temporal resolution according to its local motion. Rapidly changing motion is captured with finer temporal intervals, while slowly varying motion is represented with broader intervals, avoiding unnecessary temporal degrees of freedom and yielding a compact representation.

To ensure smooth motion across spline segments, we enforce G¹ continuity using a reflection-based control-point formulation with direction-locked tangents and learnable magnitude scaling. This yields smooth, fully differentiable trajectories while preserving local flexibility in motion speed and curvature. GaussianSpline introduces no auxiliary neural networks and integrates directly into the standard 3DGS optimization and densification pipeline, providing a compact and efficient representation for highly non-uniform dynamics.

Experiments on the Neural 3D Video benchmark, the Google Immersive dataset [BFO∗20], and synthetic scenes demonstrate that GaussianSpline significantly improves reconstruction quality for scenes with complex, highly non-uniform motion, while maintaining competitive performance on general dynamic scenes compared with state-of-the-art 4D Gaussian Splatting methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Learnable adaptive temporal parameterization. We jointly learn Bézier control points and non-uniform segment intervals to adapt temporal resolution to each Gaussian’s local motion.

  • •

    Smooth motion transitions. We introduce a reflection-based G¹ continuity constraint with learnable tangent magnitudes for smooth and flexible trajectory modeling.

  • •

    Efficient 4D representation. Our adaptive trajectories integrate seamlessly into the standard 3DGS framework, providing a compact and efficient representation of dynamic scenes.

    • 2 Related Work

    In the following we discuss recent related works on reconstruction of 3D dynamic scenes from multi-view video.

    Dynamic neural radiance fields. Dynamic extensions of NeRF [MST∗20] represent a scene as a time-varying radiance field, either conditioning the field directly on time [LSZ∗22] or warping each observation into a canonical frame through a learned deformation [PCPMMN21, PSH∗21], with later work improving robustness on casually captured monocular video [LGM∗23].

    These methods produce high-quality free-viewpoint video, but inherit NeRF’s volumetric ray marching: rendering a single pixel requires hundreds of network evaluations along a ray, so training takes hours to days and playback remains far from real time [LSZ∗22]. Grid- and plane-based factorizations [FKMW∗23] reduce this cost substantially, yet the scene stays an implicit field sampled at a fixed spatial-temporal resolution, so motion is never an explicit quantity that can be allocated where the scene actually moves.

    Dynamic 3DGS The emergence of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] has significantly advanced neural rendering by replacing implicit volumetric sampling with explicit, differentiable rasterization of anisotropic Gaussians. Building on this success, recent work has focused on extending 3DGS to dynamic scenes by modeling temporal deformation of Gaussian attributes [LKLR24, LCLX24, WYF∗24].

    Luiten et al. [LKLR24] directly optimize per-timestep Gaussian positions and rotations under local rigidity constraints, enabling dense 6-DOF tracking without an explicit deformation model. In contrast, MLP-based approaches learn continuous deformation fields in a canonical space. Deformable 3DGS [YGZ∗24] maps Gaussians from canonical to observation space via a neural deformation network, while GauFRe [LKL∗25] introduces a forward-warping formulation with an explicit static component to decouple moving and stationary regions. Although expressive, these methods require per-Gaussian MLP evaluations at render time, leading to significant computational overhead [LCLX24]. SC-GS [HSY∗23] mitigates this issue by combining deformation networks with sparse spatial constraints to reduce inference cost.

    Another line of work improves efficiency through structured spacetime factorization. Originating from NeRF-based representations such as K-Planes [FKMW∗23], these methods decompose the 4D domain into low-dimensional grids or plane representations. This idea has been adopted in 3DGS extensions such as 4DGS [WYF∗24] and 4K4D [XPL∗24], which model dynamic Gaussian attributes using structured grid-based embeddings. While computationally efficient, these methods are inherently limited by discrete resolution, leading to a trade-off between memory usage and reconstruction fidelity [WYF∗24, LCLX24].

    Explicit trajectory modeling. More recent methods abandon neural deformation networks in favor of explicit motion trajectories.

    Spacetime Gaussians (STG) [LCLX24] represent Gaussian motion using polynomial trajectories, improving temporal smoothness and efficiency. Gaussian-Flow [LDZY24] further extends this idea by combining polynomial and Fourier-based representations in a dual-domain formulation, eliminating the need for neural networks while improving expressiveness.

    However, fixed-degree polynomial models assign uniform temporal capacity to all Gaussians and may struggle to represent complex, non-linear motion patterns [LCLX24]. This limitation has motivated spline-based representations as a more flexible alternative.

    Spline-based formulations provide smooth and locally controllable representations of motion trajectories. SplineGS [PBB∗25] introduces piecewise cubic Hermite splines with motion-adaptive control-point pruning, while also reducing reliance on pre-computed camera parameters. However, its formulation targets monocular video sequences rather than multi-view dynamic 4D reconstruction, as considered in our work.

    More closely related to our setting, Yoon et al. [YHOL25] propose a method, also termed SplineGS, that employs NURBS to represent Gaussian trajectories as combinations of learned representative motion bases, improving temporal smoothness and spatial coherence in multi-view 4D dynamic scenes.

    However, both approaches rely on uniform spline parameterizations with fixed control-point distributions. In contrast, our approach jointly learns adaptive, locally refined control-point distributions based on motion complexity. This allows temporal capacity to be allocated where it is most needed, providing a more efficient representation of highly non-uniform motion and improving reconstruction quality with fewer Gaussian splats.

    3 Method

    We first review the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation and then extend it to dynamic scenes by assigning each Gaussian a learnable piecewise cubic Bézier trajectory. Unlike fixed temporal parameterizations, our formulation jointly optimizes the spline parameters and the temporal placement of control points, allowing each Gaussian to adapt its temporal resolution to the underlying motion (see Figure 1).

    3D Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussians, each parameterized by its position μ, covariance matrix Σ, opacity o, and view-dependent color c represented using spherical harmonics. Each Gaussian is defined as:

    G(x)=\exp(-1/2(x-μ)^⊤Σ⁻¹(x-μ)),

    		(1)

    with covariance parameterized as:

    Σ=RSS^⊤R^⊤,

    		(2)

    where S and R denote learnable scaling and rotation matrices, respectively.

    For rendering, Gaussians are projected onto the image plane and rasterized using differentiable alpha compositing, where Gaussians are accumulated in depth order:

    C=∑_i∈Ncᵢαᵢ∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-αⱼ),

    		(3)

    Starting from an SfM point cloud, all Gaussian parameters are optimized end-to-end through differentiable rendering, while adaptive density control dynamically splits, clones, and prunes Gaussians during training. We refer to [KKLD23] for a detailed description of the 3DGS formulation.

    4D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scenes. To reconstruct a dynamic 4D scene, we lift static Gaussian splats to a time-varying representation over a normalized timeline t∈[0,1]. In our formulation, only the Gaussian position μ(t) and rotation R(t) are time-dependent, while the scale s, opacity o, and color c are shared across all timestamps. The time-varying covariance is therefore given by:

    Σ(t)=R(t)SS^⊤R(t)^⊤,

    		(4)

    and the Gaussian at time t is obtained by evaluating Eq. (1) with μ(t) and Σ(t).

    This design reflects the observation that many real-world motions can be approximated as piecewise locally rigid deformations, with temporal variation primarily captured by translation and rotation. Restricting temporal variation to these degrees of freedom yields a compact yet flexible representation for dynamic scene modeling.

    Non-uniform Cubic Bézier Spline Trajectories To model the motion trajectory of a Gaussian splat over time, we use a piecewise cubic Bézier spline defined by K+1 joints {J₀,J₁,…,J_K}, 2K interior control points {C_k,0,C_k,1}ₖ₌₀^K-1, and K non-uniform interval widths {w₀,w₁,…,w_K-1}. Note that all spline parameters are differentiable and jointly optimized within our framework (see Figure 1 (middle)).

    To enforce monotonic partition of the entire temporal domain based on the learned adaptive non-uniform intervals we define:

    tₖ = ∑ⱼ₌₀ᵏ⁻¹w̃ⱼ,

    		(5)

    where w̃ₖ = (\exp(wₖ))/(∑ⱼ₌₀^K-1\exp(wⱼ)) is segment k’s interval width, tₖ is Jₖ’s timestamp, and the joints timestamp sequence 0=t₀

    To evaluate the trajectory at a global timestamp t∈[0,1], we locate the active segment k such that tₖ≤t

    μ(t)=(1-u)³Jₖ+3(1-u)²u C_k,0+3(1-u)u²C_k,1+u³Jₖ₊₁

    		(6)

    Learnable interval widths. Rather than using a uniform partition of the time domain [0,1], we parameterize each spline using learnable interval-width logits {w₀,w₁,…,w_K-1}, which define a non-uniform temporal segmentation. Initialized to zero, these logits yield a uniform partition at the beginning of training and are subsequently optimized jointly with the spline joints and control points.

    This allows each Gaussian to adapt its temporal resolution to the underlying motion, allocating finer intervals to rapidly changing motion and broader intervals to slowly varying motion, thereby improving reconstruction fidelity over an equivalent uniformly parameterized spline (see Figure 2).

    Learnable motion speed.C⁰ continuity is ensured by shared joints between adjacent segments. Rather than enforcing the stricter C¹ continuity, which couples both the direction and speed of motion across neighboring segments through continuity of the first derivative, we impose G¹ continuity. This preserves the tangent direction at each internal junction while allowing its magnitude to vary through a learnable positive scalar λₖ>0:

    C_k,0 = Jₖ + λₖ (Jₖ-C_k-1,1), k=1,…,K-1.

    		(7)

    The per-junction scales λₖ are initialized to 1, recovering C¹ continuity at the start of training, and are jointly optimized with the spline parameters. This relaxation allows motion speed to vary smoothly across segments while preserving kink-free trajectories and tangent continuity throughout the spline.

    Per-Gaussian polynomial rotations. To compute the per-Gaussian time-dependent rotation matrix R(t), we follow [LCLX24] and parameterize the raw quaternion as a first-degree polynomial, mapping its normalized form to the rotation group:

    q(t)=q₀+q₁t, R(t)=ℝ ((q(t))/(∥q(t)∥))

    		(8)

    where q₀ and q₁ denote the base quaternion and its linear velocity, respectively, and ℝ(·) is the standard mapping from unit quaternions to rotation matrices.

    Training. In each training iteration, we pick a random frame index from the training set, calculate its timestamp and select a subset of camera views captured at this timestamp. Then, every Gaussian is evaluated at this timestamp through its active segment (Eq. 6), and the photometric loss w.r.t. the selected views is back-propagated to the spline and Gaussian parameters.

    Together with the static initialization (all joints and control points set to x₀), this generates the Gaussian motion trajectories. Note that in near-static regions the gradients average or are near zero, leaving the trajectory approximately flat and consuming no temporal capacity.

    Furthermore, we apply Gaussians adaptive densification steps, i.e., split/clone/prune operations in early stage training iterations (as in [KKLD23]). Afterwards, the set of Gaussians remains fixed, and only the spline parameters (joints, control points, widths, G¹ scales) and the Gaussian attributes (opacity, color, covariance) are optimized.

    4 Experiments and Results

    Implementation Details. We train for 30k iterations using Adam on a single RTX 4090, optimizing an L₁ loss with a D-SSIM term (λ=0.2), SH degree 3, and batch size 2. Following 3DGS, the position learning rate decays exponentially from 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ to 1.6 × 10⁻⁶, while the learning rates for features, opacity, scaling, and rotation are 2.5 × 10⁻³, 5 × 10⁻², 5 × 10⁻³, and 10⁻³, respectively. The spline joint-width learning rate is set to 0.3× the position learning rate. Densification is performed every 100 iterations from iteration 500 to 9k, using a gradient threshold of 2 × 10⁻⁴ and a maximum of six densification events. Opacity is reset every 3k iterations, and Gaussians with opacity below 0.005 or scale above 0.1× the scene extent are pruned. Unless otherwise stated, we use K=3 spline segments with non-uniform joint spacing and G¹ continuity, initialized from approximately 8k COLMAP SfM points from a single frame on N3DV.

    Baselines We compare our method with three other SOTA methods: Gaussian-Flow [LDZY24], STG (Spacetime Gaussian)  [LCLX24] and SplineGS [YHOL25].

    We select these methods because they target the same multi-view dynamic 4D reconstruction setting and, like our approach, explicitly model Gaussian motion trajectories. They therefore provide relevant baselines for evaluating different approaches to temporal motion representation. STG represents Gaussian motion using polynomial trajectories, Gaussian-Flow combines polynomial and Fourier-based representations, and SplineGS employs piecewise cubic Hermite splines with motion-adaptive control-point pruning. These methods constitute the current set of SOTA approaches that explicitly model Gaussian motion trajectories in the multi-view dynamic 4D reconstruction setting, providing direct baselines for evaluating our adaptive temporal parameterization on highly non-uniform motion.

    In our experiments, we use the default training schedules of 30K, 30K, and 20K iterations for Gaussian-Flow, STG, and SplineGS, respectively.
