Initialization varies by scene type: for real-world sequences, we initialize from SfM, as ground-truth geometry is unavailable, while for synthetic scenes, we initialize from the ground-truth point clouds. All methods use the same views, frames, and image resolution, and are evaluated at their respective final checkpoints.

    For STG, we use the without temporal opacity configuration defined in [LCLX24], in which each Gaussian’s opacity remains constant over time. This setting enables a direct comparison of the explicit Gaussian trajectories and motion. Allowing temporal opacity could otherwise represent motion implicitly by fading Gaussians in and out rather than explicitly moving them through space. Since trajectory-based methods model motion through explicit Gaussian trajectories, we retain constant opacity for a consistent comparison.

    Datasets. The Neural 3D Video (N3DV) dataset [LSZ∗22] comprises multi-view recordings of dynamic real-world scenes captured by 21 synchronized cameras at a resolution of 2704×2028 and 30 FPS. The six publicly available scenes contain approximately 10 seconds of video and feature complex non-rigid motion. Following prior work [WYF∗24, LDZY24], we downsample the images to 1352×1014.

    We evaluate our method also on the Google Immersive light field video dataset [BFO∗20] (flame scene), captured by an outward-facing rig of 46 synchronized fisheye cameras mounted on a hemispherical dome. We use the 45 calibrated cameras, holding out camera_0001 for evaluation and training on the remaining 44, over 50 frames. Following STG [LCLX24], the fisheye images are undistorted to a pinhole model and downsampled to 1280×960. The scene features a flamethrower whose rapidly evolving, semi-transparent flame contrasts with a largely static background.

    We additionally evaluate on two ray-traced synthetic dynamic scenes, checker sphere and soft contact, with known ground-truth geometry. Both scenes use the same camera rig of 20 static cameras spanning 90^∘ in azimuth across two rings, with 60 frames captured at 30 FPS. Images are rendered at 2704×2028 and downsampled to 1352×1014, with the central view held out for evaluation.

    checker sphere features a checker-patterned sphere moving laterally within a five-plane room, following two sinusoidal motion segments with different frequencies.

    soft contact contains 16 balls with different masses (m∝r³) undergoing collisions with an invisible box. Contacts are modeled using a penalty spring-damper over a finite 0.2 s interval, producing continuous velocities with large, localized accelerations. Both scenes are procedurally generated, providing per-frame ground-truth geometry for quantitative evaluation.

    Qualitative Evaluation. Figure  compares between reconstruction with uniform-width splines (middle) and our adaptive splines with non-uniform temporal support (right). The top and bottom rows show checker sphere and cook spinach, respectively. The zoomed-in regions demonstrate the benefit of adaptive temporal allocation: GaussianSpline better recovers the earth’s sphere-geometry, texture, and shadow (top), as well as the hands, fingers, and gripper (bottom), while uniform splines produce blurred or incomplete details.

    Figure 3 provides qualitative comparisons on five dynamic scenes (rows): two synthetic sequences with known ground truth 3D motion, checker sphere (frame 59) and soft contact (frame 42), and three real-world sequences: cook spinach (frame 47) and coffee martini (frame 0) from N3DV, and flames (frame 40) from Google Immersive. Columns show the ground truth, Gaussian-Flow, STG, SplineGS, and ours with zoom-ins.

    On the checker sphere, we focus on a rapidly horizontally moving sphere with a checker pattern. Gaussian-Flow blurs the quadrant boundaries, STG completely distorts the sphere and its shadow, while SplineGS blurs the facets and completely misses the red facet. In contrast, GaussianSpline preserves the quadrant boundaries, sphere geometry, and elliptical shadow, closely matching the ground truth.

    soft contact represents the most challenging case, with rapid collisions between small spheres. Gaussian-Flow fails to preserve the boundaries of closely colliding spheres, producing bleeding artifacts between them. STG collapses colliding spheres into unified smears, while SplineGS produces inter-sphere artifacts and blur. In contrast, GaussianSpline preserves the individual sphere boundaries and geometry.

    The cook spinach real-world scene contains regions with different motion patterns. The hand and grippers move continuously, while the dog remains largely static before turning its head in the second half of the sequence. Zoom-ins show that all other methods blur the dog’s fur, whereas ours produces the sharpest reconstruction. This improvement comes from our adaptive partition, which concentrates temporal resolution around the localized head motion rather than allocating capacity uniformly across the sequence.

    In coffee martini, all other methods fail to accurately reconstruct the round cap and its pointed tip, either blurring them (Gaussian-Flow and STG) or distorting their geometry (SplineGS). In contrast, ours is the only method that faithfully reconstructs both the cap’s rounded geometry and sharp tip.

    Finally, in flames, the rapidly evolving flame and the moving hand holding the can present the greatest challenges. Gaussian-Flow, STG, and SplineGS collapse the flame into a saturated, blurry blob and smear the hand and can, whereas our method preserves more of the flame’s tongue-like structure and reconstructs the hand and can with the highest sharpness (see zoom-ins).

    Quantitative Evaluation. Table 1 summarizes the quantitative evaluation of our method in comparison with the other three SOTA methods: Gaussian-Flow, STG, and SplineGS on the five sequences, i.e., checker sphere, soft contact, cook spinach, coffee martini, and flames.

    Every method is trained with its own default iteration budget: Gaussian-Flow and STG use 30k iterations on all five sequences; SplineGS uses 20k on checker sphere, cook spinach, coffee martini and flames, and 40k on soft contact; our method uses 20k on checker sphere, 40k on soft contact, and 30k on the three real captures.

    Our method achieves the highest PSNR on all three real-world scenes, with a margin of 3.46 dB on flames, as well as on the synthetic checker sphere scene, and ranks second on soft contact.

    For SSIM, ours achieves the highest score on both synthetic scenes, i.e., checker sphere, and soft contact, as well as on coffee martini and flames, and ranks second on cook spinach.

    For LPIPS, it achieves the best score on both synthetic scenes ( checker sphere and soft contact) and on flames, and ranks second on cook spinach and coffee martini, with only a small difference from the top-performing method in both cases.

    Note that while our method ranks first or second across all tests and metrics, its performance is notably stronger on the synthetic scenes. This is expected, as our method is specifically designed to handle highly non-uniform dynamics. Our synthetic scenes were deliberately designed to exhibit such heterogeneous temporal dynamics, providing a controlled setting in which to evaluate the benefits of adaptive temporal allocation.

    Ablation Study. Table 2 ablates the two design choices of our temporal parameterization: the spline order K and the placement of the joints. For each order, we compare uniform spacing with our learnable non-uniform spacing.

    Non-uniform spacing consistently outperforms (or matches) uniform spacing across all spline orders. Interestingly, increasing the spline order does not improve reconstruction quality. Instead, the lowest-order spline with non-uniform spacing achieves the best overall results, suggesting that adaptive joint placement is more important than spline order. Moreover, the performance gap between non-uniform and uniform spacing decreases as the spline order increases, as expected, since higher-order splines provide greater flexibility even with uniformly spaced joints.

    5 Conclusions and limitations.

    We presented GaussianSpline, a dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting method in which each Gaussian follows a piecewise cubic Bézier trajectory with a learnable, non-uniform temporal partition. With a fixed segment budget, trajectories allocate temporal resolution where motion is fast and use larger intervals where it is slow. A differentiable reflection-based G¹ constraint ensures smooth trajectories without restricting local motion speed, and the method integrates directly into the standard 3DGS optimization and densification pipeline without auxiliary networks.

    Our ablation study shows that non-uniform spacing consistently outperforms or matches uniform spacing across spline orders, while increasing the order provides little benefit (Table 2). GaussianSpline achieves the best overall results on checker sphere and leads PSNR on real N3DV and Google Immersive scenes.

    Our approach has several limitations. First, while our spline representation is effective for a wide range of motion, it can struggle when the dynamics become highly transient. In Soft Contact, for example, rapid collisions produce large accelerations over very short intervals that are difficult to capture accurately with a fixed, small number of spline segments. A promising direction is therefore adaptive segment insertion, guided by local curvature or reconstruction residuals, to dynamically increase temporal resolution where needed.

    Second, our trajectories are purely temporal and optimized independently for each Gaussian, without explicit spatial motion priors or coupling between neighboring primitives. As a result, rigid and articulated structures must be learned through individual Gaussian trajectories, while topological changes, such as the appearance and disappearance of geometry, are handled implicitly through opacity and densification.

    Finally, our evaluation is limited to the publicly available N3DV scenes, one Google Immersive scene, and two synthetic sequences, with each baseline trained using its default optimization schedule. Broader evaluation is desirable, but diverse multi-view dynamic datasets with dense temporal sampling and accurate ground truth remain scarce. As more public datasets become available, evaluation across a wider range of motions and scene dynamics will provide a more comprehensive assessment.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：联合学控制点与时间分段，用反射约束保证 G¹ 连续；低阶非均匀反而打败高阶均匀。

要点：

  • 每个高斯的运动用非均匀分段三次贝塞尔样条表示，控制点与「时间怎么分段」一起学：高动态区域分到更多时间容量，接近静止的区域保持紧凑轨迹
  • 相邻贝塞尔段之间用基于反射的约束强制 G¹ 连续，于是轨迹既全局平滑又保留非均匀参数化的灵活性，且全程可微
  • 消融给出一个反直觉结论：在所有样条阶数上，非均匀间距都优于或持平均匀间距，而提高阶数几乎没收益——最低阶 + 非均匀布局效果最好，说明「自适应节点放置」比「样条多灵活」更重要

为什么值得看：动态 3DGS 的容量一直花得很平均：静止的背景和飞速的手拿同样的时间分辨率。这条把时间预算变成可学的分配问题，和渲染里「把采样率放到变化的地方」是同一个直觉，但要落到可微训练里并不容易。

中文摘要：动态 4D 高斯泼溅通常用全局形变、固定阶数多项式或均匀参数化样条来描述每个高斯的运动，结果是时间容量被平均分配。GaussianSpline 改成自适应、非均匀的分段三次贝塞尔样条：它同时学习贝塞尔控制点与每个高斯轨迹的时间分段，把更多时间容量给高动态区域、让近静态区域保持紧凑，从而还原复杂快速运动。为了让整条轨迹既平滑又保留局部分辨能力，作者在相邻段之间用基于反射的约束强制 G¹ 连续，得到完全可微的运动表示。实验在 Neural 3D Video、Google Immersive 与合成场景上均显示高非均匀动态场景的重建质量提升，消融还表明「非均匀间距」比「更高阶样条」更关键。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-10-28

GaussianSpline: Adaptive Bézier Splines for Highly Dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

We present GaussianSpline, a dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models per-Gaussian motion using adaptive, non-uniform piecewise cubic Bézier splines. Unlike approaches based on global deformations, fixed-order polynomials, or uniformly parameterized splines, GaussianSpline jointly learns the Bézier control points and the temporal partition of each Gaussian’s trajectory. This adaptive representation allocates greater temporal capacity to highly dynamic regions while maintaining compact trajectories for near-static regions, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction of complex and rapidly changing motion. To jointly achieve globally smooth motion and local adaptivity, we enforce G¹ continuity between consecutive Bézier segments using a reflection-based constraint on their control points. This produces smooth, fully differentiable trajectories while preserving the flexibility of non-uniform temporal parameterization. Experiments on the Neural 3D Video benchmark, the Google Immersive dataset [BFO∗20], as well as on synthetic scenes demonstrate that GaussianSpline substantially improves reconstruction quality in scenes with highly non-uniform and challenging dynamics, while maintaining competitive performance on general dynamic scenes compared with state-of-the-art 4D Gaussian Splatting methods.

1 Introduction

Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from multi-view video is an emerging problem in computer graphics and vision, with applications in virtual reality, telepresence, and film production. The recent success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] has demonstrated that explicit, differentiable representations based on anisotropic Gaussians can achieve high-quality reconstruction and real-time rendering of static 3D scenes, motivating their extension to dynamic 4D content. However, moving from static to dynamic Gaussian Splatting introduces a fundamental challenge: the representation must simultaneously capture the spatial structure of the scene and the complex temporal evolution of potentially millions of Gaussians. In particular, accurately modeling highly dynamic regions requires flexible motion trajectories, while avoiding unnecessary temporal degrees of freedom in near-static regions.

Existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods typically rely on neural deformation fields or fixed spatial-temporal representations. Neural deformation approaches augment canonical Gaussians with MLP-based motion predictors [HSY∗23, YGZ∗24, LKL∗25], introducing additional per-Gaussian computation during rendering. Structured 4D approaches instead factorize spacetime using voxel grids or plane-based representations [XPL∗24, WYF∗24], but rely on predefined spatial-temporal resolutions. These representations therefore face a trade-off between computational or memory cost and reconstruction fidelity, particularly for scenes with highly non-uniform dynamics, where different regions require different levels of temporal modeling.

To avoid the overhead of neural deformation networks, explicit trajectory-based methods [LCLX24, LDZY24] model Gaussian motion using global parametric functions, such as polynomials or Fourier bases. More recently, piecewise spline representations have been explored for trajectory modeling, offering local control and compact parameterization [PBB∗25, YHOL25]. However, these approaches typically employ a uniform temporal parameterization across Gaussian trajectories, allocating the same temporal capacity regardless of the underlying motion. This limits their ability to efficiently capture the highly heterogeneous dynamics of real-world scenes, where different regions may exhibit slow, smooth motion or rapid and complex changes.

To address these limitations, we introduce GaussianSpline, a per-Gaussian trajectory-based 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that models motion using adaptive piecewise cubic Bézier splines with learnable, non-uniform temporal parameterization. Each Gaussian is assigned an independent trajectory initialized with a minimal number of spline segments. During optimization, the Bézier control points and segment intervals are jointly learned, allowing each trajectory to allocate temporal resolution according to its local motion. Rapidly changing motion is captured with finer temporal intervals, while slowly varying motion is represented with broader intervals, avoiding unnecessary temporal degrees of freedom and yielding a compact representation.

To ensure smooth motion across spline segments, we enforce G¹ continuity using a reflection-based control-point formulation with direction-locked tangents and learnable magnitude scaling. This yields smooth, fully differentiable trajectories while preserving local flexibility in motion speed and curvature. GaussianSpline introduces no auxiliary neural networks and integrates directly into the standard 3DGS optimization and densification pipeline, providing a compact and efficient representation for highly non-uniform dynamics.

Experiments on the Neural 3D Video benchmark, the Google Immersive dataset [BFO∗20], and synthetic scenes demonstrate that GaussianSpline significantly improves reconstruction quality for scenes with complex, highly non-uniform motion, while maintaining competitive performance on general dynamic scenes compared with state-of-the-art 4D Gaussian Splatting methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Learnable adaptive temporal parameterization. We jointly learn Bézier control points and non-uniform segment intervals to adapt temporal resolution to each Gaussian’s local motion.

  • •

    Smooth motion transitions. We introduce a reflection-based G¹ continuity constraint with learnable tangent magnitudes for smooth and flexible trajectory modeling.

  • •

    Efficient 4D representation. Our adaptive trajectories integrate seamlessly into the standard 3DGS framework, providing a compact and efficient representation of dynamic scenes.

    • 2 Related Work

    In the following we discuss recent related works on reconstruction of 3D dynamic scenes from multi-view video.

    Dynamic neural radiance fields. Dynamic extensions of NeRF [MST∗20] represent a scene as a time-varying radiance field, either conditioning the field directly on time [LSZ∗22] or warping each observation into a canonical frame through a learned deformation [PCPMMN21, PSH∗21], with later work improving robustness on casually captured monocular video [LGM∗23].

    These methods produce high-quality free-viewpoint video, but inherit NeRF’s volumetric ray marching: rendering a single pixel requires hundreds of network evaluations along a ray, so training takes hours to days and playback remains far from real time [LSZ∗22]. Grid- and plane-based factorizations [FKMW∗23] reduce this cost substantially, yet the scene stays an implicit field sampled at a fixed spatial-temporal resolution, so motion is never an explicit quantity that can be allocated where the scene actually moves.

    Dynamic 3DGS The emergence of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] has significantly advanced neural rendering by replacing implicit volumetric sampling with explicit, differentiable rasterization of anisotropic Gaussians. Building on this success, recent work has focused on extending 3DGS to dynamic scenes by modeling temporal deformation of Gaussian attributes [LKLR24, LCLX24, WYF∗24].

    Luiten et al. [LKLR24] directly optimize per-timestep Gaussian positions and rotations under local rigidity constraints, enabling dense 6-DOF tracking without an explicit deformation model. In contrast, MLP-based approaches learn continuous deformation fields in a canonical space. Deformable 3DGS [YGZ∗24] maps Gaussians from canonical to observation space via a neural deformation network, while GauFRe [LKL∗25] introduces a forward-warping formulation with an explicit static component to decouple moving and stationary regions. Although expressive, these methods require per-Gaussian MLP evaluations at render time, leading to significant computational overhead [LCLX24]. SC-GS [HSY∗23] mitigates this issue by combining deformation networks with sparse spatial constraints to reduce inference cost.

    Another line of work improves efficiency through structured spacetime factorization. Originating from NeRF-based representations such as K-Planes [FKMW∗23], these methods decompose the 4D domain into low-dimensional grids or plane representations. This idea has been adopted in 3DGS extensions such as 4DGS [WYF∗24] and 4K4D [XPL∗24], which model dynamic Gaussian attributes using structured grid-based embeddings. While computationally efficient, these methods are inherently limited by discrete resolution, leading to a trade-off between memory usage and reconstruction fidelity [WYF∗24, LCLX24].

    Explicit trajectory modeling. More recent methods abandon neural deformation networks in favor of explicit motion trajectories.

    Spacetime Gaussians (STG) [LCLX24] represent Gaussian motion using polynomial trajectories, improving temporal smoothness and efficiency. Gaussian-Flow [LDZY24] further extends this idea by combining polynomial and Fourier-based representations in a dual-domain formulation, eliminating the need for neural networks while improving expressiveness.

    However, fixed-degree polynomial models assign uniform temporal capacity to all Gaussians and may struggle to represent complex, non-linear motion patterns [LCLX24]. This limitation has motivated spline-based representations as a more flexible alternative.

    Spline-based formulations provide smooth and locally controllable representations of motion trajectories. SplineGS [PBB∗25] introduces piecewise cubic Hermite splines with motion-adaptive control-point pruning, while also reducing reliance on pre-computed camera parameters. However, its formulation targets monocular video sequences rather than multi-view dynamic 4D reconstruction, as considered in our work.

    More closely related to our setting, Yoon et al. [YHOL25] propose a method, also termed SplineGS, that employs NURBS to represent Gaussian trajectories as combinations of learned representative motion bases, improving temporal smoothness and spatial coherence in multi-view 4D dynamic scenes.

    However, both approaches rely on uniform spline parameterizations with fixed control-point distributions. In contrast, our approach jointly learns adaptive, locally refined control-point distributions based on motion complexity. This allows temporal capacity to be allocated where it is most needed, providing a more efficient representation of highly non-uniform motion and improving reconstruction quality with fewer Gaussian splats.

    3 Method

    We first review the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation and then extend it to dynamic scenes by assigning each Gaussian a learnable piecewise cubic Bézier trajectory. Unlike fixed temporal parameterizations, our formulation jointly optimizes the spline parameters and the temporal placement of control points, allowing each Gaussian to adapt its temporal resolution to the underlying motion (see Figure 1).

    3D Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussians, each parameterized by its position μ, covariance matrix Σ, opacity o, and view-dependent color c represented using spherical harmonics. Each Gaussian is defined as:

    G(x)=\exp(-1/2(x-μ)^⊤Σ⁻¹(x-μ)),

    		(1)

    with covariance parameterized as:

    Σ=RSS^⊤R^⊤,

    		(2)

    where S and R denote learnable scaling and rotation matrices, respectively.

    For rendering, Gaussians are projected onto the image plane and rasterized using differentiable alpha compositing, where Gaussians are accumulated in depth order:

    C=∑_i∈Ncᵢαᵢ∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-αⱼ),

    		(3)

    Starting from an SfM point cloud, all Gaussian parameters are optimized end-to-end through differentiable rendering, while adaptive density control dynamically splits, clones, and prunes Gaussians during training. We refer to [KKLD23] for a detailed description of the 3DGS formulation.

    4D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scenes. To reconstruct a dynamic 4D scene, we lift static Gaussian splats to a time-varying representation over a normalized timeline t∈[0,1]. In our formulation, only the Gaussian position μ(t) and rotation R(t) are time-dependent, while the scale s, opacity o, and color c are shared across all timestamps. The time-varying covariance is therefore given by:

    Σ(t)=R(t)SS^⊤R(t)^⊤,

    		(4)

    and the Gaussian at time t is obtained by evaluating Eq. (1) with μ(t) and Σ(t).

    This design reflects the observation that many real-world motions can be approximated as piecewise locally rigid deformations, with temporal variation primarily captured by translation and rotation. Restricting temporal variation to these degrees of freedom yields a compact yet flexible representation for dynamic scene modeling.

    Non-uniform Cubic Bézier Spline Trajectories To model the motion trajectory of a Gaussian splat over time, we use a piecewise cubic Bézier spline defined by K+1 joints {J₀,J₁,…,J_K}, 2K interior control points {C_k,0,C_k,1}ₖ₌₀^K-1, and K non-uniform interval widths {w₀,w₁,…,w_K-1}. Note that all spline parameters are differentiable and jointly optimized within our framework (see Figure 1 (middle)).

    To enforce monotonic partition of the entire temporal domain based on the learned adaptive non-uniform intervals we define:

    tₖ = ∑ⱼ₌₀ᵏ⁻¹w̃ⱼ,

    		(5)

    where w̃ₖ = (\exp(wₖ))/(∑ⱼ₌₀^K-1\exp(wⱼ)) is segment k’s interval width, tₖ is Jₖ’s timestamp, and the joints timestamp sequence 0=t₀

    To evaluate the trajectory at a global timestamp t∈[0,1], we locate the active segment k such that tₖ≤t

    μ(t)=(1-u)³Jₖ+3(1-u)²u C_k,0+3(1-u)u²C_k,1+u³Jₖ₊₁

    		(6)

    Learnable interval widths. Rather than using a uniform partition of the time domain [0,1], we parameterize each spline using learnable interval-width logits {w₀,w₁,…,w_K-1}, which define a non-uniform temporal segmentation. Initialized to zero, these logits yield a uniform partition at the beginning of training and are subsequently optimized jointly with the spline joints and control points.

    This allows each Gaussian to adapt its temporal resolution to the underlying motion, allocating finer intervals to rapidly changing motion and broader intervals to slowly varying motion, thereby improving reconstruction fidelity over an equivalent uniformly parameterized spline (see Figure 2).

    Learnable motion speed.C⁰ continuity is ensured by shared joints between adjacent segments. Rather than enforcing the stricter C¹ continuity, which couples both the direction and speed of motion across neighboring segments through continuity of the first derivative, we impose G¹ continuity. This preserves the tangent direction at each internal junction while allowing its magnitude to vary through a learnable positive scalar λₖ>0:

    C_k,0 = Jₖ + λₖ (Jₖ-C_k-1,1), k=1,…,K-1.

    		(7)

    The per-junction scales λₖ are initialized to 1, recovering C¹ continuity at the start of training, and are jointly optimized with the spline parameters. This relaxation allows motion speed to vary smoothly across segments while preserving kink-free trajectories and tangent continuity throughout the spline.

    Per-Gaussian polynomial rotations. To compute the per-Gaussian time-dependent rotation matrix R(t), we follow [LCLX24] and parameterize the raw quaternion as a first-degree polynomial, mapping its normalized form to the rotation group:

    q(t)=q₀+q₁t, R(t)=ℝ ((q(t))/(∥q(t)∥))

    		(8)

    where q₀ and q₁ denote the base quaternion and its linear velocity, respectively, and ℝ(·) is the standard mapping from unit quaternions to rotation matrices.

    Training. In each training iteration, we pick a random frame index from the training set, calculate its timestamp and select a subset of camera views captured at this timestamp. Then, every Gaussian is evaluated at this timestamp through its active segment (Eq. 6), and the photometric loss w.r.t. the selected views is back-propagated to the spline and Gaussian parameters.

    Together with the static initialization (all joints and control points set to x₀), this generates the Gaussian motion trajectories. Note that in near-static regions the gradients average or are near zero, leaving the trajectory approximately flat and consuming no temporal capacity.

    Furthermore, we apply Gaussians adaptive densification steps, i.e., split/clone/prune operations in early stage training iterations (as in [KKLD23]). Afterwards, the set of Gaussians remains fixed, and only the spline parameters (joints, control points, widths, G¹ scales) and the Gaussian attributes (opacity, color, covariance) are optimized.

    4 Experiments and Results

    Implementation Details. We train for 30k iterations using Adam on a single RTX 4090, optimizing an L₁ loss with a D-SSIM term (λ=0.2), SH degree 3, and batch size 2. Following 3DGS, the position learning rate decays exponentially from 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ to 1.6 × 10⁻⁶, while the learning rates for features, opacity, scaling, and rotation are 2.5 × 10⁻³, 5 × 10⁻², 5 × 10⁻³, and 10⁻³, respectively. The spline joint-width learning rate is set to 0.3× the position learning rate. Densification is performed every 100 iterations from iteration 500 to 9k, using a gradient threshold of 2 × 10⁻⁴ and a maximum of six densification events. Opacity is reset every 3k iterations, and Gaussians with opacity below 0.005 or scale above 0.1× the scene extent are pruned. Unless otherwise stated, we use K=3 spline segments with non-uniform joint spacing and G¹ continuity, initialized from approximately 8k COLMAP SfM points from a single frame on N3DV.

    Baselines We compare our method with three other SOTA methods: Gaussian-Flow [LDZY24], STG (Spacetime Gaussian)  [LCLX24] and SplineGS [YHOL25].

    We select these methods because they target the same multi-view dynamic 4D reconstruction setting and, like our approach, explicitly model Gaussian motion trajectories. They therefore provide relevant baselines for evaluating different approaches to temporal motion representation. STG represents Gaussian motion using polynomial trajectories, Gaussian-Flow combines polynomial and Fourier-based representations, and SplineGS employs piecewise cubic Hermite splines with motion-adaptive control-point pruning. These methods constitute the current set of SOTA approaches that explicitly model Gaussian motion trajectories in the multi-view dynamic 4D reconstruction setting, providing direct baselines for evaluating our adaptive temporal parameterization on highly non-uniform motion.

    In our experiments, we use the default training schedules of 30K, 30K, and 20K iterations for Gaussian-Flow, STG, and SplineGS, respectively. Initialization varies by scene type: for real-world sequences, we initialize from SfM, as ground-truth geometry is unavailable, while for synthetic scenes, we initialize from the ground-truth point clouds. All methods use the same views, frames, and image resolution, and are evaluated at their respective final checkpoints.

    For STG, we use the without temporal opacity configuration defined in [LCLX24], in which each Gaussian’s opacity remains constant over time. This setting enables a direct comparison of the explicit Gaussian trajectories and motion. Allowing temporal opacity could otherwise represent motion implicitly by fading Gaussians in and out rather than explicitly moving them through space. Since trajectory-based methods model motion through explicit Gaussian trajectories, we retain constant opacity for a consistent comparison.

    Datasets. The Neural 3D Video (N3DV) dataset [LSZ∗22] comprises multi-view recordings of dynamic real-world scenes captured by 21 synchronized cameras at a resolution of 2704×2028 and 30 FPS. The six publicly available scenes contain approximately 10 seconds of video and feature complex non-rigid motion. Following prior work [WYF∗24, LDZY24], we downsample the images to 1352×1014.

    We evaluate our method also on the Google Immersive light field video dataset [BFO∗20] (flame scene), captured by an outward-facing rig of 46 synchronized fisheye cameras mounted on a hemispherical dome. We use the 45 calibrated cameras, holding out camera_0001 for evaluation and training on the remaining 44, over 50 frames. Following STG [LCLX24], the fisheye images are undistorted to a pinhole model and downsampled to 1280×960. The scene features a flamethrower whose rapidly evolving, semi-transparent flame contrasts with a largely static background.

    We additionally evaluate on two ray-traced synthetic dynamic scenes, checker sphere and soft contact, with known ground-truth geometry. Both scenes use the same camera rig of 20 static cameras spanning 90^∘ in azimuth across two rings, with 60 frames captured at 30 FPS. Images are rendered at 2704×2028 and downsampled to 1352×1014, with the central view held out for evaluation.

    checker sphere features a checker-patterned sphere moving laterally within a five-plane room, following two sinusoidal motion segments with different frequencies.

    soft contact contains 16 balls with different masses (m∝r³) undergoing collisions with an invisible box. Contacts are modeled using a penalty spring-damper over a finite 0.2 s interval, producing continuous velocities with large, localized accelerations. Both scenes are procedurally generated, providing per-frame ground-truth geometry for quantitative evaluation.

    Qualitative Evaluation. Figure  compares between reconstruction with uniform-width splines (middle) and our adaptive splines with non-uniform temporal support (right). The top and bottom rows show checker sphere and cook spinach, respectively. The zoomed-in regions demonstrate the benefit of adaptive temporal allocation: GaussianSpline better recovers the earth’s sphere-geometry, texture, and shadow (top), as well as the hands, fingers, and gripper (bottom), while uniform splines produce blurred or incomplete details.

    Figure 3 provides qualitative comparisons on five dynamic scenes (rows): two synthetic sequences with known ground truth 3D motion, checker sphere (frame 59) and soft contact (frame 42), and three real-world sequences: cook spinach (frame 47) and coffee martini (frame 0) from N3DV, and flames (frame 40) from Google Immersive. Columns show the ground truth, Gaussian-Flow, STG, SplineGS, and ours with zoom-ins.

    On the checker sphere, we focus on a rapidly horizontally moving sphere with a checker pattern. Gaussian-Flow blurs the quadrant boundaries, STG completely distorts the sphere and its shadow, while SplineGS blurs the facets and completely misses the red facet. In contrast, GaussianSpline preserves the quadrant boundaries, sphere geometry, and elliptical shadow, closely matching the ground truth.

    soft contact represents the most challenging case, with rapid collisions between small spheres. Gaussian-Flow fails to preserve the boundaries of closely colliding spheres, producing bleeding artifacts between them. STG collapses colliding spheres into unified smears, while SplineGS produces inter-sphere artifacts and blur. In contrast, GaussianSpline preserves the individual sphere boundaries and geometry.

    The cook spinach real-world scene contains regions with different motion patterns. The hand and grippers move continuously, while the dog remains largely static before turning its head in the second half of the sequence. Zoom-ins show that all other methods blur the dog’s fur, whereas ours produces the sharpest reconstruction. This improvement comes from our adaptive partition, which concentrates temporal resolution around the localized head motion rather than allocating capacity uniformly across the sequence.

    In coffee martini, all other methods fail to accurately reconstruct the round cap and its pointed tip, either blurring them (Gaussian-Flow and STG) or distorting their geometry (SplineGS). In contrast, ours is the only method that faithfully reconstructs both the cap’s rounded geometry and sharp tip.

    Finally, in flames, the rapidly evolving flame and the moving hand holding the can present the greatest challenges. Gaussian-Flow, STG, and SplineGS collapse the flame into a saturated, blurry blob and smear the hand and can, whereas our method preserves more of the flame’s tongue-like structure and reconstructs the hand and can with the highest sharpness (see zoom-ins).

    Quantitative Evaluation. Table 1 summarizes the quantitative evaluation of our method in comparison with the other three SOTA methods: Gaussian-Flow, STG, and SplineGS on the five sequences, i.e., checker sphere, soft contact, cook spinach, coffee martini, and flames.

    Every method is trained with its own default iteration budget: Gaussian-Flow and STG use 30k iterations on all five sequences; SplineGS uses 20k on checker sphere, cook spinach, coffee martini and flames, and 40k on soft contact; our method uses 20k on checker sphere, 40k on soft contact, and 30k on the three real captures.

    Our method achieves the highest PSNR on all three real-world scenes, with a margin of 3.46 dB on flames, as well as on the synthetic checker sphere scene, and ranks second on soft contact.

    For SSIM, ours achieves the highest score on both synthetic scenes, i.e., checker sphere, and soft contact, as well as on coffee martini and flames, and ranks second on cook spinach.

    For LPIPS, it achieves the best score on both synthetic scenes ( checker sphere and soft contact) and on flames, and ranks second on cook spinach and coffee martini, with only a small difference from the top-performing method in both cases.

    Note that while our method ranks first or second across all tests and metrics, its performance is notably stronger on the synthetic scenes. This is expected, as our method is specifically designed to handle highly non-uniform dynamics. Our synthetic scenes were deliberately designed to exhibit such heterogeneous temporal dynamics, providing a controlled setting in which to evaluate the benefits of adaptive temporal allocation.

    Ablation Study. Table 2 ablates the two design choices of our temporal parameterization: the spline order K and the placement of the joints. For each order, we compare uniform spacing with our learnable non-uniform spacing.

    Non-uniform spacing consistently outperforms (or matches) uniform spacing across all spline orders. Interestingly, increasing the spline order does not improve reconstruction quality. Instead, the lowest-order spline with non-uniform spacing achieves the best overall results, suggesting that adaptive joint placement is more important than spline order. Moreover, the performance gap between non-uniform and uniform spacing decreases as the spline order increases, as expected, since higher-order splines provide greater flexibility even with uniformly spaced joints.

    5 Conclusions and limitations.

    We presented GaussianSpline, a dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting method in which each Gaussian follows a piecewise cubic Bézier trajectory with a learnable, non-uniform temporal partition. With a fixed segment budget, trajectories allocate temporal resolution where motion is fast and use larger intervals where it is slow. A differentiable reflection-based G¹ constraint ensures smooth trajectories without restricting local motion speed, and the method integrates directly into the standard 3DGS optimization and densification pipeline without auxiliary networks.

    Our ablation study shows that non-uniform spacing consistently outperforms or matches uniform spacing across spline orders, while increasing the order provides little benefit (Table 2). GaussianSpline achieves the best overall results on checker sphere and leads PSNR on real N3DV and Google Immersive scenes.

    Our approach has several limitations. First, while our spline representation is effective for a wide range of motion, it can struggle when the dynamics become highly transient. In Soft Contact, for example, rapid collisions produce large accelerations over very short intervals that are difficult to capture accurately with a fixed, small number of spline segments. A promising direction is therefore adaptive segment insertion, guided by local curvature or reconstruction residuals, to dynamically increase temporal resolution where needed.

    Second, our trajectories are purely temporal and optimized independently for each Gaussian, without explicit spatial motion priors or coupling between neighboring primitives. As a result, rigid and articulated structures must be learned through individual Gaussian trajectories, while topological changes, such as the appearance and disappearance of geometry, are handled implicitly through opacity and densification.

    Finally, our evaluation is limited to the publicly available N3DV scenes, one Google Immersive scene, and two synthetic sequences, with each baseline trained using its default optimization schedule. Broader evaluation is desirable, but diverse multi-view dynamic datasets with dense temporal sampling and accurate ground truth remain scarce. As more public datasets become available, evaluation across a wider range of motions and scene dynamics will provide a more comprehensive assessment.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 密度控制别再靠位置梯度猜：Birth-Death 用重建损失的一阶变分给「该在哪生高斯」打分，10 万预算下全面领先 ｜ Birth-Death Structural Learning for 3D Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：把生/死决策换成变分分数：冻结当前种群、挂辅助质量坐标、对多视图损失求导。

要点：

  • 现有克隆/分裂/剪枝靠位置梯度、不透明度、图像空间误差这类代理信号，它们并不直接回答「在哪加高斯最能降多视图损失、剪掉哪些损失最小」
  • 做法：每次结构更新前冻结当前高斯种群，为每个图元附加辅助质量坐标，对多视图损失关于这些坐标求导，得到一个一阶变分分数（作者证明它是 Splat Regression Model 一阶变分的坐标）
  • 在最紧的 100k 图元预算下，该控制器在三个数据集上全面优于 3DGS-MCMC、EDGS 与 ConeGS；因为渲染器、优化器、初始化与转移都保持不变，增益可归因于这一个统计量

为什么值得看：3DGS 的密度控制十几年都是启发式。把它写成「损失对结构变量的一阶变分」，等于给了生/死决策一个可微、可解释的依据；对要在固定显存预算里榨质量的引擎团队，这是最直接能换掉的一层。

中文摘要：3DGS 的质量与效率折中高度依赖自适应密度控制，但现有的克隆、分裂与剪枝规则都建立在代理信号上（位置梯度、不透明度、图像空间误差）。这些信号在实践中有效，却没有正面回答结构问题：新增高斯放在哪里最能降低多视图重建损失，哪些现有图元剪掉代价最小。作者提出 first-variation birth-death control：每次结构更新时冻结当前高斯种群，给每个图元附加辅助质量坐标，对多视图损失关于这些坐标求导，得到一阶变分分数；他们证明这个分数正是 Splat Regression Model 一阶变分的一个坐标，因而构成严格的局部下降代理——高分处作为新生位点，低分图元优先剪除。在 100k 图元的紧预算下，该方法在三个数据集上均优于 3DGS-MCMC、EDGS 与 ConeGS。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-25

本期推送：2026-10-28

Birth-Death Structural Learning for 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a standard representation for real-time novel-view synthesis. Yet, its quality–efficiency trade-off still relies heavily on adaptive density control. Existing cloning, splitting, and pruning rules use proxy signals, such as position gradients, opacity, and image-space error. Although effective in practice, these signals do not directly answer the structural question behind density control: where should new Gaussians be allocated to reduce the multi-view reconstruction loss, and which existing primitives can be pruned with minimal penalty. To address this, we propose first-variation birth–death control for 3DGS, a principled approach that replaces heuristic structural decisions with a variational score derived from the reconstruction loss. At each structural update, we freeze the current Gaussian population, attach auxiliary mass coordinates to each primitive, and differentiate the multiview loss with respect to these coordinates. We demonstrate that this score is a coordinate of the first variation of the Splat Regression Model, giving a rigorous local descent surrogate for birth-death moves: high-score Gaussians are selected as birth sites, while low-score, low-opacity Gaussians are selected for removal. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, integrating this score into 3DGS-MCMC yields state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and outperforms existing methods, delivering the most significant gains under tight Gaussian budgets. Ultimately, our work provides compelling evidence that gradient-based variational metrics offer a principled alternative to proxy heuristics in 3DGS.

1 Introduction

High-quality photorealistic scene modeling from images is a fundamental task in computer vision and graphics, with applications spanning immersive rendering, robotics, digital humans, and geometric reconstruction [4, 38]. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [15] has emerged as a fast explicit radiance-field representation that models scenes as anisotropic Gaussian primitives and renders them by differentiable rasterization. Its speed and explicitness have led to rapid extensions in dynamic rendering, anti-aliasing, generative 3D content, and SLAM [32, 34, 28, 24, 37, 27, 14, 9, 11].

Despite this progress, 3DGS training still relies on heuristic adaptive density control (ADC). Training a 3DGS model interleaves two distinct optimization mechanisms. Continuous optimization adjusts the parameters (position, covariance, color) of existing Gaussians to fit the image data. Structural control, meanwhile, changes the population itself by creating or destroying primitives. In standard 3DGS, these population updates rely on indirect proxies: high accumulated position gradients trigger cloning or splitting, while low opacity triggers pruning [15]. These signals correlate with regions needing refinement, but they do not directly measure how a discrete birth or death event affects the photometric objective. As a result, primitive placement is sensitive to hand-tuned thresholds. The model frequently misses high-frequency details, creates floaters or needle-like artifacts, and wastes redundant Gaussians to regions that are already well covered [25, 36, 10]. The cost is most visible under tight primitive budgets, where redundant placement directly competes with missing detail [2, 19, 17].

While recent methods improve these signals through pixel-aware gradients, error-guided insertion, and budgeted densification [36, 2, 22], they remain mathematically decoupled from the empirical risk. The Splat Regression Model (SRM) framework [6] provides a rigorous lens to understand this limitation: it models splat fitting as optimization over mixing measures structured by Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry. Under this view, standard 3DGS successfully performs continuous transport (moving Gaussian parameters via gradient descent), but completely ignores the WFR mass component when deciding where to spawn or destroy primitives. Because disconnected heuristics govern these mass perturbations, a fundamental allocation problem remains unresolved: How can we identify which discrete primitives to kill, and where to spawn new ones guided by a first-order descent surrogate for the multiview reconstruction loss?

Contributions.

In this work, we propose reframing 3DGS structural updates from a collection of proxy heuristics into a formal component of empirical risk minimization. Motivated by the WFR geometry, we formulate structural control as a finite-particle birth–death process. At each control step, we freeze the continuous scene parameters and attach an auxiliary mass coordinate to each Gaussian. Differentiating the multiview reconstruction risk with respect to these coordinates yields a per-primitive first-variation score. This score is the negative directional derivative of the objective, evaluated at the frozen parameter state. It mathematically predicts the first-order descent achieved by applying an infinitesimal mass perturbation to that specific primitive. We then use score gaps to guide the birth-death process: capacity is reclaimed by killing low-score, low-opacity Gaussians and reborn at high-score sites. This provides a criterion for birth–death decisions. Because finite structural updates lack strict continuous descent guarantees, we execute them via the state transitions of 3DGS-MCMC [17]. This work bridges the theoretical view of splat fitting as mixing-measure optimization with practical 3DGS training. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We replace heuristic proxy signals with a first-variation score for 3DGS structural control, directly tying primitive allocation to the multiview empirical risk.

  • •

    We theoretically justify this framework by discretizing the SRM first variation, and by proving that restricting death to low-opacity Gaussians bounds the immediate rendering disturbance.

  • •

    We demonstrate that variational allocation outperforms proxy heuristics when representation capacity is constrained. Across standard benchmark datasets, our method achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality against matched 3DGS-MCMC and recent budget-aware baselines.

    • 1.1 Related Work

    Adaptive density control and densification.

    The original 3DGS framework couples continuous photometric optimization with adaptive density control: accumulated position-gradient statistics trigger cloning or splitting, while low opacity triggers pruning [15]. A massive body of recent work improves this controller. Revising Densification and Pixel-GS replace or reweight the growth criterion using pixel-level error or pixel-aware gradients [25, 36], while AbsGS and Improved ADC refine gradient aggregation, threshold schedules, and pruning rules [33, 10]. Other methods manage the primitive budget explicitly through resource-aware schedules, progressive propagation, or high-error insertion rules [22, 5, 2]. While these methods engineer better proxy signals or insertion heuristics, our work diverges fundamentally: we abandon proxies in favor of the structural derivative. By explicitly differentiating the multiview risk with respect to Gaussian mass, we formalize capacity allocation as a direct objective rather than a heuristic byproduct.

    Relocation, MCMC, and compact representations.

    Several methods improve 3DGS efficiency by pruning redundant Gaussians or compressing attributes post-training [8, 12, 23, 20], while others avoid incremental growth entirely by relying on dense initializations [19]. The closest backend to our method is 3DGS-MCMC [17], which rewrites densification and pruning as relocation/addition transitions. Our approach adopts these discrete transitions from 3DGS-MCMC, but completely replaces its structural selection statistic. Rather than relying on opacity-sampling to blindly select relocation targets, we use our first-variation score to predict where released capacity is most likely to reduce the reconstruction risk under a local first-order model.

    Variational splat models and first variation.

    The Splat Regression Model (SRM) formalizes splat models as optimization over mixing measures, deriving Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao gradient flows and explicit first-variation characterizations of mass rescaling [6]; related birth–death discretizations also appear in sampling theory [21]. However, while SRM establishes the continuous, measure-level WFR geometry, it does not prescribe a finite, budget-constrained training algorithm for discrete rasterizers. Our contribution bridges this gap: we derive a concrete, renderer-level mass-coordinate score and a finite score-gap birth–death controller, making this continuous variational geometry actionable for practical 3DGS training.

    2 Background

    We fix notation for the 3DGS renderer and the 3DGS-MCMC relocation backend. The SRM first-variation viewpoint is recalled at the end of the section.

    3D Gaussian Splatting.

    At iteration t, a scene is represented by a finite population Gₜ={gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^Mₜ, where

    gᵢ=(μᵢ,sᵢ,Rᵢ,αᵢ,cᵢ), μᵢ∈ℝ³, sᵢ∈ℝ_>0³, Rᵢ∈SO(3), αᵢ∈(0,1).

    Here sᵢ and Rᵢ determine the anisotropic covariance Σᵢ=RᵢDiag(sᵢ²)Rᵢ^⊤, and cᵢ denotes the view-dependent color parameters. For a fixed training view n and pixel x, let Gᵢ(x) be the projected Gaussian footprint, aᵢ(x):=αᵢGᵢ(x), and let j\precₙi denote front-to-back ordering along the ray. Suppressing the view index on projected footprints and transmittances, the rendered color is

    Îₙ(x)=∑ᵢ₌₁^MₜTᵢ(x) aᵢ(x) cᵢ(dₙ), Tᵢ(x):=∏_j\precₙi(1-aⱼ(x)).

    		(1)

    We write Îₙ=Φ(Gₜ,n) for the rasterized image. At training iteration t, a view nₜ is sampled and the photometric loss is L̂_img⁽ᵗ⁾=ℓ₁(Φ(Gₜ,nₜ),I_nₜ). The 3DGS-MCMC backend additionally uses opacity and scale regularizers to encourage unused Gaussians to disappear; we retain these terms in training but do not expand them here, since our score pass is defined from the image objective in Section 3.

    3DGS-MCMC: Markov view and relocation/addition operations.

    3DGS-MCMC [17] interprets the Gaussian population as a sample state of a Markov chain. For a regularized training objective L, the formal target density is

    p_β(G)=Z_β⁻¹\exp (-βL(G)),

    where Z_β is the normalizing constant and β>0 is an inverse temperature. Under this view, the usual gradient update is interpreted as the zero-noise limit of an SGLD step. For a parameter block θ,

    θ←θ-η ∇̂_θL(G)+σ_θ(G) ξ, ξ∼ℕ(0,I),

    where ∇̂ is a stochastic gradient and σ_θ(G) is the exploration scale. In the original 3DGS-MCMC implementation, this noise is applied to Gaussian centers, with scale depending on the current Gaussian state.

    The structural mechanism of 3DGS-MCMC realizes densification and pruning through deterministic state transitions. Let Dₜ:={i:αᵢ≤α_death} and Aₜ:={i:αᵢ>α_death} denote the candidate dead and live pools, respectively. To reallocate capacity, rⱼ recycled slots from Dₜ (or fresh slots during addition) are assigned to a target Gaussian j, yielding Nⱼ:=rⱼ+1 co-located copies parameterized as:

    μ_j,ℓ^′=μⱼ, α_j,ℓ^′=1-(1-αⱼ)^1/Nⱼ, Σ_j,ℓ^′=γ(Nⱼ,αⱼ) Σⱼ,

    		(2)

    for ℓ=1,…,Nⱼ, with color and orientation inherited from the target. The closed-form scalar γ(Nⱼ,αⱼ) rescales the covariance such that the aggregate opacity footprint of the co-located cluster matches that of the original primitive, minimizing instantaneous rendering perturbations.

    In our framework, we decouple structural decision-making from physical execution: we adopt these closed-form transitions strictly as a conservative realization backend, while entirely replacing the heuristic opacity proposals with our objective-derived first-variation score.

    SRM viewpoint: splat measures and first variation.

    Splat Regression Models (SRM) [6] formalize “splat” representations as optimization over mixing measures. Let ρ be a centered isotropic “mother” density on ℝ³. For (A,b)∈ℝ^3×3×ℝ³, define the transformed splat ρ_A,b:=(A(·)+b)_#ρ. A (vector-valued) splat measure μ over weights and splat parameters induces the mixture model

    f_μ(x):=∫v ρ_A,b(x) μ(dv,dA,db), x∈ℝ³.

    SRM endows the space of such measures with a Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao (WFR) geometry in which gradient flow decomposes into a transport component (moving A,b) and a mass component (rescaling v). The first-order object governing the mass component is the first variation of the data-fit functional. Inspired by the SRM first-variation view of splat measures, our score pass instantiates a finite-dimensional coordinate of this first-variation field for the specific mass direction that scales opacities (see Section 3.1).

    3 Method

    3.1 First-Variation Score from Splat Measures

    Let F_D(G):=N⁻¹∑ₙ₌₁^Nℓ_img(Φ(G,n),Iₙ) denote the full multiview empirical risk. The Splat Regression Model (SRM) shows that optimizing a splat-based representation involves two distinct operations: moving parameters (transport) and changing primitive weights (mass). Standard 3DGS handles transport natively via continuous gradient descent. To handle mass, we evaluate how infinitesimal changes to a Gaussian’s weight affect the empirical risk.

    At a controller step t, we freeze the current population Gₜ={gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^Mₜ and attach an auxiliary mass coordinates mᵢ for each Gaussian, initialized to the all-ones vector 1. We define a mass-perturbed population Gₜᵐ by scaling the opacity contribution of each Gaussian i by mᵢ, i.e., aᵢ(x)↦mᵢaᵢ(x). We estimate the minibatch multiview risk and its negative mass derivative from a batch of views Bₜ:

    F̂ₜ(m):=1/B∑_n∈Bₜℓ_img (Φ(Gₜᵐ,n),Iₙ), (qₜ)ᵢ:=-.(∂F̂ₜ(m))/(∂mᵢ)|ₘ₌₁.

    		(3)

    All scene parameters are detached during this computation, so a single backward pass returns the score vector qₜ. The sign of (qₜ)ᵢ gives the local mass interpretation: increasing mᵢ decreases the empirical risk by ε(qₜ)ᵢ+o(ε).

    Fix a view (Iₙ,πₙ). Under mass coordinates m, the renderer induces a map f_n,t(·;m):=Φ(Gₜᵐ,πₙ)∈L²(Ω;ℝ³). Define the per-view functional Fₙ(f):=ℓ_img(f,Iₙ). Following SRM, the relevant first-order object governing mass creation is the first variation.

    Definition 1(First variation on images [6, Def. 2]).

    Let F:L²(Ω;ℝ³)→ℝ be Fréchet differentiable at f. Its first variation δF[f]∈L²(Ω;ℝ³) is the Riesz representative of the differential: for all ξ∈L²(Ω;ℝ³),

    .d/dεF(f+εξ)|_ε=0=∫_Ω⟨ξ(x), δF[f](x)⟩ dx.

    Remark 1(On differentiability and discretization).

    Definition 1 assumes Fréchet differentiability. The practical image loss contains nonsmooth components such as ℓ₁ and differentiable image-structure terms such as DSSIM. The implemented renderer is evaluated on a pixel grid, in which case the integrals below are finite sums over pixels.

    Applying the chain rule to Fₙ∘f_n,t yields a coordinate expression for the score.

    Proposition 1(Score as a first-variation coordinate).

    Assume each Fₙ admits a first variation and f_n,t(·;m) is differentiable in m at m=1. Then the score in (3) satisfies

    (qₜ)ᵢ=-1/B∑_n∈Bₜ∫_Ω⟨δFₙ [f_n,t(·;1)](x), .(∂f_n,t(x;m))/(∂mᵢ)|ₘ₌₁⟩ dx.

    The proof is provided in Appendix A. Proposition 1 connects the SRM first-variation viewpoint to renderer-level mass coordinates. Intuitively, the integral pairs the image-space loss gradient with the image change induced by rescaling the i-th Gaussian. Ranking Gaussians by (qₜ)ᵢ therefore orders the predicted loss decrease for equal infinitesimal mass increments at the frozen state. Unlike accumulated position gradients or plain opacity [15, 17], the score directly evaluates this mass direction, providing an objective-derived criterion for allocating capacity.

    In the specific context of 3DGS alpha-compositing [39], applying the chain rule to the renderer gives a concrete pixel-level expression for this score:

    (qₜ)ᵢ=-1/B∑_n∈Bₜ∑ₓ⟨rₙ(x), Tᵢ(x)aᵢ(x)(cᵢ(dₙ)-Îᵢᵇᵃᶜᵏ(x))⟩,

    		(4)

    where Îᵢᵇᵃᶜᵏ(x) is the accumulated background color and rₙ(x) is the image-space loss gradient. Equation (4) gives the geometric intuition: a Gaussian receives a high score when its footprint is visible, meaning Tᵢ(x)aᵢ(x) is large; when its color differs from the accumulated background behind it; and when the resulting color change aligns with the negative loss gradient -rₙ(x).

    3.2 Birth–Death Allocation via Score Gaps

    The score qₜ provides a continuous mass derivative, but structural control requires a discrete allocation decision. We model reclaiming capacity from death coordinates D and assigning it to birth coordinates J_1:Rₜ through the following balanced mass perturbation:

    δm(J,D)=κ(∑ᵣ₌₁^Rₜe_Jᵣ-∑_i∈Deᵢ), |D|=Rₜ.

    Here eᵢ is the i-th coordinate vector and κ>0 sets the scale of the mass perturbation. The following bound identifies its first-order loss term under a smooth local model.

    Proposition 2(Local descent upper bound under smoothness).

    If F(m):=F̂ₜ(m) is Lₛₘ-smooth on a neighbourhood containing the segment {1+τδm:τ∈[0,1]}, then

    F(1+δm)≤F(1)-⟨qₜ,δm⟩+Lₛₘ/2∥δm∥₂².

    Proposition 2 (proof in Appendix A) identifies the score gap as the first-order predicted loss decrease:

    ⟨qₜ,δm⟩=κ(∑ᵣ₌₁^Rₜ(qₜ)_Jᵣ-∑_i∈D(qₜ)ᵢ).

    		(5)

    Proposition 3(Bounded influence of low-opacity Gaussians).

    Fix a view n and let Îₙ be the rendered image from (1). Let Îₙ⁽⁻ⁱ⁾ be the image obtained by setting αᵢ=0 while keeping all other Gaussians unchanged. Assume rendered colors and the terminal background color are bounded in [0,1]³, and define the per-image mean absolute error

    ∥J∥_1,mean:=(1)/(|Ωₚᵢₓ|)∑_x∈Ωₚᵢₓ1/3∥J(x)∥₁.

    Then

    ∥Îₙ-Îₙ⁽⁻ⁱ⁾∥_1,mean≤αᵢ.

    Consequently, if ℓ_img(·,Iₙ) is L_ℓ-Lipschitz with respect to ∥·∥_1,mean in a neighbourhood of Îₙ, then

    |ℓ_img(Îₙ,Iₙ)-ℓ_img(Îₙ⁽⁻ⁱ⁾,Iₙ)|≤L_ℓ αᵢ.

    Proposition 3 (proof in Appendix A) bounds the disturbance from an individual low-opacity removal. This motivates the candidate pool ℙₜ:={i:αᵢ≤α_death}. Within this pool, smaller scores indicate lower retention value under the local mass model.

    The final variational controller merges this continuous ideal with discrete constraints. We stabilize multi-view stochasticity using an exponentially moving averaged (EMA) score q̄ₜ. The death set Dₜ⁻ selects the Rₜ Gaussians with the lowest scores (qₜ)ᵢwithin the pool ℙₜ. The birth multiset J_1:Rₜ is sampled from live Gaussians proportional to their positive scores [(q̄ₜ)ᵢ]₊.

    3.3 Discrete Realization by the 3DGS-MCMC Kernels

    Our variational policy dictates which primitives are retired and where new capacity is sampled to approximate first-order loss descent. Once the death set Dₜ⁻ is selected from the lowest-scoring candidates in ℙₜ and the birth multiset J_1:Rₜ is sampled proportional to positive scores [(q̄ₜ)ᵢ]₊, the discrete state transition is realized by the footprint-preserving relocation kernel:

    Gₜ₊=K_reloc(Gₜ; Dₜ⁻, J_1:Rₜ).

    		(6)

    Each recycled slot in Dₜ⁻ is transferred to a sampled birth site in J_1:Rₜ, where the closed-form opacity and covariance corrections (2) preserve the aggregate optical footprint to minimize instantaneous rendering disturbance. When the population is below the prescribed cap, the addition kernel directly activates new slots at sites sampled from [(q̄ₜ)ᵢ]₊ without requiring paired deaths.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments test a single claim: the first variation of the multiview reconstruction risk is a better birth–death signal than opacity or gradient proxies. We fix the renderer, optimizer, and MCMC transitions to isolate this statistic. This allows us to answer three direct questions: Does the variational controller improve reconstruction quality at the same primitive budgets? Is the gain explicitly caused by the WFR score? And does the allocation behavior align with local descent predictions?

    4.1 Experimental setup

    Datasets and metrics.

    We evaluate on Mip-NeRF360 [3], Tanks & Temples [18], and DeepBlending [13]. Our main fixed-budget Mip-NeRF360 averages use seven scenes: Bicycle, Garden, Stump, Room, Counter, Kitchen, and Bonsai; Flowers and Treehill are excluded. Tanks & Temples uses Truck and Train, and DeepBlending uses Dr. Johnson and Playroom. We report PSNR, SSIM [30], and LPIPS [35] on held-out test views. Per-scene results are in Appendix H; compact-model comparisons use all nine Mip-NeRF360 scenes.

    Budgeted evaluation.

    We evaluate under matched Gaussian caps K∈{100k,500k,1M}. The fixed-budget setting isolates the structural decision. Every birth consumes finite capacity. Poor allocation cannot be hidden by unbounded growth.

    Baselines and protocol.

    We compare against 3DGS [15] with SfM initialization, Improved ADC [10], 3DGS-MCMC [17] with SfM initialization, EDGS [19], and ConeGS [2]. Rows marked † use published fixed-budget benchmark numbers from ConeGS under the same dataset split and Gaussian cap. Claims about the effect of the proposed controller are based on matched 3DGS-MCMC reruns: the renderer, optimizer, initialization, cap, and transition maps remain identical. Only the structural selection statistic changes.

    Implementation.

    Our implementation builds on 3DGS-MCMC. We keep the renderer, training loss, optimizer, relocation/addition kernels, and event schedule unchanged. All methods are trained for 30,000 iterations. Hyperparameters, hardware, and timing details are in Appendix B.

    4.2 Fixed-budget reconstruction quality

    Table 1 establishes fixed-budget reconstruction quality. At the tightest 100k cap, our controller outperforms 3DGS-MCMC baseline, EDGS, and ConeGS across all three datasets. This severe scarcity highlights our advantage: reallocating via WFR score derivatives yields the largest impact.

    At 500k and 1M, our method has the highest PSNR across all three datasets in Table 1. SSIM and LPIPS are metric-dependent: on Mip-NeRF360 at 500k, ConeGS has slightly higher SSIM (0.870 vs. 0.869), and competing methods achieve lower LPIPS at both larger caps. These results support the benefit of score-guided allocation under tight budgets without implying uniform superiority. Figure 3 shows the matched PSNR–budget frontier. Full metrics, random-initialization results, and runtimes are in Appendix I.
