要点：

  • 现有克隆/分裂/剪枝靠位置梯度、不透明度、图像空间误差这类代理信号，它们并不直接回答「在哪加高斯最能降多视图损失、剪掉哪些损失最小」
  • 做法：每次结构更新前冻结当前高斯种群，为每个图元附加辅助质量坐标，对多视图损失关于这些坐标求导，得到一个一阶变分分数（作者证明它是 Splat Regression Model 一阶变分的坐标）
  • 在最紧的 100k 图元预算下，该控制器在三个数据集上全面优于 3DGS-MCMC、EDGS 与 ConeGS；因为渲染器、优化器、初始化与转移都保持不变，增益可归因于这一个统计量

为什么值得看：3DGS 的密度控制十几年都是启发式。把它写成「损失对结构变量的一阶变分」，等于给了生/死决策一个可微、可解释的依据；对要在固定显存预算里榨质量的引擎团队，这是最直接能换掉的一层。

中文摘要：3DGS 的质量与效率折中高度依赖自适应密度控制，但现有的克隆、分裂与剪枝规则都建立在代理信号上（位置梯度、不透明度、图像空间误差）。这些信号在实践中有效，却没有正面回答结构问题：新增高斯放在哪里最能降低多视图重建损失，哪些现有图元剪掉代价最小。作者提出 first-variation birth-death control：每次结构更新时冻结当前高斯种群，给每个图元附加辅助质量坐标，对多视图损失关于这些坐标求导，得到一阶变分分数；他们证明这个分数正是 Splat Regression Model 一阶变分的一个坐标，因而构成严格的局部下降代理——高分处作为新生位点，低分图元优先剪除。在 100k 图元的紧预算下，该方法在三个数据集上均优于 3DGS-MCMC、EDGS 与 ConeGS。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-25

本期推送：2026-10-28

Birth-Death Structural Learning for 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a standard representation for real-time novel-view synthesis. Yet, its quality–efficiency trade-off still relies heavily on adaptive density control. Existing cloning, splitting, and pruning rules use proxy signals, such as position gradients, opacity, and image-space error. Although effective in practice, these signals do not directly answer the structural question behind density control: where should new Gaussians be allocated to reduce the multi-view reconstruction loss, and which existing primitives can be pruned with minimal penalty. To address this, we propose first-variation birth–death control for 3DGS, a principled approach that replaces heuristic structural decisions with a variational score derived from the reconstruction loss. At each structural update, we freeze the current Gaussian population, attach auxiliary mass coordinates to each primitive, and differentiate the multiview loss with respect to these coordinates. We demonstrate that this score is a coordinate of the first variation of the Splat Regression Model, giving a rigorous local descent surrogate for birth-death moves: high-score Gaussians are selected as birth sites, while low-score, low-opacity Gaussians are selected for removal. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, integrating this score into 3DGS-MCMC yields state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and outperforms existing methods, delivering the most significant gains under tight Gaussian budgets. Ultimately, our work provides compelling evidence that gradient-based variational metrics offer a principled alternative to proxy heuristics in 3DGS.

1 Introduction

High-quality photorealistic scene modeling from images is a fundamental task in computer vision and graphics, with applications spanning immersive rendering, robotics, digital humans, and geometric reconstruction [4, 38]. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [15] has emerged as a fast explicit radiance-field representation that models scenes as anisotropic Gaussian primitives and renders them by differentiable rasterization. Its speed and explicitness have led to rapid extensions in dynamic rendering, anti-aliasing, generative 3D content, and SLAM [32, 34, 28, 24, 37, 27, 14, 9, 11].

Despite this progress, 3DGS training still relies on heuristic adaptive density control (ADC). Training a 3DGS model interleaves two distinct optimization mechanisms. Continuous optimization adjusts the parameters (position, covariance, color) of existing Gaussians to fit the image data. Structural control, meanwhile, changes the population itself by creating or destroying primitives. In standard 3DGS, these population updates rely on indirect proxies: high accumulated position gradients trigger cloning or splitting, while low opacity triggers pruning [15]. These signals correlate with regions needing refinement, but they do not directly measure how a discrete birth or death event affects the photometric objective. As a result, primitive placement is sensitive to hand-tuned thresholds. The model frequently misses high-frequency details, creates floaters or needle-like artifacts, and wastes redundant Gaussians to regions that are already well covered [25, 36, 10]. The cost is most visible under tight primitive budgets, where redundant placement directly competes with missing detail [2, 19, 17].

While recent methods improve these signals through pixel-aware gradients, error-guided insertion, and budgeted densification [36, 2, 22], they remain mathematically decoupled from the empirical risk. The Splat Regression Model (SRM) framework [6] provides a rigorous lens to understand this limitation: it models splat fitting as optimization over mixing measures structured by Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry. Under this view, standard 3DGS successfully performs continuous transport (moving Gaussian parameters via gradient descent), but completely ignores the WFR mass component when deciding where to spawn or destroy primitives. Because disconnected heuristics govern these mass perturbations, a fundamental allocation problem remains unresolved: How can we identify which discrete primitives to kill, and where to spawn new ones guided by a first-order descent surrogate for the multiview reconstruction loss?

Contributions.

In this work, we propose reframing 3DGS structural updates from a collection of proxy heuristics into a formal component of empirical risk minimization. Motivated by the WFR geometry, we formulate structural control as a finite-particle birth–death process. At each control step, we freeze the continuous scene parameters and attach an auxiliary mass coordinate to each Gaussian. Differentiating the multiview reconstruction risk with respect to these coordinates yields a per-primitive first-variation score. This score is the negative directional derivative of the objective, evaluated at the frozen parameter state. It mathematically predicts the first-order descent achieved by applying an infinitesimal mass perturbation to that specific primitive. We then use score gaps to guide the birth-death process: capacity is reclaimed by killing low-score, low-opacity Gaussians and reborn at high-score sites. This provides a criterion for birth–death decisions. Because finite structural updates lack strict continuous descent guarantees, we execute them via the state transitions of 3DGS-MCMC [17]. This work bridges the theoretical view of splat fitting as mixing-measure optimization with practical 3DGS training. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We replace heuristic proxy signals with a first-variation score for 3DGS structural control, directly tying primitive allocation to the multiview empirical risk.

  • •

    We theoretically justify this framework by discretizing the SRM first variation, and by proving that restricting death to low-opacity Gaussians bounds the immediate rendering disturbance.

  • •

    We demonstrate that variational allocation outperforms proxy heuristics when representation capacity is constrained. Across standard benchmark datasets, our method achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality against matched 3DGS-MCMC and recent budget-aware baselines.

    • 1.1 Related Work

    Adaptive density control and densification.

    The original 3DGS framework couples continuous photometric optimization with adaptive density control: accumulated position-gradient statistics trigger cloning or splitting, while low opacity triggers pruning [15]. A massive body of recent work improves this controller. Revising Densification and Pixel-GS replace or reweight the growth criterion using pixel-level error or pixel-aware gradients [25, 36], while AbsGS and Improved ADC refine gradient aggregation, threshold schedules, and pruning rules [33, 10]. Other methods manage the primitive budget explicitly through resource-aware schedules, progressive propagation, or high-error insertion rules [22, 5, 2]. While these methods engineer better proxy signals or insertion heuristics, our work diverges fundamentally: we abandon proxies in favor of the structural derivative. By explicitly differentiating the multiview risk with respect to Gaussian mass, we formalize capacity allocation as a direct objective rather than a heuristic byproduct.

    Relocation, MCMC, and compact representations.

    Several methods improve 3DGS efficiency by pruning redundant Gaussians or compressing attributes post-training [8, 12, 23, 20], while others avoid incremental growth entirely by relying on dense initializations [19]. The closest backend to our method is 3DGS-MCMC [17], which rewrites densification and pruning as relocation/addition transitions. Our approach adopts these discrete transitions from 3DGS-MCMC, but completely replaces its structural selection statistic. Rather than relying on opacity-sampling to blindly select relocation targets, we use our first-variation score to predict where released capacity is most likely to reduce the reconstruction risk under a local first-order model.

    Variational splat models and first variation.

    The Splat Regression Model (SRM) formalizes splat models as optimization over mixing measures, deriving Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao gradient flows and explicit first-variation characterizations of mass rescaling [6]; related birth–death discretizations also appear in sampling theory [21]. However, while SRM establishes the continuous, measure-level WFR geometry, it does not prescribe a finite, budget-constrained training algorithm for discrete rasterizers. Our contribution bridges this gap: we derive a concrete, renderer-level mass-coordinate score and a finite score-gap birth–death controller, making this continuous variational geometry actionable for practical 3DGS training.

    2 Background

    We fix notation for the 3DGS renderer and the 3DGS-MCMC relocation backend. The SRM first-variation viewpoint is recalled at the end of the section.

    3D Gaussian Splatting.

    At iteration t, a scene is represented by a finite population Gₜ={gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^Mₜ, where

    gᵢ=(μᵢ,sᵢ,Rᵢ,αᵢ,cᵢ), μᵢ∈ℝ³, sᵢ∈ℝ_>0³, Rᵢ∈SO(3), αᵢ∈(0,1).

    Here sᵢ and Rᵢ determine the anisotropic covariance Σᵢ=RᵢDiag(sᵢ²)Rᵢ^⊤, and cᵢ denotes the view-dependent color parameters. For a fixed training view n and pixel x, let Gᵢ(x) be the projected Gaussian footprint, aᵢ(x):=αᵢGᵢ(x), and let j\precₙi denote front-to-back ordering along the ray. Suppressing the view index on projected footprints and transmittances, the rendered color is

    Îₙ(x)=∑ᵢ₌₁^MₜTᵢ(x) aᵢ(x) cᵢ(dₙ), Tᵢ(x):=∏_j\precₙi(1-aⱼ(x)).

    		(1)

    We write Îₙ=Φ(Gₜ,n) for the rasterized image. At training iteration t, a view nₜ is sampled and the photometric loss is L̂_img⁽ᵗ⁾=ℓ₁(Φ(Gₜ,nₜ),I_nₜ). The 3DGS-MCMC backend additionally uses opacity and scale regularizers to encourage unused Gaussians to disappear; we retain these terms in training but do not expand them here, since our score pass is defined from the image objective in Section 3.

    3DGS-MCMC: Markov view and relocation/addition operations.

    3DGS-MCMC [17] interprets the Gaussian population as a sample state of a Markov chain. For a regularized training objective L, the formal target density is

    p_β(G)=Z_β⁻¹\exp (-βL(G)),

    where Z_β is the normalizing constant and β>0 is an inverse temperature. Under this view, the usual gradient update is interpreted as the zero-noise limit of an SGLD step. For a parameter block θ,

    θ←θ-η ∇̂_θL(G)+σ_θ(G) ξ, ξ∼ℕ(0,I),

    where ∇̂ is a stochastic gradient and σ_θ(G) is the exploration scale. In the original 3DGS-MCMC implementation, this noise is applied to Gaussian centers, with scale depending on the current Gaussian state.

    The structural mechanism of 3DGS-MCMC realizes densification and pruning through deterministic state transitions. Let Dₜ:={i:αᵢ≤α_death} and Aₜ:={i:αᵢ>α_death} denote the candidate dead and live pools, respectively. To reallocate capacity, rⱼ recycled slots from Dₜ (or fresh slots during addition) are assigned to a target Gaussian j, yielding Nⱼ:=rⱼ+1 co-located copies parameterized as:

    μ_j,ℓ^′=μⱼ, α_j,ℓ^′=1-(1-αⱼ)^1/Nⱼ, Σ_j,ℓ^′=γ(Nⱼ,αⱼ) Σⱼ,

    		(2)

    for ℓ=1,…,Nⱼ, with color and orientation inherited from the target. The closed-form scalar γ(Nⱼ,αⱼ) rescales the covariance such that the aggregate opacity footprint of the co-located cluster matches that of the original primitive, minimizing instantaneous rendering perturbations.

    In our framework, we decouple structural decision-making from physical execution: we adopt these closed-form transitions strictly as a conservative realization backend, while entirely replacing the heuristic opacity proposals with our objective-derived first-variation score.

    SRM viewpoint: splat measures and first variation.

    Splat Regression Models (SRM) [6] formalize “splat” representations as optimization over mixing measures. Let ρ be a centered isotropic “mother” density on ℝ³. For (A,b)∈ℝ^3×3×ℝ³, define the transformed splat ρ_A,b:=(A(·)+b)_#ρ. A (vector-valued) splat measure μ over weights and splat parameters induces the mixture model

    f_μ(x):=∫v ρ_A,b(x) μ(dv,dA,db), x∈ℝ³.

    SRM endows the space of such measures with a Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao (WFR) geometry in which gradient flow decomposes into a transport component (moving A,b) and a mass component (rescaling v). The first-order object governing the mass component is the first variation of the data-fit functional. Inspired by the SRM first-variation view of splat measures, our score pass instantiates a finite-dimensional coordinate of this first-variation field for the specific mass direction that scales opacities (see Section 3.1).

    3 Method

    3.1 First-Variation Score from Splat Measures

    Let F_D(G):=N⁻¹∑ₙ₌₁^Nℓ_img(Φ(G,n),Iₙ) denote the full multiview empirical risk. The Splat Regression Model (SRM) shows that optimizing a splat-based representation involves two distinct operations: moving parameters (transport) and changing primitive weights (mass). Standard 3DGS handles transport natively via continuous gradient descent. To handle mass, we evaluate how infinitesimal changes to a Gaussian’s weight affect the empirical risk.

    At a controller step t, we freeze the current population Gₜ={gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^Mₜ and attach an auxiliary mass coordinates mᵢ for each Gaussian, initialized to the all-ones vector 1. We define a mass-perturbed population Gₜᵐ by scaling the opacity contribution of each Gaussian i by mᵢ, i.e., aᵢ(x)↦mᵢaᵢ(x). We estimate the minibatch multiview risk and its negative mass derivative from a batch of views Bₜ:

    F̂ₜ(m):=1/B∑_n∈Bₜℓ_img (Φ(Gₜᵐ,n),Iₙ), (qₜ)ᵢ:=-.(∂F̂ₜ(m))/(∂mᵢ)|ₘ₌₁.

    		(3)

    All scene parameters are detached during this computation, so a single backward pass returns the score vector qₜ. The sign of (qₜ)ᵢ gives the local mass interpretation: increasing mᵢ decreases the empirical risk by ε(qₜ)ᵢ+o(ε).

    Fix a view (Iₙ,πₙ). Under mass coordinates m, the renderer induces a map f_n,t(·;m):=Φ(Gₜᵐ,πₙ)∈L²(Ω;ℝ³). Define the per-view functional Fₙ(f):=ℓ_img(f,Iₙ). Following SRM, the relevant first-order object governing mass creation is the first variation.

    Definition 1(First variation on images [6, Def. 2]).

    Let F:L²(Ω;ℝ³)→ℝ be Fréchet differentiable at f. Its first variation δF[f]∈L²(Ω;ℝ³) is the Riesz representative of the differential: for all ξ∈L²(Ω;ℝ³),

    .d/dεF(f+εξ)|_ε=0=∫_Ω⟨ξ(x), δF[f](x)⟩ dx.

    Remark 1(On differentiability and discretization).

    Definition 1 assumes Fréchet differentiability. The practical image loss contains nonsmooth components such as ℓ₁ and differentiable image-structure terms such as DSSIM. The implemented renderer is evaluated on a pixel grid, in which case the integrals below are finite sums over pixels.

    Applying the chain rule to Fₙ∘f_n,t yields a coordinate expression for the score.

    Proposition 1(Score as a first-variation coordinate).

    Assume each Fₙ admits a first variation and f_n,t(·;m) is differentiable in m at m=1. Then the score in (3) satisfies

    (qₜ)ᵢ=-1/B∑_n∈Bₜ∫_Ω⟨δFₙ [f_n,t(·;1)](x), .(∂f_n,t(x;m))/(∂mᵢ)|ₘ₌₁⟩ dx.

    The proof is provided in Appendix A. Proposition 1 connects the SRM first-variation viewpoint to renderer-level mass coordinates. Intuitively, the integral pairs the image-space loss gradient with the image change induced by rescaling the i-th Gaussian. Ranking Gaussians by (qₜ)ᵢ therefore orders the predicted loss decrease for equal infinitesimal mass increments at the frozen state. Unlike accumulated position gradients or plain opacity [15, 17], the score directly evaluates this mass direction, providing an objective-derived criterion for allocating capacity.

    In the specific context of 3DGS alpha-compositing [39], applying the chain rule to the renderer gives a concrete pixel-level expression for this score:

    (qₜ)ᵢ=-1/B∑_n∈Bₜ∑ₓ⟨rₙ(x), Tᵢ(x)aᵢ(x)(cᵢ(dₙ)-Îᵢᵇᵃᶜᵏ(x))⟩,

    		(4)

    where Îᵢᵇᵃᶜᵏ(x) is the accumulated background color and rₙ(x) is the image-space loss gradient. Equation (4) gives the geometric intuition: a Gaussian receives a high score when its footprint is visible, meaning Tᵢ(x)aᵢ(x) is large; when its color differs from the accumulated background behind it; and when the resulting color change aligns with the negative loss gradient -rₙ(x).

    3.2 Birth–Death Allocation via Score Gaps

    The score qₜ provides a continuous mass derivative, but structural control requires a discrete allocation decision. We model reclaiming capacity from death coordinates D and assigning it to birth coordinates J_1:Rₜ through the following balanced mass perturbation:

    δm(J,D)=κ(∑ᵣ₌₁^Rₜe_Jᵣ-∑_i∈Deᵢ), |D|=Rₜ.

    Here eᵢ is the i-th coordinate vector and κ>0 sets the scale of the mass perturbation. The following bound identifies its first-order loss term under a smooth local model.

    Proposition 2(Local descent upper bound under smoothness).

    If F(m):=F̂ₜ(m) is Lₛₘ-smooth on a neighbourhood containing the segment {1+τδm:τ∈[0,1]}, then

    F(1+δm)≤F(1)-⟨qₜ,δm⟩+Lₛₘ/2∥δm∥₂².

    Proposition 2 (proof in Appendix A) identifies the score gap as the first-order predicted loss decrease:

    ⟨qₜ,δm⟩=κ(∑ᵣ₌₁^Rₜ(qₜ)_Jᵣ-∑_i∈D(qₜ)ᵢ).

    		(5)

    Proposition 3(Bounded influence of low-opacity Gaussians).

    Fix a view n and let Îₙ be the rendered image from (1). Let Îₙ⁽⁻ⁱ⁾ be the image obtained by setting αᵢ=0 while keeping all other Gaussians unchanged. Assume rendered colors and the terminal background color are bounded in [0,1]³, and define the per-image mean absolute error

    ∥J∥_1,mean:=(1)/(|Ωₚᵢₓ|)∑_x∈Ωₚᵢₓ1/3∥J(x)∥₁.

    Then

    ∥Îₙ-Îₙ⁽⁻ⁱ⁾∥_1,mean≤αᵢ.

    Consequently, if ℓ_img(·,Iₙ) is L_ℓ-Lipschitz with respect to ∥·∥_1,mean in a neighbourhood of Îₙ, then

    |ℓ_img(Îₙ,Iₙ)-ℓ_img(Îₙ⁽⁻ⁱ⁾,Iₙ)|≤L_ℓ αᵢ.

    Proposition 3 (proof in Appendix A) bounds the disturbance from an individual low-opacity removal. This motivates the candidate pool ℙₜ:={i:αᵢ≤α_death}. Within this pool, smaller scores indicate lower retention value under the local mass model.

    The final variational controller merges this continuous ideal with discrete constraints. We stabilize multi-view stochasticity using an exponentially moving averaged (EMA) score q̄ₜ. The death set Dₜ⁻ selects the Rₜ Gaussians with the lowest scores (qₜ)ᵢwithin the pool ℙₜ. The birth multiset J_1:Rₜ is sampled from live Gaussians proportional to their positive scores [(q̄ₜ)ᵢ]₊.

    3.3 Discrete Realization by the 3DGS-MCMC Kernels

    Our variational policy dictates which primitives are retired and where new capacity is sampled to approximate first-order loss descent. Once the death set Dₜ⁻ is selected from the lowest-scoring candidates in ℙₜ and the birth multiset J_1:Rₜ is sampled proportional to positive scores [(q̄ₜ)ᵢ]₊, the discrete state transition is realized by the footprint-preserving relocation kernel:

    Gₜ₊=K_reloc(Gₜ; Dₜ⁻, J_1:Rₜ).

    		(6)

    Each recycled slot in Dₜ⁻ is transferred to a sampled birth site in J_1:Rₜ, where the closed-form opacity and covariance corrections (2) preserve the aggregate optical footprint to minimize instantaneous rendering disturbance. When the population is below the prescribed cap, the addition kernel directly activates new slots at sites sampled from [(q̄ₜ)ᵢ]₊ without requiring paired deaths.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments test a single claim: the first variation of the multiview reconstruction risk is a better birth–death signal than opacity or gradient proxies. We fix the renderer, optimizer, and MCMC transitions to isolate this statistic. This allows us to answer three direct questions: Does the variational controller improve reconstruction quality at the same primitive budgets? Is the gain explicitly caused by the WFR score? And does the allocation behavior align with local descent predictions?

    4.1 Experimental setup

    Datasets and metrics.

    We evaluate on Mip-NeRF360 [3], Tanks & Temples [18], and DeepBlending [13]. Our main fixed-budget Mip-NeRF360 averages use seven scenes: Bicycle, Garden, Stump, Room, Counter, Kitchen, and Bonsai; Flowers and Treehill are excluded. Tanks & Temples uses Truck and Train, and DeepBlending uses Dr. Johnson and Playroom. We report PSNR, SSIM [30], and LPIPS [35] on held-out test views. Per-scene results are in Appendix H; compact-model comparisons use all nine Mip-NeRF360 scenes.

    Budgeted evaluation.

    We evaluate under matched Gaussian caps K∈{100k,500k,1M}. The fixed-budget setting isolates the structural decision. Every birth consumes finite capacity. Poor allocation cannot be hidden by unbounded growth.

    Baselines and protocol.

    We compare against 3DGS [15] with SfM initialization, Improved ADC [10], 3DGS-MCMC [17] with SfM initialization, EDGS [19], and ConeGS [2]. Rows marked † use published fixed-budget benchmark numbers from ConeGS under the same dataset split and Gaussian cap. Claims about the effect of the proposed controller are based on matched 3DGS-MCMC reruns: the renderer, optimizer, initialization, cap, and transition maps remain identical. Only the structural selection statistic changes.

    Implementation.

    Our implementation builds on 3DGS-MCMC. We keep the renderer, training loss, optimizer, relocation/addition kernels, and event schedule unchanged. All methods are trained for 30,000 iterations. Hyperparameters, hardware, and timing details are in Appendix B.

    4.2 Fixed-budget reconstruction quality

    Table 1 establishes fixed-budget reconstruction quality. At the tightest 100k cap, our controller outperforms 3DGS-MCMC baseline, EDGS, and ConeGS across all three datasets. This severe scarcity highlights our advantage: reallocating via WFR score derivatives yields the largest impact.

    At 500k and 1M, our method has the highest PSNR across all three datasets in Table 1. SSIM and LPIPS are metric-dependent: on Mip-NeRF360 at 500k, ConeGS has slightly higher SSIM (0.870 vs. 0.869), and competing methods achieve lower LPIPS at both larger caps. These results support the benefit of score-guided allocation under tight budgets without implying uniform superiority. Figure 3 shows the matched PSNR–budget frontier. Full metrics, random-initialization results, and runtimes are in Appendix I.

item.title: 位姿不准就别让它污染几何：SG-Splat 把几何估计与高斯属性预测拆成两条支路，再粗到细纠偏 ｜ SG-Splat: Stable Geometry Learning under Pose Uncertainty for Pose-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：残余位姿误差会扰动规范空间变换、给几何灌噪声；解耦两支路可减轻误差耦合。

要点：

  • 免位姿前馈 3DGS 直接从无位姿图像重建，但残余位姿误差会扰动规范空间的高斯变换，给几何与属性学习注入错误监督
  • SG-Splat 把几何估计与高斯属性预测解耦为两条专用支路，降低位姿敏感几何与外观属性之间的误差耦合
  • 再叠一条粗到细的细化流程：Flow-Guided Pose Refinement 用流相关特征加可微 bundle adjustment 修位姿，Residual-Guided Geometry Correction 修几何对齐；另有 GT 与预测位姿混合的非对称优化训练策略。DL3DV 与 RealEstate10K 上在稀疏与稠密输入下都改善新视角合成与相对位姿

为什么值得看：免位姿重建是「拍一段就能进引擎」的前提，而位姿误差是最难发现的一类脏数据——它不会报错，只会让几何慢慢烂。把位姿敏感路径与属性路径分开，是工程上更容易定位问题的结构。

中文摘要：免位姿前馈 3DGS 能直接从无位姿图像重建高斯表示，但对残余位姿误差敏感：位姿误差会扰动规范空间中的高斯变换，使几何与属性学习拿到带噪的监督。SG-Splat 的做法是先把几何估计与高斯属性预测解耦成两条专用支路，减少位姿敏感几何与属性之间的误差耦合；然后加一条粗到细的细化流程，包含用流相关特征与可微 bundle adjustment 的 Flow-Guided Pose Refinement，以及用于几何对齐的 Residual-Guided Geometry Correction；训练上再引入真假位姿混合的非对称优化策略，在提升鲁棒性的同时保住位姿监督的可靠性。在 DL3DV 与 RealEstate10K 上，无论稀疏还是稠密输入，新视角合成与相对位姿估计都有改善。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

本期推送：2026-10-28

SG-Splat: Stable Geometry Learning under Pose Uncertainty for Pose-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a promising representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. For practical deployment, recent studies have explored pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, which reconstructs Gaussian representations directly from unposed input images. However, these methods remain sensitive to residual pose errors, which perturb canonical-space Gaussian transformation, introducing noisy supervision for geometry and attribute learning. To address this problem, we present SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that improves robustness to pose uncertainty and stabilizes the learning of Gaussian primitives. SG-Splat decouples geometry estimation and Gaussian attribute prediction into two dedicated branches, reducing error coupling between pose-sensitive geometry and Gaussian attributes. We further introduce a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline, consisting of Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC), to improve geometric alignment before Gaussian attribute reconstruction. Specifically, FGPR refines camera poses with flow-based correlation features and differentiable bundle adjustment. RGC then corrects initial point maps using depth residuals derived from FGPR, producing more reliable Gaussian centers. To stabilize training, we introduce a dual-path strategy that mixes ground-truth and predicted poses for canonical transformation. It provides clean supervision for Gaussian attributes while improving geometry robustness to residual pose errors. Extensive experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K show that SG-Splat achieves state-of-the-art performance in both novel view synthesis and pose estimation.

Index Terms:

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, Pose-free, Novel View synthesis, Pose Estimation.

I Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)[4] has become a powerful representation for real-time photorealistic rendering and high-fidelity scene reconstruction, with growing potential in world modeling [5], autonomous driving [6], and virtual reality [7]. However, conventional 3DGS is limited by its reliance on per-scene optimization and calibrated poses, which limits scalable and efficient 3D reconstruction. This has motivated recent interest in pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, which seeks to predict camera poses and Gaussian parameters directly from input images in a single forward pass. Early pose-free feed-forward 3DGS methods [8, 9] predict 3D Gaussian primitives directly in a canonical space, thereby avoiding the explicit propagation of pose estimation errors during Gaussian aggregation. These methods have shown promising performance under sparse-view settings, typically with two to four input views. However, directly constructing a canonical Gaussian representation becomes increasingly challenging as the number of input views grows[10], due to the difficulty of maintaining cross-view geometric consistency without explicit pose-guided aggregation.

To scale to multi-view settings, recent methods such as AnySplat [1] and WorldMirror [2] predict per-view Gaussian primitives in camera coordinate systems and transform them into a canonical space using camera poses of each view, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a) and (b). At inference time, this transformation must rely on predicted poses, whose errors directly affect the alignment of Gaussian primitives across views. During training, this transformation becomes non-trivial, as the poses used for transformation affect both optimization stability and the consistency between training and inference. AnySplat uses predicted poses for transformation during training, improving consistency with inference but introducing scene-dependent pose perturbations that destabilize the learning of geometry and Gaussian attributes. In contrast, WorldMirror uses ground-truth poses for canonical transformation, which stabilizes Gaussian parameter learning but introduces a discrepancy between training and inference. In addition, both methods directly couple pose supervision with Gaussian reconstruction, introducing competing optimization objectives. This coupling becomes especially detrimental when residual pose errors perturb the canonical transformation used for rendering supervision. To remove this coupling, recent methods [11, 3] adopt a self-supervised formulation. As shown in Fig. 1(c), they discard explicit pose supervision and optimize Gaussian reconstruction solely through rendering supervision. Although this design removes the need for pose supervision, it still relies on predicted poses for canonical transformation during training. Consequently, pose errors still perturb the optimization of Gaussian geometry and attributes. In addition, without direct 3D constraints, these methods may produce visually plausible but geometrically unreliable reconstructions [12], restricting their applicability in geometry-sensitive tasks.

These observations reveal a key challenge: how can pose-free feed-forward 3DGS effectively exploit pose supervision during training while maintaining stable learning under residual pose errors? Although YoNoSplat [13] mixes predicted and ground-truth poses during training, predicted poses are sampled with a low probability. As a result, this strategy only weakly exposes the model to inference-time pose errors and still allows noisy supervision to affect Gaussian attributes when predicted poses are selected.

To address this challenge, we propose SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework with decoupled geometry and attribute branches, as shown in Fig. 1(d). This design separates geometry and camera estimation from Gaussian attribute prediction, reducing the interference between pose errors and attribute learning. We further introduce a progressive refinement pipeline with Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC). FGPR refines the initial camera poses using flow-based correlation features and differentiable bundle adjustment (DBA). RGC corrects the initial point maps using depth residuals produced by FGPR and intermediate geometry features. The refined poses stabilize canonical transformations, and the corrected point maps improve Gaussian center accuracy. Together, they reduce the discrepancy between training and inference and improve the consistency between the refined camera poses and the Gaussian centers.

In addition, we design a pose-aware dual-path training strategy that prevents the attribute branch from overfitting to alignments corrupted by residual pose errors. Specifically, either ground-truth poses or predicted poses are selected to transform Gaussian primitives into a canonical coordinate system during training. When ground-truth poses are used, the model learns geometry reconstruction and Gaussian attribute prediction under reliable alignment. When predicted poses are used, we mainly optimize the geometry branch and pose estimation modules, preventing the attribute branch from overfitting to residual pose errors. This asymmetric optimization stabilizes Gaussian attribute learning and improves geometry robustness under pose uncertainty. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework with a geometry-attribute decoupled architecture. By separating geometry and camera estimation from Gaussian attribute prediction, the framework suppresses error propagation from inaccurate pose estimates and improves the reliability of Gaussian parameter generation.

  • •

    We introduce a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline consisting of FGPR and RGC to enhance pose and Gaussian alignment. FGPR iteratively refines camera poses by combining flow-based correlation features with differentiable bundle adjustment. RGC then corrects local point maps using depth residuals from FGPR, improving the consistency between refined camera poses and Gaussian centers.

  • •

    We develop a pose-aware dual-path training strategy that integrates mixed-pose canonical transformation with asymmetric branch optimization. This strategy uses ground-truth poses to provide reliable attribute supervision, while using predicted poses to regularize geometry learning against scene-dependent pose errors.

    • II Related Work

    II-ANovel View Synthesis with Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

    Early image-based rendering methods [14, 15, 16] synthesize novel views by resampling or blending images captured from nearby viewpoints. These methods demonstrated the possibility of photorealistic view synthesis without fully explicit 3D reconstruction, but they often require dense image capture, calibrated cameras, or approximate geometry to handle large viewpoint changes and occlusions. With the advent of deep learning, learning-based NVS methods [17, 18]learn the geometry of scenes and appearance priors from data, improving flexibility under sparse-view inputs. NeRF [19] represents a scene as a continuous radiance field optimized from posed images and renders novel views via volumetric ray marching, which incurs substantial computational cost. To improve efficiency, follow-up works [20, 21, 22] introduced compact encodings or hybrid scene representations to accelerate rendering, but they still struggle to achieve real-time performance. Motivated by this limitation, 3DGS [4] and its variants [23, 24, 25] adopt explicit Gaussian primitives for scene representation, achieving high-fidelity novel view synthesis with real-time rendering efficiency. However, both NeRF and 3DGS pipelines typically rely on per-scene optimization. Recent methods extend 3DGS to sparse input views by introducing diffusion priors [26] or geometric constraints [27]. This has motivated recent feed-forward methods for NeRF [28, 29, 30] as well as feed-forward 3DGS methods [31, 32, 33, 34]. More recently, DepthSplat [35] and ProSplat [36] extend this paradigm to sparse multi-view or wide-baseline settings. In addition, recent works [37, 38, 39] decouple Gaussian primitives from pixel-aligned locations, resulting in a more flexible representation.

    Nevertheless, most of them still assume known camera poses or rely on pose-conditioned geometric cues, which limits their applicability to casually captured, unposed image collections. In contrast, our work targets pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, where camera poses, geometry, and Gaussian attributes must be jointly predicted under residual pose uncertainty.

    II-B3D Foundation Models for Geometry and Pose Priors

    Recent 3D foundation models have substantially advanced feed-forward geometry and pose estimation from unposed images. DUSt3R [40] reformulates multi-view reconstruction as point map regression from unconstrained image pairs. MASt3R [41] and its variants[42, 43] further improve dense matching accuracy and geometric consistency. Building on this line of work, VGGT [44], π³[45], and Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [46] directly predict camera poses, point maps, depth maps, and geometric tracks from a few to hundreds of views in a single forward pass, offering scalable geometry priors for downstream applications.

    These foundation models have also been increasingly adopted in feed-forward 3DGS. Splatt3R [9] and NoPoSplat [8] build upon MASt3R to obtain geometric priors and predict Gaussians in a global coordinate system from unposed images. AnySplat [1] uses VGGT as a teacher to supervise pose and geometry prediction during training. YoNoSplat [13] extends this paradigm with a π³-based architecture and introduces an intrinsic condition embedding to handle unknown camera intrinsics. AirSplat [47] leverages DA3 as a frozen geometry foundation model and trains a Gaussian generation module on top of its priors. Collectively, these methods demonstrate that 3D foundation models have become a powerful source of geometric priors for pose-free feed-forward 3DGS.

    II-CPose-Free Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

    Pose-free feed-forward 3DGS reconstructs Gaussian representations directly from unposed images, avoiding camera calibration at inference time. Existing methods mainly fall into two categories. The first line exploits 3D foundation models to provide geometry and camera priors. Methods built on DUSt3R [48] or MASt3R [9, 8, 49, 10, 50] recover geometry and camera poses before Gaussian prediction. However, these methods are mostly tailored to sparse input views, which limits their scalability to denser multi-view reconstruction. Recent methods [1, 13, 47, 51] improve scalability by using visual geometry foundation models that jointly predict point maps and camera poses in a single forward pass [44, 45, 46]. However, their Gaussian reconstruction remains sensitive to pose accuracy, because residual pose errors can perturb the transformation of Gaussian centers and introduce noisy supervision into the optimization of Gaussian geometry and attributes.

    Another line of work removes 3D supervision and trains pose-free models with self-supervised rendering objectives [52, 53, 11, 3]. Although these methods avoid explicit pose supervision, pose estimation, geometry prediction, and Gaussian attribute generation are optimized in a coupled manner through rendering losses. Consequently, pose and geometry errors may be absorbed by Gaussian attributes, leading to visually plausible but geometrically unreliable reconstructions [12].

    In contrast, our work focuses on the practical setting where explicit 3D supervision is available. We study how to effectively exploit 3D foundation priors for dense-view pose-free feed-forward 3DGS while preventing pose-corrupted supervision from destabilizing Gaussian geometry and attribute learning.

    III Method

    III-AProblem Formulation

    Given N unposed input views I={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, where Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3, the goal is to reconstruct a set of 3D Gaussian primitives for novel view synthesis. Each primitive is defined as

    g_i,j=(μ_i,j, c_i,j, r_i,j, s_i,j, α_i,j),

    		(1)

    and the complete Gaussian representation is written as

    G={g_i,j}_i=1,…,N; j=1,…,HW.

    		(2)

    The components μ∈ℝ³, r∈ℝ⁴, s∈ℝ³, α∈ℝ₊, and c∈ℝ^3×(k+1)² correspond to the 3D position, quaternion rotation, scaling factor, opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients of degree k, respectively. We assume known camera intrinsics, which are directly obtained from the capture device. In addition, the model predicts the camera poses {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N for all input views. Formally, the feed-forward model f_θ parameterized by θ learns the mapping

    f_θ:{Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N↦(G, {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N).

    		(3)

    III-BPipeline

    As illustrated in Fig. 2, SG-Splat decouples geometry and attribute modeling into two independent branches, each consisting of an encoder and a decoder. Given the input images, the two branches produce a geometry token zᵢᵍ, a camera token zᵢᶜ, and an attribute token zᵢᵃ for the i-th input view. The geometry token zᵢᵍ and attribute token zᵢᵃ are both of size ℝ^(l+5)×d, while the camera token zᵢᶜ is of size ℝ^(l/4+5)×d/4, where l=4HW/p² denotes the number of image tokens, and the additional five tokens are register tokens following π³[45]. Here, p=14 is the patch size and d=1024 is the token dimension.

    The geometry token and the camera token are then fed into a point head and a camera head to predict an initial local point map M̂ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ and an initial camera pose P̂ᵢ for each input view, respectively. The predicted pose is further refined by the proposed Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) module, which iteratively updates the pose for T rounds and produces the refined pose P̃ᵢ together with depth residual cues for geometric correction. The initial local point map M̂ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ is then refined by the Residual-Guided Geometry Correction module to obtain the refined local point map M̃ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ. Subsequently, M̃ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ is transformed from the local camera coordinate system into the shared canonical space, yielding the global Gaussian centers {μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ}ⱼ₌₁^HW.

    In parallel, the attribute token is fed into a Gaussian head to predict the remaining Gaussian attributes, which are combined with the transformed Gaussian centers to form the complete Gaussian representation:

    G={(μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ,c_i,j,r_i,j,s_i,j,α_i,j)}_i=1,…,N; j=1,…,HW.

    		(4)

    III-CFlow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR)

    Inspired by DROID-SLAM[54], we adopt an iterative pose refinement module to further correct the initial camera parameters P̂ᵢ, as shown in Fig. 4. Given the input images Iᵢ, initial camera parametersP̂ᵢ, and initial depth estimates D̂ᵢ from the z-axis M̂ᵢ, the module constructs low-based correlation features and optical flow of camera motion to refine poses iteratively.

    Inverse Depth Normalization

    To improve robustness to scene-scale variation, we use normalized inverse depth. First, we convert depth to inverse depth:

    d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ=(1)/(D̂ᵢ), d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ∈ℝ^H^′×W^′,

    		(5)

    where H^′=H/8 and W^′=W/8. We then normalize the inverse depth using only valid values,

    d̂ᵢ=(d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ)/(mean({d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ[d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ>τ]}ᵢ₌₁^N)),

    		(6)

    where τ=0.05 filters out extremely small inverse-depth values corresponding to very distant points. This normalization maintains a consistent numerical scale for the geometric input, thereby improving the robustness of pose refinement.

    Feature Extraction

    For feature extraction, input images are processed by a feature encoder and a context encoder, producing two dense feature maps at 1/8 image resolution. The feature encoder is used to compute 4D correlation volumes[55]Cᵢⱼ∈ℝ^H^′×W^′×H^′×W^′ for each pair of overlapping images (i,j). Then, a correlation lookup operator takes a H^′×W^′ grid of query coordinates and retrieves the values within a local square neighborhood of radius r from Cᵢⱼ, producing Corᵢⱼ∈ℝ^H^′×W^′×(2r+1)². The context features are injected into the update network during iterative refinement.

    Input

    Under the current pose estimates P̂ᵢ and P̂ⱼ and the inverse depth d̂ᵢ, we warp the pixel grid pᵢ from view i to view j to obtain the correspondence field:

    pᵢⱼ=Π (P̂ⱼ⁻¹∘P̂ᵢ∘Π⁻¹(pᵢ,d̂ᵢ)),

    		(7)

    where pᵢ is the pixel grid of view i, and Π⁻¹ and Π denote back-projection and projection, respectively. Based on the correspondence field pᵢ, we derive the optical flow of camera motion Fᵢ as the displacement between the projected and original pixel locations. Consequently, the update module takes the context feature h_ctx, the correlation feature Corᵢⱼ, and the optical flow Fᵢ as inputs.

    Update

    The update operator is implemented as a 3×3 convolutional GRU initialized with the context feature h_ctx. To improve feature fusion, the correlation feature Corᵢⱼ and the optical flow Fᵢ are first encoded by two convolutional layers before being injected into the GRU, while the context feature h_ctx is incorporated through element-wise addition.

    In iteration t, the operator updates the hidden state and predicts a correction term Δpᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾ for the current correspondence field pᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾:

    Δpᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾=Update (h_ctx, Corᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾, Fᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾),

    		(8)

    pᵢⱼ^*(t)=pᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾+Δpᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾.

    		(9)

    The corrected correspondence field is then fed into the DBA [56] module together with the current pose and inverse depth estimates P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾ and d̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾, to jointly update them as P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾ and d̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾. After T iterations, the final refined pose and depth are given by

    P̃ᵢ=P̃ᵢ⁽ᵀ⁾, D̃ᵢ=(1)/(d̃ᵢ⁽ᵀ⁾).

    		(10)

    The depth residual used for subsequent geometry correction is defined as

    ΔD̂ᵢ=D̃ᵢ-D̂ᵢ,

    		(11)

    where D̂ᵢ denotes the initial depth estimate.

    III-DResidual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC).

    To further improve the coarse local geometry, we introduce a lightweight Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC) module, as shown in Fig. 4. RGC takes the initial local point map together with the depth residual from FGPR as input, so that local geometry correction is explicitly guided by residual geometric cues after pose refinement.

    For each input view, the initial point map M̂ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 is concatenated with the FGPR depth residual ΔD̂ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×1 and converted into patch tokens zᵢʳ∈ℝ^4HW/p²×D through a patch embedding layer:

    zᵢʳ=PatchEmbed (Concat(M̂ᵢ,ΔD̂ᵢ)),

    		(12)

    where p=14 denotes the patch size and D=1024 is the token dimension. The residual tokens are then combined with the geometry tokens zᵢᵍ from the geometry branch, which share the same spatial resolution. We concatenate them along the channel dimension and use an MLP to obtain the correction tokens:

    zᵢ^δ=MLP (Concat_c(zᵢʳ,zᵢᵍ)),

    		(13)

    where zᵢ^δ∈ℝ^4HW/p²×D. The correction tokens are decoded into a dense point-wise correction field ΔM̂ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 through linear projection and pixel-shuffle upsampling:

    ΔM̂ᵢ=PS (Linear (zᵢ^δ)),

    		(14)

    where PS(·) denotes pixel-shuffle. Rather than directly predicting additive offsets, the module estimates a bounded multiplicative correction,

    Sᵢ=1+β\tanh(ΔM̂ᵢ),

    		(15)

    which is applied element-wise to the initial point map:

    M̃ᵢ=M̂ᵢ⊙Sᵢ,

    		(16)

    where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, and β=0.2 constrains the correction magnitude to avoid excessive corrections that could disrupt the coarse geometric structure.

    This design preserves the coarse geometric prior while enabling spatially adaptive geometry correction. Compared with direct offset regression, the multiplicative formulation yields more stable updates and is less prone to over-correction. By conditioning the refinement on FGPR depth residuals, the refined point map becomes better aligned with the corrected camera poses, providing more reliable Gaussian centers for subsequent 3D Gaussian prediction.

    III-EDual-Path Training Strategy

    We adopt a dual-branch design for SG-Splat, where the geometry branch estimates camera poses and local Gaussian centers, and the attribute branch predicts Gaussian attributes. This separation reduces error propagation from inaccurate poses and improves the reliability of Gaussian parameter generation. However, 3DGS rendering requires transforming local Gaussian centers into a shared canonical space, making cross-view alignment sensitive to pose errors. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a mixed-pose canonical transformation with asymmetric optimization, as shown in Fig. 5.

    Mixed-pose canonical transformation

    The refined point map M̃ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 provides local Gaussian centers for the i-th input view. After flattening the spatial dimensions, we obtain {μ_i,jˡᵒᶜᵃˡ}ⱼ₌₁^HW. During training, the pose used for canonical transformation is sampled from either the ground-truth pose or the refined predicted pose:

    P̄ᵢ=\begincasesPᵢ^*,&z=1, P̃ᵢ,&z=0,\endcases z∼Bernoulli(0.5),

    		(17)

    where Pᵢ^* and P̃ᵢ denote the ground-truth pose and refined predicted pose, respectively. The binary variable z is sampled once per training scene and shared across all input views. Each local center is transformed into the canonical space by

    μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ=P̄ᵢ∘μ_i,jˡᵒᶜᵃˡ.

    		(18)

    The attribute branch predicts the remaining Gaussian attributes for each center:

    {(c_i,j,r_i,j,s_i,j,α_i,j)}ⱼ₌₁^HW.

    		(19)

    Together with the transformed centers {μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ}ⱼ₌₁^HW, these predicted parameters form the Gaussian primitives for rendering. For N input views, the model generates N×H×W primitives in total.

    Asymmetric optimization under mixed poses

    The optimization rule depends on the sampled pose in Eq. (17). When z=1, ground-truth poses provide reliable canonical transformation and clean rendering supervision. We therefore update the full model, including the geometry branch, pose refinement module, and attribute branch. This path stabilizes Gaussian attribute learning under well-aligned transformations. When z=0, refined predicted poses are used, matching the inference setting where ground-truth poses are unavailable. However, residual pose errors may misalign Gaussian centers across views and introduce noisy rendering supervision. To avoid corrupting attribute learning, we detach the rendering gradients from the attribute branch and use them only to optimize the geometry branch.

    This asymmetric design combines the advantages of both paths. The ground-truth-pose path provides reliable supervision for Gaussian attribute prediction, while the predicted-pose path exposes the geometry branch to the pose distribution used during inference. By alternating between them, the proposed strategy reduces the discrepancy between training and inference and prevents the attribute branch from absorbing pose-induced noise.

    III-FTraining Objectives

    Progressive Decoupled Training

    Directly integrating FGPR and RGC into the SG-Splat pipeline leads to unstable optimization, as pose refinement, geometry correction, and Gaussian attribute prediction are optimized simultaneously. The resulting entanglement makes it difficult for the refinement modules to learn reliable corrections from noisy pose and geometry estimates. To address this issue, we adopt a progressive training strategy that decouples geometry and appearance optimization across four stages, including coupled pretraining, pose refinement, point refinement, and final joint optimization.

    Stage I: Coupled pretraining. We first train a coupled base model without FGPR and RGC, including the encoder, decoder, point head, camera head, and Gaussian head. This stage provides a stable initialization for coarse geometry reconstruction and Gaussian attribute prediction.

    Stage II: Pose refinement via FGPR. Based on the pretrained coupled model, we duplicate the encoder and decoder to initialize separate geometry and appearance branches. The point and camera heads are assigned to the geometry branch, while the Gaussian head is assigned to the appearance branch. All other modules are frozen, and only FGPR is optimized to learn stable pose refinement.

    Stage III: Point refinement via RGC. We then freeze the remaining components and optimize only the RGC, enabling geometry correction under the refined poses without interference from appearance optimization. During the refinement stages, local points are transformed into the canonical space using ground-truth poses, which removes stochastic perturbations from inaccurate pose predictions and provides stable supervision for pose and geometry refinement.

    Stage IV: Joint optimization. Finally, we fine-tune the full dual-path architecture in an end-to-end manner. With stabilized geometry and pose estimates as initialization, this stage jointly optimizes geometry and appearance, improving reconstruction fidelity, view consistency, and robustness to residual pose errors.

    Training Loss

    Our model is a joint learning framework and trained with a multi-task loss function comprising two components: camera pose loss, and 3DGS rendering loss. As for the pose loss, we only explicitly supervise the refined poses produced by the FGPR module. Given the ground-truth poses {Pᵢ^*}ᵢ₌₁^N, we supervise the refined pose estimates {P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾}ᵢ₌₁^N over T iterations by

    Lₚₒₛₑ=∑ₜ₌₁ᵀγᵀ⁻ᵗ∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥\log (Pᵢ^*⁻¹P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾)∥₂,

    		(20)

    where \log(·) denotes the SE(3) logarithm map and γ=0.9 emphasizes later refinement iterations. We do not impose direct depth supervision because 3DGS renders both images and depths via α-blending, such that accurate pixel-level depth does not necessarily imply accurate rendered depth. In addition, the predicted depths are defined in the camera coordinate system, making it difficult to enforce cross-view consistency.

    The rendering loss is defined as the sum of the MSE and LPIPS [58] losses over all target views rendered in a single forward pass:

    L_rgb=∑ₙ₌₁^N_tgt(MSE(Ĩⁿ,I_gtⁿ)+λ LPIPS(Ĩⁿ,I_gtⁿ)),

    		(21)

    where N_tgt denotes the number of target views in each forward pass, Ĩⁿ is the rendered image, and I_gtⁿ is the corresponding ground-truth image. The overall training objective is then defined as

    L=L_rgb+β Lₚₒₛₑ,

    		(22)

    where β controls the relative importance of pose supervision.

    IV Experiments

    IV-AExperimental Setup

    Implementation Details

    For both geometry and appearance branches, the encoder employs the DINOv2 Large model with 24 attention layers, and the decoder consists of 18 alternating-attention layers. The backbones, encoders, decoders, point head, camera head, and Gaussian head are initialized from the pretrained YoNoSplat [13] weights. For FGPR, the feature encoder, context encoder, and update operator are initialized from the pretrained DROID-SLAM model [54]. The newly introduced layers are initialized to zero, so that they do not perturb the pretrained representations at the beginning of training. During training, we randomly select the number of input views between 2 and 32 and sample 4 target views. All experiments are conducted at a resolution of 224×224. We train the model on a single NVIDIA L20 GPU with a batch size of 1 for 100k steps. In the FGPR module, the number of pose refinement iterations T is set to 2. For the training objective, we set λ=0.05 for the LPIPS term and β=0.02 for the pose supervision term.

    Datasets

    We train and evaluate our model on the DL3DV [57] and RealEstate10K [59] datasets. DL3DV contains 51.3 million frames captured from 10,510 real-world scenes, spanning 65 point-of-interest categories. We use the full training set for model training, while excluding the 140 benchmark scenes to avoid potential evaluation leakage. We evaluate novel view synthesis under different input-view settings, including 12, 18, 24, and 32 views, with 8 target views used for evaluation. RealEstate10K consists of real-estate videos collected from YouTube, where diverse views of a scene are obtained by sampling frames at different timestamps. We use this dataset to evaluate sparse-view reconstruction with 6 input views.

    Evaluation Metrics

    We evaluate novel view synthesis using the widely adopted metrics PSNR, SSIM[60], and LPIPS [58]. For pose estimation, we follow prior works [1, 13] and report the area under the cumulative angular pose error curve (AUC) at angular thresholds of 5^∘, 10^∘, and 20^∘.

    Baselines

    We compare our method with representative state-of-the-art feed-forward 3DGS methods under both pose-free and pose-dependent settings. For pose-free reconstruction, we consider the following methods:

  • •

    YoNoSplat[13] is a unified feed-forward 3DGS model designed for both pose-dependent and pose-free reconstruction. It predicts per-view Gaussian primitives and camera poses and aggregates them into a global representation using the predicted camera poses. In our experiments, we use the publicly released checkpoints trained on DL3DV and RealEstate10K at 224×224 resolution, respectively.

  • •

    NoPoSplat[8] reconstructs 3D Gaussians from sparse unposed images by anchoring one input view as the canonical coordinate system, thereby avoiding explicit local-to-global Gaussian transformation with estimated poses. For a fair comparison, we retrain NoPoSplat under the corresponding multi-view settings on each dataset for 150K steps. On RealEstate10K, we initialize the model from the official pretrained 3-view weights, while keeping the remaining training configurations consistent with the original paper.

  • •

    AnySplat[1] targets feed-forward 3DGS from unconstrained image collections. It jointly predicts Gaussian parameters, depth maps, and camera poses from uncalibrated inputs, with geometry supervision provided by pretrained VGGT priors.

  • •

    WorldMirror[2] is a general-purpose feed-forward 3D geometric prediction model that can incorporate different geometric priors and output multiple 3D representations, including camera parameters, depth maps, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. We use its publicly released checkpoint trained on multiple large-scale datasets, including DL3DV and RealEstate10K.

    • We further compare with pose-dependent feed-forward 3DGS methods, where ground-truth camera poses are provided as input:

  • •

    MVSplat[61] constructs plane-sweeping cost volumes from posed sparse-view images and uses the estimated depth maps to localize Gaussian centers. For RealEstate10K, we evaluate the official checkpoint released by the authors. For DL3DV, no official checkpoint is available for our multi-view setting. Therefore, we retrain MVSplat for 300K iterations following the original training protocol and extend the number of input views to 32 views.

  • •

    DepthSplat[35] enhances cost-volume depth estimation with pretrained monocular depth features, leading to more robust Gaussian center prediction under challenging matching conditions. We use the official checkpoints trained on DL3DV and RealEstate10K.

    • For camera pose estimation, we additionally report results from recent feed-forward 3D Foundation Models, including MASt3R[41], VGGT[44] and π³[45].

    IV-BNovel View Synthesis

    Tab. I and Tab. II show the quantitative results for novel view synthesis on DL3DV and RealEstate10K. The symbol p indicates whether ground-truth camera poses are provided as input. On DL3DV, our method achieves the best results across all evaluated view settings in both pose-dependent and pose-free configurations. In the posed setting, SG-Splat achieves the best quantitative results across all view settings. This demonstrates that the proposed framework remains effective even when accurate camera poses are available. In the pose-free setting, SG-Splat also achieves the best quantitative results across all view settings, with a maximum PSNR gain of 0.91 dB over the second-best result. Although the absolute difficulty varies across view settings, the relative advantage of our method becomes more pronounced under denser input settings. This property is particularly important for feed-forward 3DGS, where dense inputs introduce more view-dependent Gaussian primitives, making accurate geometric correction crucial for mitigating pose-induced errors and ensuring reliable Gaussian reconstruction.

    On RealEstate10K, SG-Splat further demonstrates its effectiveness under the pose-free sparse-view setting. It achieves the best overall quantitative performance across the evaluation metrics, outperforming all baselines. This confirms that our method remains robust in sparse real-world scenes, rather than being limited to dense-view reconstruction.

    Qualitative comparisons are shown in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7. Our method produces sharper textures, cleaner object boundaries, and more complete scene structures. In contrast, AnySplat tends to generate blurred details because inaccurate predicted poses perturb the transformed Gaussian centers and degrade the supervision of Gaussian attributes. Other methods often suffer from distorted geometry or missing structures due to inaccurate pose estimation and geometric reconstruction. With the proposed FGPR module, our method improves pose accuracy before Gaussian reconstruction, leading to more reliable geometric alignment and more stable Gaussian parameter prediction. As a result, the rendered novel views are visually sharper and geometrically more consistent.

    IV-CRelative Pose Estimation

    We further evaluate the relative pose estimation on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, as reported in Tab. III. DL3DV is evaluated under dense-view settings with 12, 18, 24, and 32 input views, while RealEstate10K is evaluated under the sparse-view setting with 6 input views. The comparison includes pose-free feed-forward 3DGS methods and 3D foundation models, including MASt3R, VGGT, and π³.

    Our method achieves the best or comparable-best pose estimation accuracy across the evaluated settings. Our method achieves the highest AUC values on DL3DV under most evaluated view settings and consistently outperforms the compared methods on RealEstate10K across all AUC thresholds. The consistent performance across dense-view DL3DV and sparse-view RealEstate10K demonstrates the robustness of the proposed pose estimation framework.

    The comparison with π³ and VGGT is particularly informative. These models are trained on large-scale multi-dataset corpora that include DL3DV and RealEstate10K, whereas our method is designed and trained for the feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction task. Despite this strong comparison setting, our method still achieves superior or comparable pose accuracy on most evaluated protocols. These results indicate that the proposed FGPR module effectively improves both fine-grained pose accuracy and coarse relative pose estimation, which further contributes to the superior rendering quality reported in Tab. I and Tab. II.

    IV-DAblation Study

    We conduct ablation experiments on DL3DV under the 24-view setting. The base model adopts the same architecture but excludes the proposed Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC) modules, and is trained with ground-truth (GT) poses. We progressively incorporate FGPR, different pose selection strategies, and RGC to evaluate their individual contributions to rendering performance.

    Effect of FGPR

    As shown in Tab. IV, introducing FGPR alone (FGPR*) leads to only marginal improvements over the base model. This suggests that while pose refinement is beneficial, its effectiveness is limited when optimized in isolation with all other components frozen, and cannot fully compensate for pose inaccuracies during training.

    Effect of Dual-Branch Pose Selection Strategy

    We further investigate different pose selection strategies for training FGPR. Training with predicted poses (Pred Pose) leads to a noticeable performance degradation, indicating that noisy pose estimates introduce instability and hinder effective optimization. In contrast, using only GT poses achieves strong performance but suffers from exposure bias, as the model is not exposed to pose perturbations during training. Our proposed dual-branch strategy (Mix Pose), which adaptively combines predicted and GT poses, achieves the best results. This demonstrates that jointly leveraging accurate poses and realistic pose perturbations effectively reduces the discrepancy between training and inference, resulting in more robust rendering quality.

    Effect of RGC

    Building upon FGPR with the proposed dual-path training strategy, further incorporating RGC consistently improves all metrics. This suggests that point-map correction driven by depth residuals improves the reliability of Gaussian centers, thereby enhancing rendering fidelity.

    Effect of the Number of Iterations

    Tab. V evaluates the effect of the number of FGPR iterations T. A single iteration (T=1) yields suboptimal performance, indicating that one-step refinement is insufficient to fully correct pose errors. Increasing T to 2 significantly improves all metrics, demonstrating that iterative refinement is effective in enhancing pose quality and rendering accuracy. Increasing T from 2 to 3 slightly improves LPIPS and AUC@5∘, but reduces PSNR and SSIM while increasing computational cost. We therefore set T=2 as a practical trade-off between reconstruction quality, pose accuracy, and efficiency.

    V Conclusion

    In this paper, we presented SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for robust reconstruction under inaccurate pose estimation. To reduce the impact of residual pose errors, SG-Splat decouples geometry estimation from Gaussian attribute prediction and introduces a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline with Flow-Guided Pose Refinement and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction. We further proposed a dual-path training strategy that mixes ground-truth and predicted poses with asymmetric optimization, improving robustness to pose errors while maintaining reliable pose supervision. Extensive experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K show that SG-Splat achieves improved novel view synthesis and relative pose estimation under both sparse and dense input-view settings.

    Despite these improvements, several limitations remain. First, our method assumes known camera intrinsics, limiting its applicability to in-the-wild images with unavailable or unreliable intrinsics. Second, pixel-aligned feed-forward reconstruction tends to produce view-dependent and redundant Gaussian primitives, resulting in less compact representations. Third, high-resolution reconstruction still incurs substantial training and inference costs. Future work will explore intrinsic-free reconstruction, more efficient high-resolution architectures, and non-pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction to obtain more compact and effective 3DGS representations.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：残余位姿误差会扰动规范空间变换、给几何灌噪声；解耦两支路可减轻误差耦合。

要点：

  • 免位姿前馈 3DGS 直接从无位姿图像重建，但残余位姿误差会扰动规范空间的高斯变换，给几何与属性学习注入错误监督
  • SG-Splat 把几何估计与高斯属性预测解耦为两条专用支路，降低位姿敏感几何与外观属性之间的误差耦合
  • 再叠一条粗到细的细化流程：Flow-Guided Pose Refinement 用流相关特征加可微 bundle adjustment 修位姿，Residual-Guided Geometry Correction 修几何对齐；另有 GT 与预测位姿混合的非对称优化训练策略。DL3DV 与 RealEstate10K 上在稀疏与稠密输入下都改善新视角合成与相对位姿

为什么值得看：免位姿重建是「拍一段就能进引擎」的前提，而位姿误差是最难发现的一类脏数据——它不会报错，只会让几何慢慢烂。把位姿敏感路径与属性路径分开，是工程上更容易定位问题的结构。

中文摘要：免位姿前馈 3DGS 能直接从无位姿图像重建高斯表示，但对残余位姿误差敏感：位姿误差会扰动规范空间中的高斯变换，使几何与属性学习拿到带噪的监督。SG-Splat 的做法是先把几何估计与高斯属性预测解耦成两条专用支路，减少位姿敏感几何与属性之间的误差耦合；然后加一条粗到细的细化流程，包含用流相关特征与可微 bundle adjustment 的 Flow-Guided Pose Refinement，以及用于几何对齐的 Residual-Guided Geometry Correction；训练上再引入真假位姿混合的非对称优化策略，在提升鲁棒性的同时保住位姿监督的可靠性。在 DL3DV 与 RealEstate10K 上，无论稀疏还是稠密输入，新视角合成与相对位姿估计都有改善。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-10-28

SG-Splat: Stable Geometry Learning under Pose Uncertainty for Pose-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a promising representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. For practical deployment, recent studies have explored pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, which reconstructs Gaussian representations directly from unposed input images. However, these methods remain sensitive to residual pose errors, which perturb canonical-space Gaussian transformation, introducing noisy supervision for geometry and attribute learning. To address this problem, we present SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that improves robustness to pose uncertainty and stabilizes the learning of Gaussian primitives. SG-Splat decouples geometry estimation and Gaussian attribute prediction into two dedicated branches, reducing error coupling between pose-sensitive geometry and Gaussian attributes. We further introduce a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline, consisting of Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC), to improve geometric alignment before Gaussian attribute reconstruction. Specifically, FGPR refines camera poses with flow-based correlation features and differentiable bundle adjustment. RGC then corrects initial point maps using depth residuals derived from FGPR, producing more reliable Gaussian centers. To stabilize training, we introduce a dual-path strategy that mixes ground-truth and predicted poses for canonical transformation. It provides clean supervision for Gaussian attributes while improving geometry robustness to residual pose errors. Extensive experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K show that SG-Splat achieves state-of-the-art performance in both novel view synthesis and pose estimation.

Index Terms:

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, Pose-free, Novel View synthesis, Pose Estimation.

I Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)[4] has become a powerful representation for real-time photorealistic rendering and high-fidelity scene reconstruction, with growing potential in world modeling [5], autonomous driving [6], and virtual reality [7]. However, conventional 3DGS is limited by its reliance on per-scene optimization and calibrated poses, which limits scalable and efficient 3D reconstruction. This has motivated recent interest in pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, which seeks to predict camera poses and Gaussian parameters directly from input images in a single forward pass. Early pose-free feed-forward 3DGS methods [8, 9] predict 3D Gaussian primitives directly in a canonical space, thereby avoiding the explicit propagation of pose estimation errors during Gaussian aggregation. These methods have shown promising performance under sparse-view settings, typically with two to four input views. However, directly constructing a canonical Gaussian representation becomes increasingly challenging as the number of input views grows[10], due to the difficulty of maintaining cross-view geometric consistency without explicit pose-guided aggregation.

To scale to multi-view settings, recent methods such as AnySplat [1] and WorldMirror [2] predict per-view Gaussian primitives in camera coordinate systems and transform them into a canonical space using camera poses of each view, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a) and (b). At inference time, this transformation must rely on predicted poses, whose errors directly affect the alignment of Gaussian primitives across views. During training, this transformation becomes non-trivial, as the poses used for transformation affect both optimization stability and the consistency between training and inference. AnySplat uses predicted poses for transformation during training, improving consistency with inference but introducing scene-dependent pose perturbations that destabilize the learning of geometry and Gaussian attributes. In contrast, WorldMirror uses ground-truth poses for canonical transformation, which stabilizes Gaussian parameter learning but introduces a discrepancy between training and inference. In addition, both methods directly couple pose supervision with Gaussian reconstruction, introducing competing optimization objectives. This coupling becomes especially detrimental when residual pose errors perturb the canonical transformation used for rendering supervision. To remove this coupling, recent methods [11, 3] adopt a self-supervised formulation. As shown in Fig. 1(c), they discard explicit pose supervision and optimize Gaussian reconstruction solely through rendering supervision. Although this design removes the need for pose supervision, it still relies on predicted poses for canonical transformation during training. Consequently, pose errors still perturb the optimization of Gaussian geometry and attributes. In addition, without direct 3D constraints, these methods may produce visually plausible but geometrically unreliable reconstructions [12], restricting their applicability in geometry-sensitive tasks.

These observations reveal a key challenge: how can pose-free feed-forward 3DGS effectively exploit pose supervision during training while maintaining stable learning under residual pose errors? Although YoNoSplat [13] mixes predicted and ground-truth poses during training, predicted poses are sampled with a low probability. As a result, this strategy only weakly exposes the model to inference-time pose errors and still allows noisy supervision to affect Gaussian attributes when predicted poses are selected.

To address this challenge, we propose SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework with decoupled geometry and attribute branches, as shown in Fig. 1(d). This design separates geometry and camera estimation from Gaussian attribute prediction, reducing the interference between pose errors and attribute learning. We further introduce a progressive refinement pipeline with Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC). FGPR refines the initial camera poses using flow-based correlation features and differentiable bundle adjustment (DBA). RGC corrects the initial point maps using depth residuals produced by FGPR and intermediate geometry features. The refined poses stabilize canonical transformations, and the corrected point maps improve Gaussian center accuracy. Together, they reduce the discrepancy between training and inference and improve the consistency between the refined camera poses and the Gaussian centers.

In addition, we design a pose-aware dual-path training strategy that prevents the attribute branch from overfitting to alignments corrupted by residual pose errors. Specifically, either ground-truth poses or predicted poses are selected to transform Gaussian primitives into a canonical coordinate system during training. When ground-truth poses are used, the model learns geometry reconstruction and Gaussian attribute prediction under reliable alignment. When predicted poses are used, we mainly optimize the geometry branch and pose estimation modules, preventing the attribute branch from overfitting to residual pose errors. This asymmetric optimization stabilizes Gaussian attribute learning and improves geometry robustness under pose uncertainty. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework with a geometry-attribute decoupled architecture. By separating geometry and camera estimation from Gaussian attribute prediction, the framework suppresses error propagation from inaccurate pose estimates and improves the reliability of Gaussian parameter generation.

  • •

    We introduce a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline consisting of FGPR and RGC to enhance pose and Gaussian alignment. FGPR iteratively refines camera poses by combining flow-based correlation features with differentiable bundle adjustment. RGC then corrects local point maps using depth residuals from FGPR, improving the consistency between refined camera poses and Gaussian centers.

  • •

    We develop a pose-aware dual-path training strategy that integrates mixed-pose canonical transformation with asymmetric branch optimization. This strategy uses ground-truth poses to provide reliable attribute supervision, while using predicted poses to regularize geometry learning against scene-dependent pose errors.

    • II Related Work

    II-ANovel View Synthesis with Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

    Early image-based rendering methods [14, 15, 16] synthesize novel views by resampling or blending images captured from nearby viewpoints. These methods demonstrated the possibility of photorealistic view synthesis without fully explicit 3D reconstruction, but they often require dense image capture, calibrated cameras, or approximate geometry to handle large viewpoint changes and occlusions. With the advent of deep learning, learning-based NVS methods [17, 18]learn the geometry of scenes and appearance priors from data, improving flexibility under sparse-view inputs. NeRF [19] represents a scene as a continuous radiance field optimized from posed images and renders novel views via volumetric ray marching, which incurs substantial computational cost. To improve efficiency, follow-up works [20, 21, 22] introduced compact encodings or hybrid scene representations to accelerate rendering, but they still struggle to achieve real-time performance. Motivated by this limitation, 3DGS [4] and its variants [23, 24, 25] adopt explicit Gaussian primitives for scene representation, achieving high-fidelity novel view synthesis with real-time rendering efficiency. However, both NeRF and 3DGS pipelines typically rely on per-scene optimization. Recent methods extend 3DGS to sparse input views by introducing diffusion priors [26] or geometric constraints [27]. This has motivated recent feed-forward methods for NeRF [28, 29, 30] as well as feed-forward 3DGS methods [31, 32, 33, 34]. More recently, DepthSplat [35] and ProSplat [36] extend this paradigm to sparse multi-view or wide-baseline settings. In addition, recent works [37, 38, 39] decouple Gaussian primitives from pixel-aligned locations, resulting in a more flexible representation.

    Nevertheless, most of them still assume known camera poses or rely on pose-conditioned geometric cues, which limits their applicability to casually captured, unposed image collections. In contrast, our work targets pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, where camera poses, geometry, and Gaussian attributes must be jointly predicted under residual pose uncertainty.

    II-B3D Foundation Models for Geometry and Pose Priors

    Recent 3D foundation models have substantially advanced feed-forward geometry and pose estimation from unposed images. DUSt3R [40] reformulates multi-view reconstruction as point map regression from unconstrained image pairs. MASt3R [41] and its variants[42, 43] further improve dense matching accuracy and geometric consistency. Building on this line of work, VGGT [44], π³[45], and Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [46] directly predict camera poses, point maps, depth maps, and geometric tracks from a few to hundreds of views in a single forward pass, offering scalable geometry priors for downstream applications.

    These foundation models have also been increasingly adopted in feed-forward 3DGS. Splatt3R [9] and NoPoSplat [8] build upon MASt3R to obtain geometric priors and predict Gaussians in a global coordinate system from unposed images. AnySplat [1] uses VGGT as a teacher to supervise pose and geometry prediction during training. YoNoSplat [13] extends this paradigm with a π³-based architecture and introduces an intrinsic condition embedding to handle unknown camera intrinsics. AirSplat [47] leverages DA3 as a frozen geometry foundation model and trains a Gaussian generation module on top of its priors. Collectively, these methods demonstrate that 3D foundation models have become a powerful source of geometric priors for pose-free feed-forward 3DGS.

    II-CPose-Free Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

    Pose-free feed-forward 3DGS reconstructs Gaussian representations directly from unposed images, avoiding camera calibration at inference time. Existing methods mainly fall into two categories. The first line exploits 3D foundation models to provide geometry and camera priors. Methods built on DUSt3R [48] or MASt3R [9, 8, 49, 10, 50] recover geometry and camera poses before Gaussian prediction. However, these methods are mostly tailored to sparse input views, which limits their scalability to denser multi-view reconstruction. Recent methods [1, 13, 47, 51] improve scalability by using visual geometry foundation models that jointly predict point maps and camera poses in a single forward pass [44, 45, 46]. However, their Gaussian reconstruction remains sensitive to pose accuracy, because residual pose errors can perturb the transformation of Gaussian centers and introduce noisy supervision into the optimization of Gaussian geometry and attributes.

    Another line of work removes 3D supervision and trains pose-free models with self-supervised rendering objectives [52, 53, 11, 3]. Although these methods avoid explicit pose supervision, pose estimation, geometry prediction, and Gaussian attribute generation are optimized in a coupled manner through rendering losses. Consequently, pose and geometry errors may be absorbed by Gaussian attributes, leading to visually plausible but geometrically unreliable reconstructions [12].

    In contrast, our work focuses on the practical setting where explicit 3D supervision is available. We study how to effectively exploit 3D foundation priors for dense-view pose-free feed-forward 3DGS while preventing pose-corrupted supervision from destabilizing Gaussian geometry and attribute learning.

    III Method

    III-AProblem Formulation
