    Given N unposed input views I={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, where Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3, the goal is to reconstruct a set of 3D Gaussian primitives for novel view synthesis. Each primitive is defined as

    g_i,j=(μ_i,j, c_i,j, r_i,j, s_i,j, α_i,j),

    		(1)

    and the complete Gaussian representation is written as

    G={g_i,j}_i=1,…,N; j=1,…,HW.

    		(2)

    The components μ∈ℝ³, r∈ℝ⁴, s∈ℝ³, α∈ℝ₊, and c∈ℝ^3×(k+1)² correspond to the 3D position, quaternion rotation, scaling factor, opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients of degree k, respectively. We assume known camera intrinsics, which are directly obtained from the capture device. In addition, the model predicts the camera poses {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N for all input views. Formally, the feed-forward model f_θ parameterized by θ learns the mapping

    f_θ:{Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N↦(G, {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N).

    		(3)

    III-BPipeline

    As illustrated in Fig. 2, SG-Splat decouples geometry and attribute modeling into two independent branches, each consisting of an encoder and a decoder. Given the input images, the two branches produce a geometry token zᵢᵍ, a camera token zᵢᶜ, and an attribute token zᵢᵃ for the i-th input view. The geometry token zᵢᵍ and attribute token zᵢᵃ are both of size ℝ^(l+5)×d, while the camera token zᵢᶜ is of size ℝ^(l/4+5)×d/4, where l=4HW/p² denotes the number of image tokens, and the additional five tokens are register tokens following π³[45]. Here, p=14 is the patch size and d=1024 is the token dimension.

    The geometry token and the camera token are then fed into a point head and a camera head to predict an initial local point map M̂ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ and an initial camera pose P̂ᵢ for each input view, respectively. The predicted pose is further refined by the proposed Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) module, which iteratively updates the pose for T rounds and produces the refined pose P̃ᵢ together with depth residual cues for geometric correction. The initial local point map M̂ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ is then refined by the Residual-Guided Geometry Correction module to obtain the refined local point map M̃ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ. Subsequently, M̃ᵢˡᵒᶜᵃˡ is transformed from the local camera coordinate system into the shared canonical space, yielding the global Gaussian centers {μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ}ⱼ₌₁^HW.

    In parallel, the attribute token is fed into a Gaussian head to predict the remaining Gaussian attributes, which are combined with the transformed Gaussian centers to form the complete Gaussian representation:

    G={(μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ,c_i,j,r_i,j,s_i,j,α_i,j)}_i=1,…,N; j=1,…,HW.

    		(4)

    III-CFlow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR)

    Inspired by DROID-SLAM[54], we adopt an iterative pose refinement module to further correct the initial camera parameters P̂ᵢ, as shown in Fig. 4. Given the input images Iᵢ, initial camera parametersP̂ᵢ, and initial depth estimates D̂ᵢ from the z-axis M̂ᵢ, the module constructs low-based correlation features and optical flow of camera motion to refine poses iteratively.

    Inverse Depth Normalization

    To improve robustness to scene-scale variation, we use normalized inverse depth. First, we convert depth to inverse depth:

    d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ=(1)/(D̂ᵢ), d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ∈ℝ^H^′×W^′,

    		(5)

    where H^′=H/8 and W^′=W/8. We then normalize the inverse depth using only valid values,

    d̂ᵢ=(d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ)/(mean({d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ[d̂ᵢʳᵃʷ>τ]}ᵢ₌₁^N)),

    		(6)

    where τ=0.05 filters out extremely small inverse-depth values corresponding to very distant points. This normalization maintains a consistent numerical scale for the geometric input, thereby improving the robustness of pose refinement.

    Feature Extraction

    For feature extraction, input images are processed by a feature encoder and a context encoder, producing two dense feature maps at 1/8 image resolution. The feature encoder is used to compute 4D correlation volumes[55]Cᵢⱼ∈ℝ^H^′×W^′×H^′×W^′ for each pair of overlapping images (i,j). Then, a correlation lookup operator takes a H^′×W^′ grid of query coordinates and retrieves the values within a local square neighborhood of radius r from Cᵢⱼ, producing Corᵢⱼ∈ℝ^H^′×W^′×(2r+1)². The context features are injected into the update network during iterative refinement.

    Input

    Under the current pose estimates P̂ᵢ and P̂ⱼ and the inverse depth d̂ᵢ, we warp the pixel grid pᵢ from view i to view j to obtain the correspondence field:

    pᵢⱼ=Π (P̂ⱼ⁻¹∘P̂ᵢ∘Π⁻¹(pᵢ,d̂ᵢ)),

    		(7)

    where pᵢ is the pixel grid of view i, and Π⁻¹ and Π denote back-projection and projection, respectively. Based on the correspondence field pᵢ, we derive the optical flow of camera motion Fᵢ as the displacement between the projected and original pixel locations. Consequently, the update module takes the context feature h_ctx, the correlation feature Corᵢⱼ, and the optical flow Fᵢ as inputs.

    Update

    The update operator is implemented as a 3×3 convolutional GRU initialized with the context feature h_ctx. To improve feature fusion, the correlation feature Corᵢⱼ and the optical flow Fᵢ are first encoded by two convolutional layers before being injected into the GRU, while the context feature h_ctx is incorporated through element-wise addition.

    In iteration t, the operator updates the hidden state and predicts a correction term Δpᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾ for the current correspondence field pᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾:

    Δpᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾=Update (h_ctx, Corᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾, Fᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾),

    		(8)

    pᵢⱼ^*(t)=pᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾+Δpᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾.

    		(9)

    The corrected correspondence field is then fed into the DBA [56] module together with the current pose and inverse depth estimates P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾ and d̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾, to jointly update them as P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾ and d̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾. After T iterations, the final refined pose and depth are given by

    P̃ᵢ=P̃ᵢ⁽ᵀ⁾, D̃ᵢ=(1)/(d̃ᵢ⁽ᵀ⁾).

    		(10)

    The depth residual used for subsequent geometry correction is defined as

    ΔD̂ᵢ=D̃ᵢ-D̂ᵢ,

    		(11)

    where D̂ᵢ denotes the initial depth estimate.

    III-DResidual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC).

    To further improve the coarse local geometry, we introduce a lightweight Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC) module, as shown in Fig. 4. RGC takes the initial local point map together with the depth residual from FGPR as input, so that local geometry correction is explicitly guided by residual geometric cues after pose refinement.

    For each input view, the initial point map M̂ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 is concatenated with the FGPR depth residual ΔD̂ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×1 and converted into patch tokens zᵢʳ∈ℝ^4HW/p²×D through a patch embedding layer:

    zᵢʳ=PatchEmbed (Concat(M̂ᵢ,ΔD̂ᵢ)),

    		(12)

    where p=14 denotes the patch size and D=1024 is the token dimension. The residual tokens are then combined with the geometry tokens zᵢᵍ from the geometry branch, which share the same spatial resolution. We concatenate them along the channel dimension and use an MLP to obtain the correction tokens:

    zᵢ^δ=MLP (Concat_c(zᵢʳ,zᵢᵍ)),

    		(13)

    where zᵢ^δ∈ℝ^4HW/p²×D. The correction tokens are decoded into a dense point-wise correction field ΔM̂ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 through linear projection and pixel-shuffle upsampling:

    ΔM̂ᵢ=PS (Linear (zᵢ^δ)),

    		(14)

    where PS(·) denotes pixel-shuffle. Rather than directly predicting additive offsets, the module estimates a bounded multiplicative correction,

    Sᵢ=1+β\tanh(ΔM̂ᵢ),

    		(15)

    which is applied element-wise to the initial point map:

    M̃ᵢ=M̂ᵢ⊙Sᵢ,

    		(16)

    where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, and β=0.2 constrains the correction magnitude to avoid excessive corrections that could disrupt the coarse geometric structure.

    This design preserves the coarse geometric prior while enabling spatially adaptive geometry correction. Compared with direct offset regression, the multiplicative formulation yields more stable updates and is less prone to over-correction. By conditioning the refinement on FGPR depth residuals, the refined point map becomes better aligned with the corrected camera poses, providing more reliable Gaussian centers for subsequent 3D Gaussian prediction.

    III-EDual-Path Training Strategy

    We adopt a dual-branch design for SG-Splat, where the geometry branch estimates camera poses and local Gaussian centers, and the attribute branch predicts Gaussian attributes. This separation reduces error propagation from inaccurate poses and improves the reliability of Gaussian parameter generation. However, 3DGS rendering requires transforming local Gaussian centers into a shared canonical space, making cross-view alignment sensitive to pose errors. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a mixed-pose canonical transformation with asymmetric optimization, as shown in Fig. 5.

    Mixed-pose canonical transformation

    The refined point map M̃ᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 provides local Gaussian centers for the i-th input view. After flattening the spatial dimensions, we obtain {μ_i,jˡᵒᶜᵃˡ}ⱼ₌₁^HW. During training, the pose used for canonical transformation is sampled from either the ground-truth pose or the refined predicted pose:

    P̄ᵢ=\begincasesPᵢ^*,&z=1, P̃ᵢ,&z=0,\endcases z∼Bernoulli(0.5),

    		(17)

    where Pᵢ^* and P̃ᵢ denote the ground-truth pose and refined predicted pose, respectively. The binary variable z is sampled once per training scene and shared across all input views. Each local center is transformed into the canonical space by

    μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ=P̄ᵢ∘μ_i,jˡᵒᶜᵃˡ.

    		(18)

    The attribute branch predicts the remaining Gaussian attributes for each center:

    {(c_i,j,r_i,j,s_i,j,α_i,j)}ⱼ₌₁^HW.

    		(19)

    Together with the transformed centers {μ_i,jᵍˡᵒᵇᵃˡ}ⱼ₌₁^HW, these predicted parameters form the Gaussian primitives for rendering. For N input views, the model generates N×H×W primitives in total.

    Asymmetric optimization under mixed poses

    The optimization rule depends on the sampled pose in Eq. (17). When z=1, ground-truth poses provide reliable canonical transformation and clean rendering supervision. We therefore update the full model, including the geometry branch, pose refinement module, and attribute branch. This path stabilizes Gaussian attribute learning under well-aligned transformations. When z=0, refined predicted poses are used, matching the inference setting where ground-truth poses are unavailable. However, residual pose errors may misalign Gaussian centers across views and introduce noisy rendering supervision. To avoid corrupting attribute learning, we detach the rendering gradients from the attribute branch and use them only to optimize the geometry branch.

    This asymmetric design combines the advantages of both paths. The ground-truth-pose path provides reliable supervision for Gaussian attribute prediction, while the predicted-pose path exposes the geometry branch to the pose distribution used during inference. By alternating between them, the proposed strategy reduces the discrepancy between training and inference and prevents the attribute branch from absorbing pose-induced noise.

    III-FTraining Objectives

    Progressive Decoupled Training

    Directly integrating FGPR and RGC into the SG-Splat pipeline leads to unstable optimization, as pose refinement, geometry correction, and Gaussian attribute prediction are optimized simultaneously. The resulting entanglement makes it difficult for the refinement modules to learn reliable corrections from noisy pose and geometry estimates. To address this issue, we adopt a progressive training strategy that decouples geometry and appearance optimization across four stages, including coupled pretraining, pose refinement, point refinement, and final joint optimization.

    Stage I: Coupled pretraining. We first train a coupled base model without FGPR and RGC, including the encoder, decoder, point head, camera head, and Gaussian head. This stage provides a stable initialization for coarse geometry reconstruction and Gaussian attribute prediction.

    Stage II: Pose refinement via FGPR. Based on the pretrained coupled model, we duplicate the encoder and decoder to initialize separate geometry and appearance branches. The point and camera heads are assigned to the geometry branch, while the Gaussian head is assigned to the appearance branch. All other modules are frozen, and only FGPR is optimized to learn stable pose refinement.

    Stage III: Point refinement via RGC. We then freeze the remaining components and optimize only the RGC, enabling geometry correction under the refined poses without interference from appearance optimization. During the refinement stages, local points are transformed into the canonical space using ground-truth poses, which removes stochastic perturbations from inaccurate pose predictions and provides stable supervision for pose and geometry refinement.

    Stage IV: Joint optimization. Finally, we fine-tune the full dual-path architecture in an end-to-end manner. With stabilized geometry and pose estimates as initialization, this stage jointly optimizes geometry and appearance, improving reconstruction fidelity, view consistency, and robustness to residual pose errors.

    Training Loss

    Our model is a joint learning framework and trained with a multi-task loss function comprising two components: camera pose loss, and 3DGS rendering loss. As for the pose loss, we only explicitly supervise the refined poses produced by the FGPR module. Given the ground-truth poses {Pᵢ^*}ᵢ₌₁^N, we supervise the refined pose estimates {P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾}ᵢ₌₁^N over T iterations by

    Lₚₒₛₑ=∑ₜ₌₁ᵀγᵀ⁻ᵗ∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥\log (Pᵢ^*⁻¹P̃ᵢ⁽ᵗ⁾)∥₂,

    		(20)

    where \log(·) denotes the SE(3) logarithm map and γ=0.9 emphasizes later refinement iterations. We do not impose direct depth supervision because 3DGS renders both images and depths via α-blending, such that accurate pixel-level depth does not necessarily imply accurate rendered depth. In addition, the predicted depths are defined in the camera coordinate system, making it difficult to enforce cross-view consistency.

    The rendering loss is defined as the sum of the MSE and LPIPS [58] losses over all target views rendered in a single forward pass:

    L_rgb=∑ₙ₌₁^N_tgt(MSE(Ĩⁿ,I_gtⁿ)+λ LPIPS(Ĩⁿ,I_gtⁿ)),

    		(21)

    where N_tgt denotes the number of target views in each forward pass, Ĩⁿ is the rendered image, and I_gtⁿ is the corresponding ground-truth image. The overall training objective is then defined as

    L=L_rgb+β Lₚₒₛₑ,

    		(22)

    where β controls the relative importance of pose supervision.

    IV Experiments

    IV-AExperimental Setup

    Implementation Details

    For both geometry and appearance branches, the encoder employs the DINOv2 Large model with 24 attention layers, and the decoder consists of 18 alternating-attention layers. The backbones, encoders, decoders, point head, camera head, and Gaussian head are initialized from the pretrained YoNoSplat [13] weights. For FGPR, the feature encoder, context encoder, and update operator are initialized from the pretrained DROID-SLAM model [54]. The newly introduced layers are initialized to zero, so that they do not perturb the pretrained representations at the beginning of training. During training, we randomly select the number of input views between 2 and 32 and sample 4 target views. All experiments are conducted at a resolution of 224×224. We train the model on a single NVIDIA L20 GPU with a batch size of 1 for 100k steps. In the FGPR module, the number of pose refinement iterations T is set to 2. For the training objective, we set λ=0.05 for the LPIPS term and β=0.02 for the pose supervision term.

    Datasets

    We train and evaluate our model on the DL3DV [57] and RealEstate10K [59] datasets. DL3DV contains 51.3 million frames captured from 10,510 real-world scenes, spanning 65 point-of-interest categories. We use the full training set for model training, while excluding the 140 benchmark scenes to avoid potential evaluation leakage. We evaluate novel view synthesis under different input-view settings, including 12, 18, 24, and 32 views, with 8 target views used for evaluation. RealEstate10K consists of real-estate videos collected from YouTube, where diverse views of a scene are obtained by sampling frames at different timestamps. We use this dataset to evaluate sparse-view reconstruction with 6 input views.

    Evaluation Metrics

    We evaluate novel view synthesis using the widely adopted metrics PSNR, SSIM[60], and LPIPS [58]. For pose estimation, we follow prior works [1, 13] and report the area under the cumulative angular pose error curve (AUC) at angular thresholds of 5^∘, 10^∘, and 20^∘.

    Baselines

    We compare our method with representative state-of-the-art feed-forward 3DGS methods under both pose-free and pose-dependent settings. For pose-free reconstruction, we consider the following methods:

  • •

    YoNoSplat[13] is a unified feed-forward 3DGS model designed for both pose-dependent and pose-free reconstruction. It predicts per-view Gaussian primitives and camera poses and aggregates them into a global representation using the predicted camera poses. In our experiments, we use the publicly released checkpoints trained on DL3DV and RealEstate10K at 224×224 resolution, respectively.

  • •

    NoPoSplat[8] reconstructs 3D Gaussians from sparse unposed images by anchoring one input view as the canonical coordinate system, thereby avoiding explicit local-to-global Gaussian transformation with estimated poses. For a fair comparison, we retrain NoPoSplat under the corresponding multi-view settings on each dataset for 150K steps. On RealEstate10K, we initialize the model from the official pretrained 3-view weights, while keeping the remaining training configurations consistent with the original paper.

  • •

    AnySplat[1] targets feed-forward 3DGS from unconstrained image collections. It jointly predicts Gaussian parameters, depth maps, and camera poses from uncalibrated inputs, with geometry supervision provided by pretrained VGGT priors.

  • •

    WorldMirror[2] is a general-purpose feed-forward 3D geometric prediction model that can incorporate different geometric priors and output multiple 3D representations, including camera parameters, depth maps, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. We use its publicly released checkpoint trained on multiple large-scale datasets, including DL3DV and RealEstate10K.

    • We further compare with pose-dependent feed-forward 3DGS methods, where ground-truth camera poses are provided as input:

  • •

    MVSplat[61] constructs plane-sweeping cost volumes from posed sparse-view images and uses the estimated depth maps to localize Gaussian centers. For RealEstate10K, we evaluate the official checkpoint released by the authors. For DL3DV, no official checkpoint is available for our multi-view setting. Therefore, we retrain MVSplat for 300K iterations following the original training protocol and extend the number of input views to 32 views.

  • •

    DepthSplat[35] enhances cost-volume depth estimation with pretrained monocular depth features, leading to more robust Gaussian center prediction under challenging matching conditions. We use the official checkpoints trained on DL3DV and RealEstate10K.

    • For camera pose estimation, we additionally report results from recent feed-forward 3D Foundation Models, including MASt3R[41], VGGT[44] and π³[45].

    IV-BNovel View Synthesis

    Tab. I and Tab. II show the quantitative results for novel view synthesis on DL3DV and RealEstate10K. The symbol p indicates whether ground-truth camera poses are provided as input. On DL3DV, our method achieves the best results across all evaluated view settings in both pose-dependent and pose-free configurations. In the posed setting, SG-Splat achieves the best quantitative results across all view settings. This demonstrates that the proposed framework remains effective even when accurate camera poses are available. In the pose-free setting, SG-Splat also achieves the best quantitative results across all view settings, with a maximum PSNR gain of 0.91 dB over the second-best result. Although the absolute difficulty varies across view settings, the relative advantage of our method becomes more pronounced under denser input settings. This property is particularly important for feed-forward 3DGS, where dense inputs introduce more view-dependent Gaussian primitives, making accurate geometric correction crucial for mitigating pose-induced errors and ensuring reliable Gaussian reconstruction.

    On RealEstate10K, SG-Splat further demonstrates its effectiveness under the pose-free sparse-view setting. It achieves the best overall quantitative performance across the evaluation metrics, outperforming all baselines. This confirms that our method remains robust in sparse real-world scenes, rather than being limited to dense-view reconstruction.

    Qualitative comparisons are shown in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7. Our method produces sharper textures, cleaner object boundaries, and more complete scene structures. In contrast, AnySplat tends to generate blurred details because inaccurate predicted poses perturb the transformed Gaussian centers and degrade the supervision of Gaussian attributes. Other methods often suffer from distorted geometry or missing structures due to inaccurate pose estimation and geometric reconstruction. With the proposed FGPR module, our method improves pose accuracy before Gaussian reconstruction, leading to more reliable geometric alignment and more stable Gaussian parameter prediction. As a result, the rendered novel views are visually sharper and geometrically more consistent.

    IV-CRelative Pose Estimation

    We further evaluate the relative pose estimation on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, as reported in Tab. III. DL3DV is evaluated under dense-view settings with 12, 18, 24, and 32 input views, while RealEstate10K is evaluated under the sparse-view setting with 6 input views. The comparison includes pose-free feed-forward 3DGS methods and 3D foundation models, including MASt3R, VGGT, and π³.

    Our method achieves the best or comparable-best pose estimation accuracy across the evaluated settings. Our method achieves the highest AUC values on DL3DV under most evaluated view settings and consistently outperforms the compared methods on RealEstate10K across all AUC thresholds. The consistent performance across dense-view DL3DV and sparse-view RealEstate10K demonstrates the robustness of the proposed pose estimation framework.

    The comparison with π³ and VGGT is particularly informative. These models are trained on large-scale multi-dataset corpora that include DL3DV and RealEstate10K, whereas our method is designed and trained for the feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction task. Despite this strong comparison setting, our method still achieves superior or comparable pose accuracy on most evaluated protocols. These results indicate that the proposed FGPR module effectively improves both fine-grained pose accuracy and coarse relative pose estimation, which further contributes to the superior rendering quality reported in Tab. I and Tab. II.

    IV-DAblation Study

    We conduct ablation experiments on DL3DV under the 24-view setting. The base model adopts the same architecture but excludes the proposed Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC) modules, and is trained with ground-truth (GT) poses. We progressively incorporate FGPR, different pose selection strategies, and RGC to evaluate their individual contributions to rendering performance.

    Effect of FGPR

    As shown in Tab. IV, introducing FGPR alone (FGPR*) leads to only marginal improvements over the base model. This suggests that while pose refinement is beneficial, its effectiveness is limited when optimized in isolation with all other components frozen, and cannot fully compensate for pose inaccuracies during training.

    Effect of Dual-Branch Pose Selection Strategy

    We further investigate different pose selection strategies for training FGPR. Training with predicted poses (Pred Pose) leads to a noticeable performance degradation, indicating that noisy pose estimates introduce instability and hinder effective optimization. In contrast, using only GT poses achieves strong performance but suffers from exposure bias, as the model is not exposed to pose perturbations during training. Our proposed dual-branch strategy (Mix Pose), which adaptively combines predicted and GT poses, achieves the best results. This demonstrates that jointly leveraging accurate poses and realistic pose perturbations effectively reduces the discrepancy between training and inference, resulting in more robust rendering quality.

    Effect of RGC

    Building upon FGPR with the proposed dual-path training strategy, further incorporating RGC consistently improves all metrics. This suggests that point-map correction driven by depth residuals improves the reliability of Gaussian centers, thereby enhancing rendering fidelity.

    Effect of the Number of Iterations

    Tab. V evaluates the effect of the number of FGPR iterations T. A single iteration (T=1) yields suboptimal performance, indicating that one-step refinement is insufficient to fully correct pose errors. Increasing T to 2 significantly improves all metrics, demonstrating that iterative refinement is effective in enhancing pose quality and rendering accuracy. Increasing T from 2 to 3 slightly improves LPIPS and AUC@5∘, but reduces PSNR and SSIM while increasing computational cost. We therefore set T=2 as a practical trade-off between reconstruction quality, pose accuracy, and efficiency.

    V Conclusion

    In this paper, we presented SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for robust reconstruction under inaccurate pose estimation. To reduce the impact of residual pose errors, SG-Splat decouples geometry estimation from Gaussian attribute prediction and introduces a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline with Flow-Guided Pose Refinement and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction. We further proposed a dual-path training strategy that mixes ground-truth and predicted poses with asymmetric optimization, improving robustness to pose errors while maintaining reliable pose supervision. Extensive experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K show that SG-Splat achieves improved novel view synthesis and relative pose estimation under both sparse and dense input-view settings.

    Despite these improvements, several limitations remain. First, our method assumes known camera intrinsics, limiting its applicability to in-the-wild images with unavailable or unreliable intrinsics. Second, pixel-aligned feed-forward reconstruction tends to produce view-dependent and redundant Gaussian primitives, resulting in less compact representations. Third, high-resolution reconstruction still incurs substantial training and inference costs. Future work will explore intrinsic-free reconstruction, more efficient high-resolution architectures, and non-pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction to obtain more compact and effective 3DGS representations.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 复杂区域不该和高斯一样稀疏：用局部熵当复杂度先验，人物高斯 PSNR 最多提 2.30 dB、还能跑 7.7 FPS ｜ Complexity-guided Regularization for Generalizable Human Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：用几何与纹理的局部熵当复杂度先验，既约束高斯密度也决定 patch 采样位置。

要点：

  • 问题：泛化型人物高斯在细节密集区渲染发糊，因为这些方法没有约束高斯该放多密，复杂区域被粗放地摆几个高斯
  • 做法：用服装人体几何与纹理的局部熵算复杂度先验，用它阻止高斯在复杂区域被粗放放置，同时按该先验主要从复杂区域采局部 patch，让监督集中在细节上
  • PSNR 提升：DNA-Rendering +0.79 dB、ZJU-MoCap +1.33 dB（对比 RoGSplat），THuman2.0 +1.50 dB、X-Humans +2.30 dB（对比 GHGS-MVSC）；另一组对比里 +4.12 dB、LPIPS 降 59.31，同时 7.7 FPS 对 1.0 FPS

为什么值得看：「高斯该放多密」是 3DGS 系的通用难题，用信息熵做成可计算先验，比再加一个损失项更有依据；而且它同时解决了训练时的 patch 采样偏向问题，是一处改动解两个坑。

中文摘要：泛化型人物高斯泼溅已能从多视图图像合成未见过的人，但细节仍然糊：根本原因是这些方法没有约束高斯的放置密度，几何与纹理都很复杂的区域被粗放地摆上少量高斯。作者提出复杂度引导的正则：先用服装人体在几何与纹理上的局部熵计算复杂度先验，用它阻止高斯在复杂区域被粗放放置，从而保住精细结构；同一个先验还用来决定训练时局部 patch 的采样位置，让监督集中到真正复杂的区域。在多个基准上方法达到 SOTA 且维持实时：DNA-Rendering 上比次优的 RoGSplat 高 0.79 dB、ZJU-MoCap 高 1.33 dB，THuman2.0 与 X-Humans 上分别高 1.50 与 2.30 dB；另一组对比中 PSNR 提升 4.12 dB、LPIPS 降低 59.31，同时做到 7.7 FPS。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-10-28

Complexity-guided Regularization for Generalizable Human Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

Recent studies on generalizable human Gaussian splatting have achieved the notable progress in synthesizing novel views of unseen human subjects from multi-view images. Despite this progress, existing methods still struggle to represent fine-grained details of human subjects, which inherently involve high geometric and textural complexity. This is because previous methods do not impose a constraint on how densely Gaussians are placed, which often leads to blurry rendering results in complex regions. To address this problem, we propose a complexity-guided regularization scheme. The key idea is to leverage a complexity prior computed via the local entropy in geometric and textural characteristics of a clothed human. This effectively prevents Gaussians from being coarsely placed in complex regions, which facilitates the faithful reconstruction of intricate structures. Furthermore, we sample local patches predominantly from complex regions according to this complexity prior, which allows the model to be sufficiently supervised by local details. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method delivers state-of-the-art performance while maintaining the real-time inference speed in generalizable human Gaussian splatting. The code and model are publicly available at link111https://github.com/DCVL-3D/CGR-GS_release.

1 Introduction

Realistic 3D human reconstruction has gained the significant interest due to its wide range of applications in virtual reality, telepresence, gaming, content creation, etc. In recent literature, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [1], which explicitly represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussian primitives while enabling real-time rendering, has been widely adopted for this task. Most recently, various studies [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] have begun to integrate human body templates, e.g., SMPL [9], to improve the rendering performance. However, since previous methods rely on the per-subject optimization scheme, they cannot be directly applied to unseen individuals without repeating the entire training procedure, which severely restricts their practicality in real-world scenarios.

To overcome the aforementioned limitation, recent studies have explored generalizable approaches, which regress Gaussian attributes for unseen human subjects in a single forward pass. Due to the absence of the iterative refinement process, the majority of generalizable methods rely on an explicit structural prior to mitigate the difficulty of directly predicting Gaussian attributes. For example, some methods [10, 11, 12] have exploited geometric constraints between view pairs as a structural prior to determine the spatial layout of Gaussians. A skinned human model has also been employed [13, 14, 15] to enable the feed-forward model to place Gaussians directly on the body surface. Even though considerable efforts have been devoted to determining where to place Gaussians via feed-forward approaches, how densely they should be placed across different regions of the human subject has not been sufficiently explored.

In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for effectively handling generalizable human Gaussian splatting. Due to the inherent smoothness of Gaussian primitives, Gaussians need to be densely placed to faithfully reconstruct high-frequency details. However, previous feed-forward methods localize Gaussians based on the pixel grid [10, 11, 12] or vertices of the skinned mesh [15, 13, 14], whose density is highly related to the image resolution or the skinned mesh template rather than the visual properties of the target subject itself. While this may not be significant in simple regions (e.g., plain areas), it often leads to an insufficient number of Gaussians in complex regions (e.g., fingers or textured clothes), which produces blurry rendering results as shown in Figs. 1(b) and (c). To deal with this problem, we propose a complexity-guided regularization scheme. The key idea is to allocate Gaussians in proportion to the local complexity of the clothed human mesh. Specifically, we define the complexity prior as the entropy of the local geometric and textural information around each vertex of the human mesh. Guided by this prior, we regularize the local density of Gaussians to be positively correlated with the complexity. This helps the model faithfully reconstruct high-frequency details with sufficient Gaussians, as shown in Fig. 1(d). Moreover, we find that supervising the model with the entire image is suboptimal for reconstructing fine-grained details. This is because supervisory signals from complex regions, which often occupy only a small portion of the human-centric image, e.g., fingers, facial features, etc., are easily dominated by those from surrounding simple regions. Accordingly, during the training phase, we use the complexity prior as sampling weights to select local patches, where regions of higher complexity are more frequently sampled. This training strategy enables the model to receive sufficient supervision on fine details. The main contribution of the proposed method can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We define a complexity prior as a per-vertex scalar value, which is computed via the local entropy in geometric and textural characteristics of the clothed human mesh. Leveraging this prior, we propose a novel regularization scheme to guide the model to adjust the local Gaussian density according to the complexity. This encourages the model to allocate Gaussians densely in complex regions, which enables faithful reconstruction of fine-grained details.

  • •

    To effectively provide sufficient supervisory signals on intricate details, we introduce a patch-based training strategy, which samples local patches with probability proportional to the complexity prior.

    • 2 Related work

    Per-subject optimization-based 3DGS for human rendering. Motivated by the great success of 3D Gaussian splatting [1] in novel view synthesis, several studies have begun to apply 3DGS to human rendering based on the point-based representation. For example, Gaussian points are initialized on faces of the human mesh and optimized to represent the detailed appearance while preserving the geometric structure of the target subject [5, 7]. On the other hand, other methods [16, 4, 3, 2, 6, 8] optimize Gaussian attributes to reconstruct the human in a canonical pose, which are rendered in arbitrary poses via forward skinning. Although these approaches have demonstrated the impressive performance, they typically require the per-subject optimization, which restricts their generalizability to unseen human subjects.

    Generalizable 3DGS for human rendering. To overcome this limitation, recent studies have explored generalizable human Gaussian splatting, which regress Gaussian attributes for unseen subjects in a single forward pass. As a pioneer, Zheng et al.[10] estimated per-pixel Gaussian attributes based on the depth map, which is predicted through stereo matching between adjacent views. In a similar vein, Hu et al.[11] improved the regression process by employing the 1D-window attention along epipolar lines between view pairs. More recently, Kim et al.[12] leveraged a foundation model [17] to inject the implicit 3D geometric knowledge, while recalibrating multi-view features via semantic consistency-based cross-view attention, which helps the model robustly estimate Gaussian attributes in visually complex regions. Instead of estimating per-pixel Gaussian attributes, skinned human models have been adopted as a structural prior to directly place Gaussians on the body surface. In this direction, Wen et al.[14] attached Gaussians to the skinned mesh surface and iteratively refined Gaussian attributes through a feedback mechanism. Similarly, Xiao et al.[15] densified SMPL vertices to align with the actual human geometry and predicted Gaussian attributes on such densified points. Kwon et al.[13] regressed Gaussian attributes in the 2D UV space of the SMPL template and introduced a multi-scaffold representation to effectively mitigate the geometric discrepancy between the skinned body and clothed human. While previous efforts have focused on accurately estimating the position of Gaussians, we shift our focus to how densely Gaussians should be placed and propose an effective regularization scheme, which significantly improves the rendering performance of generalizable human Gaussian splatting.

    3 Method

    3.1 Architecture details

    The overall architecture of the proposed method is shown in Fig. 2. Given N multi-view RGB images {Iₙ}ₙ₌₁^N∈ℝ^3×H×W of a clothed human subject with the corresponding Plücker ray [18] maps {Pₙ}ₙ₌₁^N∈ℝ^6×H×W and human masks {Mₙ}ₙ₌₁^N∈{0,1}^H×W, our goal is to regress a set of Gaussian attributes in a single feed-forward pass. Following previous feed-forward approaches [19, 20], each input image is concatenated with the corresponding Plücker ray map along the channel dimension, which yields a per-view feature map Ĩₙ=[Iₙ;Pₙ]∈ℝ^9×H×W. The resulting feature map Ĩₙ is partitioned into non-overlapping p×p patches, which are subsequently flattened and projected into tokens. Since the target subject only occupies a small area of the human-centric image, we discard tokens whose patch lies entirely outside the human mask Mₙ, which yields Tₙ foreground tokens for the n-th view. This significantly reduces the number of tokens fed into transformer layers, which leads to the real-time inference. Following Long-LRM++ [21], a Gaussian decoder regresses attributes of K Gaussians from each token. Specifically, the decoder predicts depth d∈ℝ, 3D spatial offset Δx∈ℝ³, scale s∈ℝ³, rotation quaternion q∈ℝ⁴, opacity o∈ℝ, and color ρ∈ℝ³. The 3D position of each Gaussian is computed by unprojecting the predicted depth d along the ray as rₒ+d r_d, which is further shifted by the spatial offset Δx. Note that rₒ∈ℝ³ and r_d∈ℝ³ denote directional vectors of the origin and the center ray of the patch, respectively. Consequently, the model produces K×T Gaussians, where T=∑ₙ₌₁^NTₙ is the total number of foreground tokens across all views, which are rasterized to synthesize the target view image.

    3.2 Complexity prior of the human subject

    A clothed human is inherently a complex subject whose surface contains structural and visual information at a wide range of spatial scales. Moreover, such complexity varies significantly across different regions of the surface. Properly accounting for this variation is essential to faithfully reconstruct the human subject. To this end, we quantitatively define the local complexity of a clothed human, which can serve as an explicit guidance signal for the reconstruction process. Specifically, we represent the clothed human as a textured mesh M=(V,F,T), whose components are defined as follows: V={vᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^|V| is the set of vertices, where vᵢ∈ℝ³ represents a point in the 3D space. F={fₖ}ₖ₌₁^|F| is the set of triangular faces, where fₖ=(v_k₁,v_k₂,v_k₃) denotes a triplet of vertices which constitute a face. T∈ℝ^H×W×3 is a UV map for the human mesh, which stores RGB color values. Each pixel in T corresponds to a point on the mesh surface via UV coordinates. On this mesh, we define the complexity prior as a scalar value cᵢ∈[0,1] for vertex vᵢ.

    Geometric complexity. We denote the set of faces including the vertex vᵢ as Fᵢ. For each vertex vᵢ, we compute an area-weighted unit normal nᵢ, which represents the dominant normal direction of the local surface as follows:

    nᵢ=(mᵢ)/(∥mᵢ∥), where mᵢ=∑_fₖ∈FᵢA_fₖ n_fₖ,

    		(1)

    where n_fₖ∈ℝ³ and A_fₖ∈ℝ_>0 denote the unit normal and the area of face fₖ, respectively. We further find a local neighborhood ℕᵢ={vⱼ:j≠i, ∥vⱼ-vᵢ∥≤r} of vᵢ within a radius r to measure how the unit normal varies around it. For neighbor vⱼ∈ℕᵢ, the angular deviation of its area-weighted unit normal nⱼ from nᵢ is defined as sᵍᵉᵒⱼ=(1-nᵢ·nⱼ)/2∈[0,1]. Subsequently, we construct a histogram pᵍᵉᵒᵢ=(pᵍᵉᵒ₁,…,pᵍᵉᵒ_B) of the deviations {sᵍᵉᵒⱼ}_j∈ℕᵢ over B equal-width bins on [0,1], where pᵍᵉᵒ_b denotes the proportion of deviations falling into bin b. The geometric complexity at vᵢ is finally computed by the normalized Shannon entropy [22] of this histogram, as follows:

    Hᵍᵉᵒᵢ=-(1)/(\log₂B)∑_b=1^Bpᵍᵉᵒ_b\log₂pᵍᵉᵒ_b.

    		(2)

    Textural complexity. Similarly, we compute the textural complexity around each vertex. The RGB color tᵢ of the vertex vᵢ is retrieved from the location (uᵢ,vᵢ) of the corresponding UV map T. For vⱼ∈ℕᵢ, the chromatic deviation of its color tⱼ from the color tᵢ is defined as sᵗᵉˣⱼ=∥tⱼ-tᵢ∥/√3∈[0,1]. Subsequently, we construct a histogram pᵗᵉˣᵢ=(pᵗᵉˣ₁,…,pᵗᵉˣ_B) of the deviations {sᵗᵉˣⱼ}_j∈ℕᵢ over B equal-width bins on [0,1], where pᵗᵉˣ_b denotes the proportion of deviations falling into bin b. The textural complexity at vᵢ is also computed by the normalized Shannon entropy [22] of this histogram, as follows:

    Hᵗᵉˣᵢ=-(1)/(\log₂B)∑_b=1^Bpᵗᵉˣ_b\log₂pᵗᵉˣ_b.

    		(3)

    Multi-scale aggregation. To account for complexity at multiple spatial scales, we repeat above computations at S different scales with radii {rₛ}ₛ₌₁^S, where rₛ is set to a different fraction of the bounding box diagonal of M. Entropies Hᵍᵉᵒ_i,s and Hᵗᵉˣ_i,s at scale s are averaged to obtain the multi-scale complexities, as follows: H̄ᵍᵉᵒᵢ=1/S∑ₛ₌₁^SHᵍᵉᵒ_i,s and H̄ᵗᵉˣᵢ=1/S∑ₛ₌₁^SHᵗᵉˣ_i,s, respectively. Consequently, the per-vertex complexity prior cᵢ is finally defined as the maximum between the geometric and textural complexities as follows:

    cᵢ=\max (H̄ᵍᵉᵒᵢ, H̄ᵗᵉˣᵢ).

    		(4)

    This maximum operation ensures a high complexity value whenever at least one of these cues shows a high degree of local variations. As shown in Figs. 3(b), (c), and (d), the complexity prior effectively captures the local variation in both geometric and textural characteristics of the clothed human, where higher values are attributed to structurally or visually intricate regions (e.g., fingers or textured clothes). The resulting complexity prior {cᵢ} serves as the guidance signal for regularization and patch-based supervision, which are explained in the following subsections.

    3.3 Complexity-guided regularization

    Due to the inherent smoothness of Gaussian primitives, the local density of Gaussians should be properly taken into account for faithfully reconstructing fine-grained details. However, previous methods allocate Gaussians without regard to the local complexity of the human subject, which leaves fine-grained regions under-represented. To address this problem, we introduce a regularization scheme, which couples the local Gaussian density with the complexity prior {cᵢ} and explicitly guides the model to allocate Gaussians densely in complex regions. An overview of this scheme is shown in Fig. 3(e). Since the complexity prior is defined at mesh vertices, we first sample a set of points on the surface of the human mesh. Specifically, we randomly sample M points on the mesh surface with the probability proportional to the area of the corresponding face fₘ. The complexity value cₘ∈[0,1] at sampled point pₘ∈ℝ³ of face fₘ is obtained by interpolating the complexity values at three vertices {vⱼ}_j∈fₘ as follows:

    cₘ=∑_j∈fₘαⱼ cⱼ,

    		(5)

    where {αⱼ}_j∈fₘ are the barycentric weights of pₘ, which satisfies pₘ=∑_j∈fₘαⱼ vⱼ and ∑_j∈fₘαⱼ=1. Following CDC-GS [23], we measure the local Gaussian density at sampled point pₘ based on the distances to the k-nearest Gaussian centers. Note that Gaussians whose opacity is below 0.1 are excluded from the nearest-neighbor search. Specifically, the local density score sₘ is defined as follows:

    sₘ=-\log (1/k∑ⱼ₌₁ᵏd_m,j+ε),

    		(6)

    where d_m,j denotes the Euclidean distance from pₘ to its j-th nearest Gaussian center and ε is a small positive constant for numerical stability. To encourage sₘ to be positively correlated with cₘ, we adopt a pairwise monotonic ranking regularization scheme. Given a pair of points on the mesh surface (pₐ,p_b) with cₐ>c_b, the regularization penalizes the case in which the point with higher complexity has a lower density score, i.e., sₐ

    L_comp=(1)/(|ℙ|)∑_(a,b)∈ℙ(cₐ-c_b)·softplus (-(sₐ-s_b)),

    		(7)

    where ℙ denotes the set of sampled pairs (a,b) and softplus(x)=\ln(1+eˣ). Each pair is weighted by the complexity gap cₐ-c_b to impose a strong penalty on pairs with a significant complexity difference. This regularization scheme encourages the model to place Gaussians densely in complex regions, which enables the faithful reconstruction of fine-grained details.

    3.4 Complexity-aware patch-based supervision

    Complex regions often occupy only a small portion of the human-centric image, which makes their supervisory signals easily dominated by those from surrounding simple regions during training. To address this issue, we introduce a patch-based supervision strategy which leverages the complexity prior to concentrate the supervisory signal on intricate regions. For target view q, we first render a 2D complexity map C^2D_q∈[0,1]^H×W by rasterizing the per-vertex complexity values {cᵢ} onto the image plane. From this map, we sample Nₚ patch centers per view with the per-pixel sampling probability given by C^2D_q. Based on sampled centers, pₛ×pₛ local patches are constructed for the supervision. During the training phase, the model is supervised on either the entire image or these local patches with the equal probability at each iteration, as shown in Fig. 2. We further adopt a progressive schedule for the size of the patch pₛ, which gradually decreases from pₘₐₓ to pₘᵢₙ during training. This provides a coarse-to-fine supervisory signal, where larger patches in the early stages capture broader structural context and smaller patches in later stages focus on fine-grained details.

    3.5 Loss function

    The proposed method is trained based on three terms, i.e., the rendering loss L_render, the depth regularization L_depth, and the proposed complexity-guided regularization L_comp. Following [20], the rendering loss L_render consists of a photometric loss L₁, a perceptual loss Lₗₚᵢₚₛ, and an alpha regularization L_α, which aligns the rendered alpha map with the ground-truth human mask. The depth regularization L_depth enforces the consistency between rendered and ground-truth depth maps [10]. The overall training objective is formulated as follows:

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ=λ₁L₁+λₗₚᵢₚₛLₗₚᵢₚₛ+λ_αL_α+λ_depthL_depth+λ_compL_comp,

    		(8)

    where λ₁, λₗₚᵢₚₛ, λ_α, λ_depth, and λ_comp are balancing factors for each loss term, which are set to 2.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.25, and 0.1, respectively. Note that the same training objective is applied when patch-based supervision, which is explained in the previous subsection, is activated.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation details

    The proposed method is implemented on the PyTorch [27] framework. All the experiments were performed on a single PC with an Intel Xeon w5-3433@2.0 GHz CPU and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. By following [19], all the parameters of the proposed network are updated by the AdamW optimizer, where the momentum factors are set to 0.9 and 0.95, respectively. The learning rate is set to 2×10⁻⁴. Each input feature map is tokenized with a non-overlapping patch size of 8, and the Gaussian decoder predicts 64 Gaussians per token. For computing the complexity prior, the number of histogram bins B is set to 20. The complexity prior is computed at three different radii {rₛ}ₛ₌₁³. Each radius is defined as rₛ=αₛ·d_bbox, where d_bbox denotes the diagonal length of the bounding box for the clothed human mesh and α₁, α₂, and α₃ are set to 0.02, 0.01, and 0.005, respectively. For the complexity-guided regularization, the number of nearest neighbors k is set to 7. At each iteration, 2048 points are sampled on the mesh surface and 4096 pairs are sampled for pairwise ranking regularization. For patch-based supervision, the number of patch centers per target image Nₚ is set to 2. The patch size is linearly decreased from 512 to 64 over 600,000 iterations.

    4.2 Datasets and evaluation metrics

    Datasets. For the performance evaluation of the proposed method, three human-centric multi-view datasets, i.e., THuman2.0 [24], 2K2K [25], and X-Humans [26], are adopted. All three datasets provide high-quality textured 3D human scans, which are rendered into multi-view images at the resolution of 512×512 pixels under known camera parameters. For THuman2.0, we follow train and test splits adopted in prior works [15, 13, 12]. For 2K2K, we follow the split adopted in HART [28]. For X-Humans, the official split is used. The proposed method is trained on each dataset independently for in-domain evaluations. We further evaluate the cross-domain generalization ability of our method by training on THuman2.0 and directly testing on 2K2K and X-Humans datasets without any fine-tuning. We additionally provide experimental results on real-world datasets (i.e., DNA-Rendering [29] and ZJU-MoCap [30]) in the appendix.

    Evaluation metrics. Following previous works [15, 13, 12], the reconstruction performance is evaluated by using three metrics, i.e., Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) [31], and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [32]. PSNR and SSIM measure pixel-wise similarity and structural fidelity between the rendered image and the ground truth, while LPIPS reflects the perceptual similarity in the feature domain. We additionally report frames per second (FPS) to evaluate the inference speed. Since FPS values of our method vary depending on the number of foreground tokens per input image, we report the average value measured on the THuman2.0 dataset [24].

    4.3 Performance evaluation

    Quantitative evaluation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we compare our method with previous generalizable human Gaussian splatting methods, i.e., GPS-Gaussian [10], GHG [13], RoGSplat [15], and GHGS-MVSC [12]. Note that GPS-Gaussian is evaluated under a 6-view setting following [15], while other methods use 4-view inputs. The result of in-domain generalization comparisons is shown in Table 1. As can be seen, the proposed method consistently achieves the best performance across all three datasets and all three metrics. Specifically, the proposed method achieves 32.42 dB PSNR on THuman2.0, 31.68 dB on 2K2K, and 31.96 dB on X-Humans, which outperforms the second-best method by 1.49 dB, 1.01 dB, and 1.36 dB, respectively. Similar improvements are observed in SSIM and LPIPS metrics, which indicates that the proposed method better represents both pixel-wise and perceptual fidelity. Notably, the proposed method achieves these improvements while running at 33.96 FPS, which is substantially faster than RoGSplat (5.42 FPS) and GHGS-MVSC (2.79 FPS). The cross-domain generalization comparison is also presented in Table 2. Our approach improves PSNR values by a notable margin, which demonstrates the robust generalization capability compared to previous methods (+0.93 dB over GHGS-MVSC on 2K2K and +0.96 dB over RoGSplat on X-Humans).

    Qualitative evaluation. The qualitative comparisons on in-domain and cross-domain evaluations are presented in Figs. 4 and 5, respectively. Compared to existing methods, the proposed method reconstructs the target-view human image accurately in fine-grained regions, such as fingers, facial details, and textured clothes (see Fig. 4(e) and Fig. 5(e)). In contrast, previous methods often fail to faithfully recover such intricate details due to the insufficient Gaussian density, which leads to the noticeable degradation in these regions (see Figs. 4(b)(c)(d) and Figs. 5(b)(c)(d)). These visual comparisons confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method in faithfully reconstructing fine-scale human details.

    4.4 Ablation study

    Effectiveness of the proposed components. In Table 3, we conduct ablation studies on the THuman2.0 dataset to validate the effectiveness of the proposed components. The complexity-guided

    regularization scheme improves PSNR by 0.47 dB and noticeably reduces the LPIPS value, which confirms that the explicit guidance of the Gaussian density by the local complexity is effective for reconstructing fine-grained details. The complexity-aware patch-based supervision strategy substantially improves all metrics by concentrating the supervisory signal on intricate regions. Consequently, the synergy among the proposed components encourages the local Gaussian density to be positively correlated with the complexity prior, which yields superior performance in generalizable human Gaussian splatting, as shown in Fig. 6.

    Performance variations according to different k values. We investigate the influence of the number of nearest neighbors k for computing the local density of Gaussians as defined in Eq. 6. As

    shown in Table 4, the performance improves as k increases from 3 to 7, where k=7 achieves the best PSNR and LPIPS values. When k is further increased to 9, the performance remains comparable across all metrics. This suggests that an excessively small k makes the density score sensitive to the noise. Based on the trade-off between the performance and the computational cost, we set k=7 in our experiments.

    Effectiveness of complexity-aware patch sampling. For our patch-based supervision, patch centers are sampled with probabilities proportional to the local complexity. To validate this strategy,

    we compare the complexity-aware sampling with two alternative strategies, as shown in Table 5. For the image-gradient-based sampling, the gradient magnitude map computed by the Sobel operator with 3×3 kernels is used as the sampling probability instead of the 2D complexity map. The complexity-aware sampling consistently outperforms both alternatives across all metrics. Specifically, the image-gradient-based sampling improves PSNR by only 0.18 dB over random sampling, whereas the complexity-aware sampling achieves an improvement of 0.43 dB. This confirms that incorporating the local complexity of the human subject into the training scheme effectively guides the model to learn fine-grained details.

    Effectiveness of complexity components. To examine the contribution of the geometric and textural complexities in Eq. 4, we conduct an ablation study of complexity components. As shown in Table 6, combining geometric and textural complexity yields better reconstruction quality than using either component alone. Furthermore, the maximum operation achieves the best performance across all metrics, outperforming the average operation by 0.11 dB in PSNR. This result indicates that the maximum operation effectively preserves a strong complexity cue when either geometric or textural variation is prominent.

    Correlation between complexity and density of Gaussians. To directly verify that the

    proposed regularization scheme changes the distribution of Gaussians, we measure the Spearman rank correlation between the local complexity and the local density of estimated Gaussians on the THuman2.0 dataset. As shown in Table 7, the correlation coefficient increases from 0.1086 to 0.4262 with the complexity-guided regularization scheme. This result confirms that the distribution of Gaussians is closely aligned with the complexity prior.

    Performance comparison under different regularization settings. Since the complexity prior is computed from the textured clothed human mesh, the proposed method relies on an additional

    3D prior which is not used by previous methods. For a fair comparison, we evaluate a variant of the proposed method which computes the complexity prior directly from input images by applying Eqs. 2 and 3 to normal maps predicted by an off-the-shelf monocular normal estimator [33] and RGB pixels, respectively. As shown in Table 8, the proposed method consistently outperforms previous methods under both regularization settings. Without the depth regularization scheme, the proposed method achieves 31.83 dB in PSNR, which surpasses GHGS-MVSC [12] by 0.90 dB. When the depth regularization scheme is additionally employed, the proposed method reaches 32.04 dB in PSNR, which outperforms RoGSplat [15] by 3.21 dB. These results are slightly lower than those obtained with a textured mesh, which may be attributed to inaccuracies in the image-derived complexity maps. This is because complexity maps derived from a monocular normal estimator may be inconsistent across views. Nevertheless, the competitive performance of this variant suggests that the proposed method can be extended to settings where textured meshes are unavailable.

    5 Conclusion

    In this paper, we introduce a novel method for generalizable human Gaussian splatting. The key idea of the proposed method is to allocate Gaussians in proportion to the local complexity of a clothed human, which is quantified through the entropy of geometric and textural variations. This approach allocates Gaussians densely in fine-grained regions, which effectively contributes to the faithful reconstruction of intricate human details. Additionally, the proposed complexity-aware patch-based supervision concentrates the supervisory signal on complex regions, which provides the model with sufficient supervision on fine-scale details. As a result, the proposed method consistently produces high-fidelity rendering results. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generalizable human Gaussian splatting on both in-domain and cross-domain settings.
